questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50 year old male presents with pain in his right ear. He is diagnosed with right sided otitis media after investigations. He also adds that he recurrently gets these ear infections. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

The most probable diagnosis in a 50 year old male with recurrent otitis media is most likely nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx. The theories for etiology include genetics, infection with Epstein-Barr virus, air pollution, and smoking. It commonly occurs in males in the 5th to 7th decade. The most common site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rosenmuller. From here, it can spread extensively in any direction locally. It also can spread lymphatically to the cervical, retropharyngeal, or parapharyngeal lymph nodes.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents with the following symptoms:

* Nasal - obstruction, discharge, rhinolalia clausa, epistaxis

* Ear - eustachian tube obstruction leading to conductive hearing loss or recurrent otitis media.

* Ophthalmoneurologic - all the cranial nerves (CN) may be involved.

* CN VI - squint and diplopia

* CN III, IV, VI, - ophthalmoplegia

* CN V - reduced corneal reflex

* CN II - exophthalmos

* CN IX, X, XI - jugular foramen syndrome

* Horner’s syndrome

* Cervical lymph node metastasis

* Distant metastasis to the bone, liver, and lung.

Examination of the ear shows a dull tympanic membrane and audiometry shows a Type B curve due to the presence of fluid in the middle ear. The presence of unilateral serous otitis media in an adult suggests nasopharyngeal growth.

Trotter's triad consists of ipsilateral conductive hearing loss (eustachian tube blockage), trigeminal neuralgia of the mandibular division, and palatal asymmetry due to the involvement of the CN X may be seen. This triad occurs in malignant tumors of the lateral nasopharyngeal wall due to extensive invasion.
questions.learning: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma — The most probable diagnosis in a 50 year old male with recurrent otitis media is most likely nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about thymoma?
options: Usually symptomatic with dyspnoea, dysphagia and SVC syndrome
Chest Xray is the investigation of choice
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Most common neoplasm of thymus

The true statement is that thymoma is the most common neoplasm of the thymus.

Thymoma is the most frequently encountered neoplasm of the anterior mediastinum (Option B) in adults and is rare in children. It is seen most frequently in the age group of 40 and 60 years. Most patients with thymoma are asymptomatic (Option C). Large thymic tumors may present with symptoms related to a mass effect, which may include cough, chest pain, dyspnea, or SVC syndrome. Around 10% to 50% of patients with thymoma may have symptoms suggestive of myasthenia gravis or have circulating antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor. Other paraneoplastic syndromes, including red cell aplasia, hypogammaglobulinemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Cushing’s syndrome, or SIADH, may be present.

While the mediastinal mass can be identified on screening chest X-ray, imaging with contrast-enhanced CT and MRI (Option D) have a critical role in characterizing the mediastinal masses. The diagnosis may be suspected based on history and CT imaging but imaging alone is not diagnostic. The diagnosis is usually made after surgical resection due to the relative difficulty of obtaining a needle biopsy. Biopsy should be avoided in cases where imaging is highly suggestive of thymoma. Masaoka staging system is used for thymomas and is based on the gross or microscopic invasion of the capsule and of surrounding structures, as well as on the presence of metastases.

The definitive treatment for thymoma is complete surgical removal. Thymectomy leads to improvement or resolution of symptoms of myasthenia gravis in only about 25% of patients with thymomas.
questions.learning: Most common neoplasm of thymus — The true statement is that thymoma is the most common neoplasm of the thymus. Thymoma is the most frequently encountered neoplasm of the anterior mediastinum (Option B) in adults and is rare in children.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient presents with antepartum hemorrhage. Previous ultrasound showed placenta previa, and Doppler demonstrates the placenta adherent to the uterus with invasion and extension into the urinary bladder. What is this pathology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Placenta percreta

The clinical scenario of a patient with antepartum hemorrhage, known placenta previa on ultrasound, and a placenta adherent to the uterus with invasion and extension into the urinary bladder is most consistent with placenta percreta.

The placenta accreta spectrum is characterized by abnormally implanted, invasive, or adhered placenta. This occurs due to partial or complete absence of the decidua basalis and imperfect development of the Nitabuch layer. Risk factors include associated placenta previa and previous cesarean delivery as seen in this patient.

There are three variants of this condition based on the depth of trophoblastic growth.

* Placenta accreta, the villi are attached to the myometrium. (Option A)

* Placenta increta, the villi invades into the myometrium.( Option B)

* Placenta percreta, the villi penetrate the myometrium into the serosa. (Option C)

Ultrasound findings in placenta percreta:

* Loss of normal hypoechoic retroplacental zone between uterus and placenta

* Placental vascular lacunae

* Placental bulging into the posterior bladder wall

* Attenuation of retroplacental myometrium

Based on the adherence of placental lobules, all three types of morbidly adherent placenta can be:

* Total - involving all lobules of the placenta

* Focal - involving a single lobule or part of a lobule of the placenta

Morbidly adherent placenta can lead to torrential post-partum hemorrhage. It is managed via C-section and peripartum hysterectomy.

Other options:

Option D: Placental abruption is the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from its bed before delivery, which causes antepartum haemorrhage. It might present as external bleeding or maybe concealed. Risk factors include hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, trauma, Multifetal pregnancy, polyhydramnios, PROM, cigarette smoking, and thrombophilias.
questions.learning: Placenta percreta — The clinical scenario of a patient with antepartum hemorrhage, known placenta previa on ultrasound, and a placenta adherent to the uterus with invasion and extension into the urinary bladder is most consistent with placenta percreta.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with a painless, palpable hard mass arising near the metaphyseal region of a long bone. Radiographic evaluation shows characteristic X-ray features associated with this lesion. Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A painless, palpable bony mass located near the metaphysis is the classic clinical presentation of an Osteochondroma (exostosis). It is the most common benign bone tumor and is essentially an outgrowth of the growth plate. The pathognomonic radiographic finding is a bony projection that is continuous with the cortex and medullary cavity of the host bone, often pointing away from the nearest joint. Osteosarcoma (Option A) is a highly malignant tumor that presents with severe pain, swelling, and aggressive bone destruction (e.g., "sunburst" appearance). Multiple myeloma (Option B) typically presents in older adults with systemic bone pain and "punched-out" lytic lesions. Osteoid Osteoma (Option D) is a very small lesion ( cm) that characteristically causes intense night pain which is relieved by aspirin. Osteochondromas typically stop growing once skeletal maturity is reached. While generally benign, a sudden increase in size or pain after puberty may signal a rare malignant transformation into a chondrosarcoma
questions.learning: A painless, palpable bony mass located near the metaphysis is the classic clinical presentation of an Osteochondroma (exostosis). It is the most common benign bone tumor and is essentially an outgrowth of the growth plate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following vessels will serve as an alternate source of blood supply to prevent uterine ischaemia, in case the primary artery is ligated in the event of PPH?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ovarian artery

In the event of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), bleeding occurs from the uterine artery which is the primary vessel ligated, and the inflow from the ovarian artery compensates to prevent ischaemia.

The arterial supply to the uterus is by two main arteries: the uterine artery, which is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, and the ovarian artery which is a direct branch of the abdominal aorta. Ligating the uterine artery limits the supply from the internal iliac artery and hence the ovarian artery serves as the alternate blood supply.

The uterine artery runs from its origin towards the cervix, crosses the ureter and then ascends with a tortuous course along the lateral aspect of the uterus up to ovary, where it anastomoses with the ovarian artery.  It is based on this anatomical relationship that the order of ligation of vessels to arrest bleeding in atonic postpartum haemorrhage is the uterine artery > ovarian artery > internal iliac artery.

Other Options:

Option C: The arcuate artery is a branch of the uterine artery itself.

Option D: The artery to the round ligament artery is a branch from the ovarian artery.
questions.learning: Ovarian artery — In the event of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), bleeding occurs from the uterine artery which is the primary vessel ligated, and the inflow from the ovarian artery compensates to prevent ischaemia.

questions.text: Identify the anti-apoptotic factor among the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bcl-2

BCl-2 is an anti-apoptotic factor.

The intrinsic pathway of apoptosis is initiated by the permeabilization of the mitochondrial membrane. This is facilitated by pro-apoptotic proteins (BAX and BAK) and inhibited by anti-apoptotic proteins.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are true about PR interval? 1. It denotes atrial depolarization. 2. Normal duration is 0.12–0.20 second. 3. Prolongation denotes impaired AV nodal conduction. 4. A short PR interval occurs in WPW syndrome. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

The PR interval is the time from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS complex. It represents the time taken for the electrical impulse to travel from the atria through the AV node, bundle of His, and Purkinje system to the ventricles.

• Statement 1. It denotes atrial depolarization: Incorrect.

• The P wave denotes atrial depolarization.
• The PR interval represents AV conduction time, not atrial depolarization alone.

• Statement 2. Normal duration is 0.12–0.20 second: Correct. Normal PR interval = 0.12–0.20 seconds (3–5 small squares).
• Statement 3. Prolongation denotes impaired AV nodal conduction: Correct. PR interval >0.20 seconds indicates delayed AV nodal conduction, classically seen in first-degree AV block.
• Statement 4. A short PR interval occurs in WPW syndrome: Correct. A short PR interval (<0.12 seconds) is seen in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome due to conduction through an accessory pathway (Bundle of Kent), bypassing the AV node.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the cause of the appearance observed in intravenous pyelography (IVP)?
questions.explanation: The IVP image shows a classic "cobra head" or "spring onion" sign — a well-defined radiolucent halo surrounding a contrast-filled dilation at the distal ureter as it enters the bladder. This pathognomonic appearance represents a ureterocele — a cystic dilation of the distal intravesical ureter. Key Radiological Features visible: 1. Cobra head deformity at distal ureter 2. Contrast filled dilated distal ureteric segment 3. Radiolucent halo surrounding it within bladder 4. Bilateral renal collecting system otherwise visible Why other options are wrong: (A) Horseshoe kidney is incorrect because horseshoe kidney shows fused lower poles of both kidneys across midline with medially rotated collecting systems and abnormally low positioned kidneys — none of which are seen here. (C) Bladder tumor is incorrect because bladder tumors appear as irregular filling defects within the bladder without the characteristic cobra head appearance at the ureterovesical junction seen in this IVP. (D) Posterior urethral valve is incorrect because PUV causes bladder trabeculation, dilated posterior urethra, and bilateral hydronephrosis — the findings here are localized to distal ureter showing classic ureterocele morphology

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What do apoptotic bodies consist of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All cellular content

An apoptotic body is formed during the late stages of apoptosis when a cell undergoes controlled self-destruction. Apoptotic bodies contain all the cellular components such as organelles and fragmented DNA and are typically smaller than the cell undergoing apoptosis.

Apoptosis, also known as programmed cell death, plays a vital role in the normal development and renewal of tissues. It can be initiated by external triggers like cytotoxic T cells or inflammatory molecules, as well as internal factors such as DNA damage or cellular stress.

Mitochondria play a key role in processing signals that determine whether a cell will undergo apoptosis or not. If there's a predominance of signals favoring cell death, mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) occurs, releasing cytochrome C and other proteins into the cytoplasm. These proteins then activate internal pathways leading to programmed cell death.

Apoptosis has two pathways:

A. Mitochondrial or intrinsic pathway:

* Cell injury results in the release of cytochrome C and other pro-apoptotic proteins from mitochondria.

* These then activate caspase 9 which causes nuclear fragmentation and formation of apoptotic bodies.

B. Death receptor or extrinsic pathway:

* In this pathway, activation of death receptors causes apoptosis by activating caspase-8.

* Prototypic death receptors are the type I TNF receptor and Fas (CD95).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old female patient with HIV infection is started on antiretroviral therapy. After a year of treatment, the patient develops back pain. X-ray LS spine is shown below. Which of the following antiretroviral drugs could be the potential cause of these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tenofovir

Tenofovir, a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) used in HIV treatment, is associated with decreased bone mineral density and osteoporosis, which can lead to vertebral compression fractures and back pain. Causes renal proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome).

Why other options are less likely

A. Didanosine – associated with pancreatitis and peripheral neuropathy.

C. Zidovudine – causes bone marrow suppression (anemia, neutropenia) and myopathy.

D. Ritonavir – causes metabolic syndrome, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cell marked in the below slide is inhibitory to
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Deep nuclei of cerebellum

The structure marked in the image is a flask-shaped neuron in the cerebellar cortex, which is a Purkinje cell. It is inhibitory to deep cerebellar nuclei.

Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum. They are evenly spaced and arranged in a single layer between molecular and granular cell layers. The dendrite from each cell passes upward to enter the molecular layer and the axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer, and terminates on the deep cerebellar nuclei. They are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter.

Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex. They receive excitatory input from the climbing fibers from the inferior olivary nucleus and mossy fibers.

Pathological significance of Purkinje cells:

• Negri bodies in rabies are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum.
• In paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells due to antibodies directed against them.
• Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of the hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.
questions.learning: Deep nuclei of cerebellum — The structure marked in the image is a flask-shaped neuron in the cerebellar cortex, which is a Purkinje cell. It is inhibitory to deep cerebellar nuclei.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which is the type of cataract seen following a blunt trauma?
questions.explanation: A Rosette-shaped cataract is the classic finding associated with blunt (concussive) trauma to the eye. The mechanical shock causes fluid to infiltrate the lens fibers, typically following the lines of the lens sutures, which creates a characteristic flower-like or star-shaped opacity. Christmas tree cataract (Option B) is a polychromatic opacity seen in myotonic dystrophy. Snowflake cataract (Option C) is the hallmark of uncontrolled, acute juvenile diabetes mellitus. Sunflower cataract (Option D) is caused by copper deposition (chalcosis) and is classically seen in Wilson's disease. While traumatic cataracts can also appear as a "Vossius ring" (pigment deposit on the lens), the rosette pattern is the most frequently tested morphological description for trauma. Surgery is required if the opacity significantly impairs the patient's vision or if there is associated lens instability

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents with hirsutism, delayed or irregular menstrual cycles, and obesity. Ultrasonography findings are provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of hirsutism, obesity, and oligomenorrhea (delayed periods), combined with the "necklace pattern" or "string of pearls" of follicles on ultrasound, is diagnostic of PCOS. PCOS is a metabolic-endocrine disorder characterized by hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction. Regarding the distractors, POI (Option B) involves premature menopause with amenorrhea and depleted follicles, not multiple cysts. OHSS (Option C) is an acute, severe complication of fertility treatment presenting with massive ovarian enlargement and ascites. Thecal luteal cysts (Option D) are large, bilateral multiloculated cysts caused by high hCG levels in molar pregnancies. Since this patient presents with chronic symptoms and the classic sub-capsular follicular arrangement on ultrasound, PCOS is the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical triad of hirsutism, obesity, and oligomenorrhea (delayed periods), combined with the "necklace pattern" or "string of pearls" of follicles on ultrasound, is diagnostic of PCOS.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the conversion of T4 to T3, in the peripheral tissue?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iodothyronine deiodinase I

Peripheral T3 conversion from T4 is catalyzed by the enzyme iodothryronine deiodinase I. T4 undergoes deiodination in extrathyroidal tissue to form T3, which is the active form of the hormone. It is expressed predominantly in the peripheral tissues.

Iodothyronine deiodinase II: Iodothyronine deiodinase type II (DIO2) is an enzyme responsible for the activation of T4 to T3 in certain specific tissues, such as the hypothalamus and pituitary gland.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: On ocular examination, a teenage girl with a low body weight is found to have the ocular abnormality shown. According to the WHO classification, which grade does this finding correspond to?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a Bitot's spot, which is a characteristic finding of Vitamin A deficiency (Xerophthalmia). Bitot's spots are dry, foamy, triangular patches of keratinized epithelium typically located on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification for Xerophthalmia, the specific grades are: 1. X1A: Conjunctival xerosis (dryness) 2. X1B: Bitot's spot 3. X2: Corneal xerosis 4. X3A/B: Corneal ulceration/keratomalacia Options A (1A), C (2A), and D (2B) are incorrect as they represent different stages or are not standard WHO xerophthalmia codes. The "teenage girl with low body weight" suggests chronic malnutrition, which is the primary risk factor for this deficiency. Bitot's spots are reversible with high-dose Vitamin A supplementation. Therefore, based on the pathognomonic visual finding shown in the image, WHO grade 1B is the correct classification

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following PDE-5 inhibitor is the longest acting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tadalafil

Tadalafil is the longest acting PDE-5 inhibitor with duration of action lasting 24-36 hours.

Duration of action of other PDE5 inhibitors:

* Sildenafil: 10-12 hours

* Vardenafil: 8-10 hours

* Avanafil: 4-6 hours

Clinical correlation:

* Nitrates administration can be done usually after 24 hours of PDE-5 inhibitors intake. But for tadalafil, nitrates are generally not indicated for 2-3 days.

* Tadalafil can also be given at any time without regard to sexual activity because of the long duration of action (low dose).

* Used in erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension.

Drug interactions: Nitrates cause activation of guanylyl cyclase → ↑ cGMP → relaxation of vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation. PDE-5 inhibitors enhance the accumulation of cGMP by preventing its degradation and therefore cause vasodilation. Since nitrates also act by increasing cyclic GMP, they can potentiate the effects of PDE-5 inhibitors. Hence, men treated with PDE-5 inhibitors and nitrates are at risk for severe hypotension and syncope.

Adverse effects:

* The most common side effects reported include headache, flushing, nasal congestion, nasopharyngitis, and dyspepsia. Rare but serious reports of prolonged erections lasting more than 4 hours and priapism (painful erections lasting more than 6 hours) have been reported with PDE5 inhibitors.

* Sildenafil and Vardenafil also cause retinal PDE-6 inhibition and can result in blurring of vision and blue-green tinting of the vision.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the cell seen in the image below?
questions.explanation: The cell shown is a Reed–Sternberg (RS) cell, which is the diagnostic hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma. RS cells are large, abnormal B-lymphocytes, typically binucleated or bilobed, with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli that give the characteristic “owl-eye” appearance. Faggot cells (Option A) are seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) and contain multiple Auer rods bundled together, giving a stick-like or “faggot” appearance. Mott cells (Option C) are plasma cells filled with Russell bodies, appearing as multiple round, grape-like cytoplasmic inclusions due to accumulated immunoglobulins, commonly seen in plasma cell dyscrasias. Sézary–Lutzner cells (Option D) are atypical T-lymphocytes with cerebriform (brain-like) nuclei, characteristic of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome). Thus, the distinctive morphology of a large binucleated cell with owl-eye nucleoli confirms the diagnosis of a Reed–Sternberg cell, which is essential for distinguishing Hodgkin lymphoma from non-Hodgkin lymphomas

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are the features of post-lumbar puncture headache? 1. Dull aching occipitofrontal headache. 2. Worse on waking but improves during the day. 3. Recumbency usually improves the headache within minutes. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 3 only

Post-lumbar puncture headache (PLPH) is caused by CSF leakage through the dural puncture site, leading to intracranial hypotension. It is typically a dull occipitofrontal headache that is postural—worsens on sitting or standing and improves rapidly on lying down (recumbency).

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Dull aching occipitofrontal headache ✔️ – Characteristic feature.
• 2. Worse on waking but improves during the day ❌ – Incorrect. The headache is worse in the upright position and improves when lying down, irrespective of the time of day.
• 3. Recumbency usually improves the headache within minutes ✔️ – Classical feature due to restoration of CSF pressure.

questions.text: In a male child having recurrent urinary problems, an imaging as done as shown. What is the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endoscopic Ablation

This is a VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram) showing dilated posterior urethra, enlarged bladder, urinary obstruction which suggests Posterior Urethral Valves (PUV).

This condition occurs only in male children and causes recurrent urinary infections and obstructive uropathy.

Posterior urethral valves are congenital obstructing membranes in the posterior urethra, causing:

• Bladder outlet obstruction
• Recurrent UTIs
• Hydronephrosis
• Renal damage if untreated

The standard treatment is:

Endoscopic valve ablation (valve fulguration) using a cystoscope removes the obstructing valve and restores urine flow.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which hormone plays a major role in home based pregnancy tests?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Beta-HCG

Beta Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is the basis of home-based pregnancy tests.

hCG is produced by the syncitiotrophoblasts of the placenta. It is a glycoprotein hormone with two subunits. The alpha-subunit is similar to LH, FSH and TSH. The beta-subunit is specific and is measured by pregnancy tests.

hCG can be detected in maternal blood 8 days after fertilisation. Thus, it can help in diagnosis of pregnancy even before the period is missed. Its levels nearly doubles every 48 hours in early pregnancy reaching a maximum of 50000 - 100000 IU/L by 60-70 days of gestation. Then the level starts falling reaching a minimum at 16 weeks, which continues throughout pregnancy.

The various placental hormones and their functions are given below.

Placental hormones
Functions

Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)

Structurally similar to - LH, FSH, TSH

• Maintains corpus luteum function
• Regulates testosterone secretion from fetal testes
• Stimulates maternal thyroid

Placental lactogen (PL)

Structurally similar to - GH, Prolactin

• Helps the mother adapt to fetal energy requirements

Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH)

• Vascular and myometrial smooth muscle relaxation
• Initiation of parturition
• Stimulates placental ACTH production

Placental adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)

Stimulates fetal and maternal adrenal glucocorticoid production

Other placental hormones include:

* GnRH, TRH, GHRH, Growth hormone variant (hGH-V)

* Parathyroid hormone-releasing protein (PTH-rP)

* Inhibin

* Activin

* Relaxin
questions.learning: Beta-HCG Beta Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is the basis of home-based pregnancy tests. hCG is produced by the syncitiotrophoblasts of the placenta.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 20-year-old male came with complaints of pain over the left flank associated with fever and chills. On examination, the patient had pain on the passive extension of the hip over the left side. Lab investigations reveal leucocytosis. CT scan shows findings as shown. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Psoas Abscess

The clinical vignette of a patient with flank pain, fever, leucocytosis, positive psoas sign, and the CT scan showing a mass in the psoas muscle lateral to the vertebral column is diagnostic of a psoas abscess.

Psoas Abscess -

Commonly presents in males > females. In developed countries, the age of presentation is between 44 - 58 years and in developing countries <20 years of age.

Clinical features include fever, pain in the back or flank region, mass in the inguinal region, anorexia, and unintentional weight reduction. "Psoas sign" is pain brought on by extension of the hip.

Lab investigation - Leucocytosis, increased ESR, and mild anemia may be seen.

Diagnosis - Commonly confirmed using a CT scan. Blood culture and abscess material should be obtained in all cases to guide therapy.

Treatment - Percutaneous or surgical drainage plus Antibiotics
questions.learning: Psoas Abscess — The clinical vignette of a patient with flank pain, fever, leucocytosis, positive psoas sign, and the CT scan showing a mass in the psoas muscle lateral to the vertebral column is diagnostic of a psoas abscess.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The below image is of a femur bone. Which of the following muscles is attached to "A"?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iliopsoas

The image shows the posterior surface of the right femur and the structure marked "A" is the lesser trochanter where the iliopsoas muscle is attached.

The Iliopsoas comprises of Psoas major and Iliacus. They arise from the lumbar spine and the inner surface of the ilium bone respectively, and insert on the lesser trochanter. The iliopsoas cause flexion of the hip.

The femur can be divided into the proximal femur, shaft, and distal femur.

* The proximal femur consists of the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters. The intertrochanteric line is present on the anterior surface at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur while the intertrochanteric crest is present on the posterior surface. The lesser trochanter is the posteromedial projection of the femur arising posteroinferiorly from the neck-shaft junction.

* The shaft of the femur consists of linea aspera (bony crest present on the posterior surface), gluteal tuberosity, and pectineal line.

* The distal femur consists of the medial condyle, lateral condyle, intercondylar fossa, and patellar surface.

The image below shows attachments of various muscles over the posterior surface of the right femur.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury at which of the following marked sites causes failure of dorsiflexion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3

The site marked as '3' in the x-ray given above is the neck of the fibula. Injury at this site causes failure of dorsiflexion (foot drop) due to injury to the common fibular nerve (also know as common peroneal nerve)

The common fibular nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st and 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves.

Superficial fibular nerve
Deep fibular nerve

Motor innervation

• Peroneus longus
• Peroneus brevis

• Extensor digitorum longus
• Extensor hallucis longus
• Tibialis anterior
• Peroneus tertius

Sensory innervation

• Lateral aspect of the lower leg
• Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital web-space

• The first interdigital space

Injury to the common peroneal nerve (common fibular nerve) at the level of the neck of the fibula causes foot drop. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion of the foot are lost, while the inversion and plantar flexion are usually preserved. Sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot, including the first web space, is lost. The ankle reflex is usually preserved.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Modified shock index is calculated using?

HR: Heart rate

MAP: Mean arterial pressure

SBP: Systolic blood pressure

DBP: Diastolic blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HR/MAP

• Modified shock index = HR/MAP
• Original shock index = HR/SBP

The shock index is a hemodynamic stability indicator. In patients with shock, it is a better predictor of mortality than blood pressure or heart rate alone. A shock index >0.9 is indicative of higher mortality.

The modified shock index is a more sensitive indicator of tissue perfusion than the original shock index. In critically ill patients, the DBP decreases earlier than SBP, hence, the modified shock index using MAP is better suited to assess the severity of shock.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A postmenopausal woman presents with irregular uterine bleeding, and endometrial biopsy reveals endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia is a benign condition with a low risk of progressing to cancer. In postmenopausal women with irregular bleeding, the first-line medical management is progestin therapy to reverse the hyperplasia. The Levonorgestrel Intrauterine System (LNG-IUS) is highly effective as it provides high local progestin concentrations to the endometrium. OCPs (Option A) and Estradiol (Option B) are contraindicated because estrogen stimulates further endometrial proliferation, worsening the condition and increasing malignancy risk. Danazol (Option D) is an androgenic agent with significant side effects and is far less effective than modern progestin options. If medical management fails or symptoms recur, a hysterectomy may be considered as the definitive surgical option
questions.learning: Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia is a benign condition with a low risk of progressing to cancer. In postmenopausal women with irregular bleeding, the first-line medical management is progestin therapy to reverse the hyperplasia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is a bioterrorism category A agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anthrax

Bacillus anthracis which causes anthrax is categorized under category A bioterrorism agent.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman is diagnosed with locally advanced breast carcinoma. The multidisciplinary tumor board recommends systemic chemotherapy before definitive surgery to reduce tumor size and improve the likelihood of breast-conserving surgery. This treatment strategy is best described as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) is systemic chemotherapy administered before definitive surgery (or other local therapy). Its goals are to downstage the tumor, improve resectability, facilitate organ conservation, eradicate micrometastatic disease early, and assess in vivo tumor chemosensitivity. In breast cancer, achieving a pathological complete response (pCR) is associated with a favorable prognosis, especially in HER2-positive and triple-negative tumors.

Why not the other options?

• B. Adjuvant chemotherapy: Given after surgery to eliminate residual microscopic disease and reduce recurrence.
• C. Definitive chemotherapy: Used as the primary treatment without planned surgery, such as in certain leukemias, lymphomas, or metastatic disease.
• D. Concurrent chemoradiotherapy: Chemotherapy administered simultaneously with radiotherapy, not before surgery.

High-Yield Pearl:

"Neo = Before, Adjuvant = After."

Common indications for neoadjuvant chemotherapy:

• Locally advanced or inflammatory breast cancer
• Osteosarcoma
• Rectal carcinoma (often with radiotherapy)
• Esophageal carcinoma
• Muscle-invasive bladder cancer
• Advanced ovarian cancer
• Wilms tumor

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a low grade fever, sore mouth and painful vesicular rash on the hands, feet and inside the mouth as shown in image below. The child attends daycare and similar cases have been reported among classmates. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coxsackie A16

A child with low-grade fever, painful oral ulcers, and vesicular lesions on the hands and feet in a daycare setting is characteristic of hand, foot and mouth disease caused most commonly by Coxsackievirus A16.

• Spread is via feco-oral and respiratory routes, leading to outbreaks in children
• Typical features include oral ulcers, vesicles on palms and soles, and mild fever
• Illness is self-limiting and resolves within about a week

Differentials:

• Varicella: lesions in different stages, predominantly on trunk
• Epstein–Barr virus: pharyngitis with lymphadenopathy, no vesicular rash
• Coxsackie B  → Myocarditis, pleurodynia

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with diabetes asks for dietary advice, and you recommend foods with a low glycemic index. Which of the following options would be most appropriate to suggest?
questions.explanation: The glycemic index (GI) measures how quickly a food raises blood glucose levels. For diabetic patients, low GI foods (<55) are preferred because they cause a slow, gradual rise in blood sugar, helping maintain better glycemic control. Among the given options, papaya has a low to moderate GI and is rich in fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants, which help slow glucose absorption and improve overall metabolic health. Hence, it is the most appropriate choice. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Corn flakes : Very high GI (~80–85) → causes rapid spike in blood glucose (B) Brown rice : Moderate GI (~65–70) → better than white rice but not low GI (C) Sucrose : Simple sugar with high GI (~65) → quickly raises blood glucose
questions.learning: The glycemic index (GI) measures how quickly a food raises blood glucose levels. For diabetic patients, low GI foods (<55) are preferred because they cause a slow, gradual rise in blood sugar, helping maintain better glycemic control.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the most commonly used test for newborn hearing screening?
questions.explanation: Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) is the primary screening tool used in universal newborn hearing screening programs worldwide. It is quick (taking only minutes), non-invasive, and can be performed while the baby is awake. OAE measures the soft sounds produced by the outer hair cells of the cochlea in response to an acoustic click. Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA/AABR) (Option B) is used as a second-tier test for those who fail OAE or as a primary test in high-risk infants (e.g., NICU graduates) to detect auditory neuropathy. Pure Tone Audiometry (Option C) requires the patient to indicate when they hear a sound, which is impossible for newborns. Tympanometry (Option D) measures middle ear pressure/function but is not a hearing threshold test. Early detection through OAE is crucial because timely intervention (before 6 months) is necessary for normal speech and language development in children with congenital hearing loss
questions.learning: Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) is the primary screening tool used in universal newborn hearing screening programs worldwide. It is quick (taking only minutes), non-invasive, and can be performed while the baby is awake.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which pneumoconiosis is caused by exposure to cotton dust?
questions.explanation: Byssinosis is an occupational lung disease caused by the inhalation of dust from cotton, flax, or hemp. It is often called "Monday morning fever" because symptoms like chest tightness and dyspnea are typically most severe when workers return to the textile mill after a weekend break. Bagassosis (Option B) is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhaling dust from moldy sugar cane fiber (bagasse). Anthracosis (Option C) is caused by the inhalation of coal dust or carbon particles and is commonly found in miners. Silicosis (Option D) is caused by inhaling crystalline silica dust in industries like stone cutting or sandblasting. Long-term chronic exposure to cotton dust can eventually lead to permanent, irreversible obstructive lung disease. Prevention focuses on industrial hygiene, including improved local exhaust ventilation, the use of personal protective masks, and regular medical screening of workers to detect early respiratory decline

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with abdominal pain, irritability, and developmental delay. On examination, pallor and a bluish line along the gums are noted. Laboratory investigations show microcytic anemia, and peripheral blood smear reveals basophilic stippling of red blood cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of abdominal pain (painter's colic), irritability, and developmental delay in a child is highly suggestive of lead poisoning. The most specific physical finding is the Burtonian line (Burton's line), a stippled blue line on the gums caused by subepithelial granules of lead. Laboratory findings of microcytic anemia accompanied by basophilic stippling (punctate basophilia) on the peripheral smear are pathognomonic for this toxicity. Lead inhibits essential enzymes like ferrochelatase and ALA-dehydratase. Iron deficiency (Option A) lacks the gum line and basophilic stippling. Sideroblastic anemia (Option B) shows ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow but not the neurological or gingival signs. Thalassemia minor (Option D) is often asymptomatic or mild and does not explain the developmental delay. Treatment requires removing the lead source and initiating chelation therapy
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of abdominal pain (painter's colic), irritability, and developmental delay in a child is highly suggestive of lead poisoning.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Patients diagnosed with breast cancer are usually advised to undergo ER screening test. What is its significance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prognostic marker

Estrogen receptor (ER) is used as a prognostic marker.

The term prognostic marker generally is used to describe molecular markers that predict disease-free survival, disease- specific survival, and overall survival, whereas the term predictive marker often is used in the context of predicting response to certain therapies.

Other options

Option A: A diagnostic biomarker detects or confirms the presence of a disease or condition of interest, or identifies an individual with a subtype of the disease.

Option C:When a biomarker can be measured serially to assess the status of a disease or medical condition for evidence of exposure to a medical product or environmental agent, or to detect an effect of a medical product or biological agent, it is a monitoring biomarker

Option D: The most common and serious error in evaluating biomarkers is assuming that a correlation between a biomarker's level and a clinical outcome means the biomarker is a valid surrogate. However, for a biomarker to be a valid surrogate, it must not only be correlated with the outcome but also explain the change in the clinical outcome.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Blue

According to biomedical waste management, used pacemakers should be disposed of in a blue colored bag. All the metallic body implants and glasswares are discarded in a blue colored bag.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents to the emergency department with lethargy. On examination, the child is unresponsive, unable to take oral feeds, eyes dry and sunken, and severely malnourished. What is the fluid of choice in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose

A child with features of severe dehydration like sunken dry eyes, lethargy and being unable to take oral feeds must be started on IV fluid correction for dehydration. Since the child has severe malnutrition as well, the fluid of choice is ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose.

Intravenous therapy should be given only for severe dehydration and shock or if the enteral route cannot be used. IV fluids that can be used in these children are

* Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose

* Half-normal saline with 5% dextrose

* Half-strength Darrow solution with 5% dextrose.

Children are given a total of 100 ml/kg of fluid for severe dehydration. Children below 1 year of age are administered that amount over 6 hours. Children over 1 year of age are given that amount over 3 hours.

The treatment of some dehydration in a child with severe acute malnutrition is half-strength WHO low-osmolarity ORS with glucose and potassium.

ReSoMal is another oral rehydration salt or ORS for severely malnourished children. It is used in in-patient centres for the treatment of children with severe acute malnutrition. ReSoMal contains a higher amount of glucose (125mmol/L) and a lower amount of sodium (45mmol/L) than the standard WHO-ORS.

Pearl PF1945: Treatment of dehydration based on severity

Plan A: For no dehydration or minimal dehydration. ORS is administered after each loose stool.

Plan C: For severe dehydration, treatment includes IV fluid administration.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman reports a one-month history of greenish, frothy vaginal discharge with associated vulvovaginal erythema. Saline wet mount examination reveals motile organisms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a greenish-frothy vaginal discharge coupled with vulvovaginal erythema (often described as a "strawberry cervix") is highly characteristic of Trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis. The definitive diagnostic clue provided is the presence of motile organisms on saline wet mount microscopy, which identifies the pear-shaped, flagellated trophozoites. Bacterial vaginosis (Option B) typically presents with a thin, greyish-white discharge with a "fishy" odor and "clue cells" but lacks motile protozoa. Chlamydial cervicitis (Option C) often presents with mucopurulent discharge and cervical friability but is usually diagnosed via molecular testing rather than wet mount. Candidiasis (Option D) is characterized by a thick, "curd-like" white discharge and the presence of pseudohyphae on microscopy, with intense pruritus rather than frothiness. Treatment for Trichomoniasis involves oral metronidazole or tinidazole for both the patient and their sexual partner to prevent reinfection. Early diagnosis is essential as the infection can increase the risk of acquiring other STIs

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In which condition is excessive urinary excretion of 5- hydroxy indole acetic acid seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carcinoid syndrome

Excessive urinary excretion of 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) is seen in carcinoid syndrome.

Carcinoid syndrome is marked by symptoms of bronchospasm, cutaneous flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea. It occurs due to excessive production of serotonin, a specialized product of tryptophan metabolism by tumors commonly in the small intestine, liver and lungs. It is then metabolized and excreted in urine as 5-HIAA.
questions.learning: Carcinoid syndrome Excessive urinary excretion of 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid (5-HIAA) is seen in carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid syndrome is marked by symptoms of bronchospasm, cutaneous flushing, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male presents with purulent discharge from a perianal opening. Examination in the lithotomy position reveals an external opening at the 11 o’clock position, about 4 cm from the anal verge. What is the most likely location of the internal opening, and from where does it originate?
options: 12 o'clock and at external anal sphincter
11 o'clock and at internal anal sphincter
6 o'clock and crypt of the dentate line
questions.explanation: The management of a fistula-in-ano is guided by Goodsall’s Law. According to this rule, an external opening located posterior to a transverse line through the anus (such as the 11 o'clock position) will have a curved tract that enters the anal canal at the midline posterior (6 o'clock position). Furthermore, most fistulae originate in an infected anal crypt at the dentate line . Option B describes a straight tract, which according to Goodsall's law, only applies to anterior fistulae located within 3 cm of the anus. Option A and C do not follow standard anatomical tract guidelines. Because the external opening is both posterior and relatively far from the anus (4 cm), the track is expected to be complex and curved, meeting at the midline posterior crypt. Understanding these landmarks is essential for successful fistulectomy or seton placement

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following characteristics accurately describes Taenia solium?
options: Eggs are not infective to man
The eggs do not float in saturated salt solution
questions.explanation: Taenia solium (the pork tapeworm) has several distinct features. Statement C is correct; its eggs are "heavy" and do not float in a saturated salt solution during fecal concentration tests. Statement A is incorrect because the "eggs are highly infective to man," leading to cysticercosis (larval infection) if ingested. This distinguishes it from T. saginata, whose eggs are not infective to humans. Statement B is incorrect; T. solium is an "armed tapeworm," meaning it has a rostellum with two rows of "hooks" for attachment. T. saginata lacks hooks. Statement D is incorrect; the intermediate host for T. solium is the "pig," while the cow is the intermediate host for T. saginata. Understanding these differences is vital for diagnosing neurocysticercosis, which is a major cause of adult-onset seizures in developing countries
questions.learning: Taenia solium (the pork tapeworm) has several distinct features. Statement C is correct; its eggs are "heavy" and do not float in a saturated salt solution during fecal concentration tests.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-week-old infant presents with elevated conjugated bilirubin levels, dark urine, and clay-colored stools. Upon examination, the infant appears jaundiced but is feeding normally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Biliary atresia

The given clinical vignette suggests a probable diagnosis of biliary atresia.

Biliary atresia presents with progressive jaundice, persistent acholic stools, and hepatomegaly at a peak age of incidence between 2 - 6 weeks.

Biliary atresia is characterised by inflammatory fibrosis of the biliary tree, resulting in bile flow obstruction and conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. The clinical features include persistent jaundice, clay-coloured stools, and hepatomegaly. The meconium may be slightly bile-stained, but later, the stools will be pale, and the urine will be dark. Untreated newborns will show signs of liver cirrhosis and failure (ascites, portal hypertension, and failure to thrive). Associated anomalies include cardiac lesions, polysplenia, situs inversus, absent vena cava, and preduodenal portal vein.

Laboratory evaluation will show elevated direct and indirect bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase. An ultrasound of the abdomen will show a hypoplastic or absent gall bladder and a triangular cord sign.

Biliary atresia may also be termed as noncystic obliterative cholangiopathy. It is a disease of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts of unknown aetiology.

The HIDA test is used for screening, and liver biopsy is diagnostic for biliary atresia. A biopsy shows proliferation of the bile ductule, the presence of bile plugs, and portal or perilobular edema and fibrosis, with the basic hepatic lobular architecture intact.

The Japanese and Anglo-Saxon classification describes three main types (Kasai):

* Type I – Common bile duct

* Type II – Common hepatic duct

* Type IIa – only common hepatic duct

* Type IIb – Common bile duct, hepatic duct, cystic duct.

* Type III (most common type) – Common bile duct, right and left hepatic ducts, cystic duct; no anastomosable ducts at porta hepatis.

Clinical features include persistent jaundice, clay-coloured stools, and hepatomegaly. Untreated newborns will show signs of liver cirrhosis and failure (ascites, portal hypertension, and failure to thrive).

The definitive diagnosis is by intraoperative cholangiography. Preoperative percutaneous transhepatic cholecystocholangiography combined with liver biopsy in cholestatic infants has a sensitivity of 100% and a specificity of 93% for diagnosing biliary atresia.

According to Bailey's 28th edition:

* Fasting USG is the gold standard for diagnosis

* MRCP is highly sensitive and specific

* Cholangiography defines surgical anatomy.

Management of extrahepatic biliary atresia:

Type I

Atresia restricted to the common bile duct (CBD)
Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy

Type II

Atresia of the CBD + common hepatic duct (CHD)

Kasai procedure (Roux-en-Y hepatoportoenterostomy)

Type III
Atresia of the CBD + CHD + right and left hepatic duct
Kasai procedure (Roux-en-Y hepatoportoenterostomy)

The image given below shows the Kasai procedure.

Other options:

Option A: Accumulation of lipofuscin pigments in hepatocytes is seen in Gilbert's syndrome. Gilbert syndrome is a benign, familial disorder characterised by mild intermittent jaundice usually seen during stress, fatigue, or alcohol use. The condition is recognised to arise from a mutation in the UGT1A1 gene, which results in mildly decreased UDP-glucuronyltransferase production. This causes a reduction in the liver's ability to conjugate bilirubin, thus causing unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The total bilirubin value is usually < 3 mg/dL.

Option B: Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I is due to the absence of the UDP-glucuronyl transferase enzyme. It is an autosomal recessive hyperbilirubinemia syndrome characterised by severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and usually presents with kernicterus. It is usually fatal in the neonatal period.

Option C: Physiological jaundice occurs due to increased bilirubin production due to the destruction of the foetal RBCs, along with a transient limitation in bilirubin conjugation in the immature neonatal liver. It first appears on the 2nd or 3rd day, usually peaks between the 2nd and 4th days, and decreases between the 5th and 7th days after birth.
questions.learning: Biliary atresia — The given clinical vignette suggests a probable diagnosis of biliary atresia. Biliary atresia presents with progressive jaundice, persistent acholic stools, and hepatomegaly at a peak age of incidence between 2 - 6 weeks.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 23-year-old primigravida at 25 weeks of gestation presents with right upper abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and generalized edema. Peripheral smear shows evidence of hemolysis. Her vital signs are stable, with a blood pressure of 104/72 mm Hg and pulse rate of 72/min. Laboratory investigations reveal leukocyte count of 10,500/mm³, platelet count of 62,000/mm³, hematocrit of 26%, and elevated AST levels (90 IU/L). Based on this clinical and laboratory profile, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis of HELLP syndrome is based on the laboratory triad of Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets. This patient satisfies all criteria: "hemolysis" on peripheral smear (also suggested by low hematocrit), elevated AST (90 IU/L), and a significantly low platelet count (62,000/mm3). Although her blood pressure is currently 104/72 mm Hg, HELLP can occur in the absence of overt hypertension or proteinuria in up to 15-20% of cases. Hepatitis B (Option B) and obstetric cholestasis (Option D) do not cause hemolysis or severe thrombocytopenia. Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy (AFLP, Option C) is a close differential but typically presents later in the third trimester and is often associated with coagulopathy and hypoglycemia. The right upper quadrant pain is a classic symptom caused by Glisson’s capsule distension. HELLP syndrome is an obstetric emergency requiring stabilization and usually prompt delivery, as it carries high risks of maternal morbidity and fetal mortality

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient complained of acute painful diminution of vision in the left eye for the past 2 days. On ophthalmic examination, circumcorneal congestion and irregularly shaped pupil were noted as shown below, with the left eye visual acuity at 6/60 and the right eye at 6/12. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute anterior uveitis

Given the patient's symptoms—acute pain, decreased vision in the left eye, circumcorneal congestion, irregularly shaped pupil and keratic precipitates, as shown in the image—the most likely diagnosis is acute anterior uveitis. This condition, also known as iritis, involves inflammation of the iris and anterior chamber.

Key features of acute anterior uveitis include unilateral eye pain, circumcorneal redness, photophobia, and reduced visual acuity. The pupil may appear irregular or constricted, and keratic precipitates (KP) on the corneal endothelium are pathognomonic for this condition. Inflammation leads to pseudo-rubeosis iridis and aqueous flare, a hazy appearance in the anterior chamber due to inflammatory exudate.

Anterior uveitis involves inflammation of the uvea, which can cause sluggish pupillary reactions and a "muddy" appearance of the iris. Aqueous flare is often the earliest sign seen during slit-lamp examination, alongside Koeppe and Busacca nodules and potential posterior synechiae formation.

Management focuses on reducing inflammation and managing symptoms, typically using topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics like homatropine or atropine to relieve pain and prevent synechiae. Monitoring intraocular pressure is also essential, as cycloplegics are contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma due to the risk of exacerbating the condition.

Other options:

Option A: Angle-closure glaucoma involves a sudden increase in intraocular pressure due to blockage of the anterior chamber angle. It is characterized by severe eye pain, blurred vision, and a mid-dilated pupil, with diffuse redness rather than the circumcorneal congestion seen in uveitis.

Option C: Acute conjunctivitis typically presents with diffuse redness, discharge, and mild irritation, without significant pupil changes or severe vision loss.

Option D: Episcleritis features sectoral or diffuse redness with mild tenderness but does not cause severe pain, irregular pupil, or substantial visual changes seen in anterior uveitis.
questions.learning: Acute anterior uveitis Given the patient's symptoms—acute pain, decreased vision in the left eye, circumcorneal congestion, irregularly shaped pupil and keratic precipitates, as shown in the image—the most likely diagnosis is acute anterior uveitis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with a history of cervical erosion and spotting since 2 months. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LBC + HPV + cervical biopsy

Liquid Based Cytology

Advantages:

• Better sample preservation
• Reduced false negatives
• Allows HPV testing from same sample

Human Papillomavirus

High-risk types:

• HPV 16
• HPV 18

These cause \~70% of cervical cancers.

Cervical Biopsy

This confirms the definitive diagnosis.

Suspicious cervix

↓

Screening test (LBC)

↓

HPV testing

↓

Biopsy for confirmation

In a 45-year-old with persistent spotting and cervical erosion, cervical cancer must be ruled out. Liquid-Based-Cytology + HPV testing is the recommended screening combination. Biopsy is mandatory when symptoms persist or lesion appears suspicious.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the tarsal bone labelled in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Navicular

The image shows the navicular bone which is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

There are 7 tarsal bones and they occupy the proximal half of foot. The proximal row is made up of the talus and calcaneum. The distal row from medial to lateral contains, the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiforms and the cuboid. Medially the navicular bone is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with several weeks of eye dryness and discomfort, along with complaints of night blindness. The history reveals a poor diet deficient in fruits and vegetables. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A (retinol) is essential for maintaining the health of the ocular surface and the function of the retina. Night blindness (nyctalopia) is often the earliest clinical symptom of Vitamin A deficiency because the vitamin is a precursor to rhodopsin, the pigment in the retina's rod cells responsible for low-light vision. Prolonged deficiency leads to xerophthalmia, a spectrum of eye disease starting with conjunctival dryness (xerosis) and discomfort, potentially progressing to Bitot's spots (foamy keratin plaques), corneal xerosis, and eventually keratomalacia (corneal melting and blindness). The patient's history of a poor diet lacking fruits and vegetables (sources of beta-carotene) is a significant risk factor. Vitamin B (Option B) deficiencies cause conditions like beriberi or pellagra. Vitamin C deficiency (Option C) causes scurvy, and Vitamin D deficiency (Option D) leads to rickets or osteomalacia; neither primarily presents with night blindness and xerosis. Therefore, based on the specific combination of night blindness and ocular dryness, Vitamin A deficiency is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient who is a known case of COPD presented with acute exacerbation and is admitted to the ICU. Which of the following statements is correct with regards to the initial management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Non-Invasive PPV should be given

Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) should be the first mode of ventilation used in COPD patients with acute respiratory failure provided there are no absolute contraindications. This approach improves gas exchange, reduces work of breathing and the need for intubation, decreases hospitalization duration and enhances overall survival outcomes.

Invasive positive pressure ventilation is only considered after failure of NIPPV, resulting in severe respiratory distress, life threatening hypoxemia, severe hypercarbia and/or acidosis, markedly impaired mental status, respiratory arrest or hemodynamic instability (Option B).

Apart from NIPPV, short-acting inhaled beta 2 agonists (albuterol, salbutamol) with or without short-acting anticholinergics (ipratropium) and Long-acting anticholinergics (tiotropium) are recommended as the initial bronchodilators. Maintenance therapy with long-acting beta 2 agonists (formoterol) must be started as soon as possible.

Systemic corticosteroids are useful in the treatment of acute exacerbations of COPD as they reduce airway inflammation and improve lung function over time. However, the effects are not immediate. NIPPV on the other hand provides immediate relief to the patient and reduces the work of breathing. Therefore, it would not be the best choice in this case. (Option C)

Antibiotics can also be considered, as they reduce duration of hospitalisation. Treatment is given for 5 days.

Permissive hypercapnia refers to a ventilation strategy where tidal volume is reduced in order to avoid hyperinflation-associated lung trauma. It is not preferred at the initial presentation. It is only permitted once invasive PPV is started following NIPPV failure (Option D)

An exacerbation of COPD is defined as an event characterized by dyspnea and/or cough and sputum that worsen over < 14 days. Exacerbations of COPD are often associated with increased local and systemic inflammation caused by airway infection, pollution, or other insults to the lungs.
questions.learning: Non-Invasive PPV should be given Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) should be the first mode of ventilation used in COPD patients with acute respiratory failure provided there are no absolute contraindications.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient presents with respiratory depression suspected due to opioid overdose. What should be the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Naloxone

A patient with respiratory depression due to suspected opioid overdose requires immediate reversal of opioid effects.

Naloxone is the drug of choice because it is a pure opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses the effects of opioids at µ-opioid receptors, restoring respiratory drive and consciousness.

Key points about Naloxone:

• Given IV, IM, SC, or intranasal
• Rapid onset of action
• Used specifically for acute opioid overdose
• May require repeat dosing because its duration is shorter than many opioids

Why other options are incorrect:

• Naltrexone: Long-acting opioid antagonist used for maintenance therapy in opioid or alcohol dependence, not acute overdose.
• Buprenorphine: Partial opioid agonist used for opioid dependence treatment, not overdose reversal.
• Methadone: Long-acting opioid agonist used for maintenance therapy in opioid dependence.

Therefore, the immediate management is Naloxone.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presented with history of dysphagia, halitosis and aspiration pneumonia. A barium swallow was done and is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zenker’s diverticulum

The given image shows the collection of contrast in a pouch-like structure, which favours the diagnosis of Zenker's diverticulum.

Zenker’s diverticulum is a pulsion-type pseudodiverticulum. It occurs due to the protrusion of mucosa and submucosa through Killian’s triangle. Killian’s triangle represents a weak muscular space located between two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle - the oblique fibres of the thyropharyngeus and the transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus. This phenomenon may lead to the creation of a sac with a narrow neck that can trap liquid and food. The distended sac may compress the cervical oesophagus.

Clinical presentation:

The entrapment of liquid and/or food within the diverticulum may result in:

* Globus sensation

* Dysphagia

* Halitosis

* Regurgitation

* Aspiration pneumonia

Diagnosis is by Barium swallow studies and video laryngoscopy.

Pearl PF1662: Zenker’s Diverticulum

Zenker's diverticulum occurs due to herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the Killian's triangle, which is a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor - (thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus) in the posterior pharyngeal wall. It is usually seen in elderly patients (>60 years).

Characteristics of Zenker's diverticulum:

* Hypopharyngeal

* False diverticula - doesn't have a muscle coat

* Acquired

* Pulsion diverticulum

Pathophysiology: Impaired relaxation and spasm of the cricopharyngeus muscle after swallowing can result in increased pressure within the distal pharynx, and cause the diverticulum.Clinical features:

* Dysphagia

* Regurgitation

* Halitosis

* Aspiration

* Gurgling sound during swallowing

The investigation of choice is barium swallow (lateral X-ray).

It is treated with:

* Cricopharyngeal myotomy

* Surgical diverticulectomy

* Marsupialization

* Dohlman’s procedure
questions.learning: Zenker’s diverticulum — The given image shows the collection of contrast in a pouch-like structure, which favours the diagnosis of Zenker's diverticulum.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Revised Which of the following is most likely to be released from the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hexokinase IV

Hexokinase type IV/ glucokinase is most likely to be released from the hypothalamus (ventromedial hypothalamus)

Glucokinase, also known as hexokinase IV, catalyses the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, which constitutes the first step of glycolysis.

The hypothalamus is an important centre for the regulation of glucose homeostasis. It contains glucokinase/hexokinase IV which plays a central role in the counterregulatory response, which is a feedback system to counteract hypoglycemia by increasing the production of glucose and limiting its utilization.

There are four isoforms of hexokinase:

* Hexokinase type I: major isoform in the brain but also ubiquitously expressed

* Hexokinase type II: predominant in insulin-sensitive tissues such as adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and cardiac muscle.

* Hexokinase type III: not predominant in any tissue.

* Hexokinase type IV: primarily in the liver, pancreas, hypothalamus, small intestine and other neuroendocrine tissue.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the lesion shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Incised looking laceration

The image depicts a wound with linear splitting of the tissue, sharp margins, and crushed hair follicles, which is suggestive of an incised-looking lacerated wound.

Incised-looking lacerated wounds are seen at sites where the skin overlies an area of the bone where there is scanty underlying subcutaneous tissue. A blunt force causes linear splitting of the tissue which results in the laceration resembling an incised wound. There will be extensive tissue crushing but the margins will be clear and delineable.

Common areas are Scalp, Forehead, Eyebrows, Zygoma, Lower jaw, Perineum, Shin, and Iliac crest.

Laceration (Option-A)

A laceration is a tear or a split in the skin, mucous membrane, muscle, or any internal organ produced by blunt force. The full thickness of the skin is penetrated.

Features of laceration:

• Margins are irregular with pieces of tissue attached in between called tissue tags or bridges. Tears that are seen at the ends, diverging away from the main laceration are called swallow tails.
• Bruising is seen around the margins.
• Deeper tissues are unevenly divided with tissue tags.
• Hair bulbs are crushed.
• Depth of the wound contains abundant foreign material such as dust particles, paint material of the vehicle involved, etc
• In skin lacerations, usually one of the margins overhangs the other. This helps in assessing the direction of the force.
• A laceration, on healing, produces a permanent scar.

Classification of a laceration:

• Split laceration (incised - like laceration)

• This occurs when the skin is crushed between two hard objects
• For example, during a fall, the scalp gets crushed between the skull from inside and hard ground outside. This results in a wound, which usually mimics an incised one unless examined closely.

• Stretch laceration

• As the name implies, it occurs due to the over-stretching of the skin, beyond its elasticity.
• This typically occurs in the setting of a fracture, where the fracture fragment may stretch and pierce the skin to project out

• Avulsed laceration

• An avulsion is a lesion where the skin separates or peels off by tearing from the underlying tissues. It may overhang the wound.
• This is common in road traffic accidents.

• Tears - Tearing of skin and subcutaneous tissue can occur from localized impact
• Cuts - Injury leads to a deep and wide injury leading to a cut

Incised wound (Option-B)

An incised wound is a clean-cut wound made with a sharp-edged instrument, through the skin and subcutaneous tissues, including blood vessels. It is more in length than depth. The edges are well-defined and usually everted, free from contusions and abrasions. It is generally spindle-shaped. The depth is more at the commencement and progressively becomes shallower, known as tailing. Tailing determines the direction of the force applied when creating the wound.

The image below shows two spindle-shaped incisions.

Laceration-looking incised wounds (Option C)

In areas of the body where a loose layer of muscle fibres is attached to the skin, the edges of the incision may become inverted, adherent, and wrinkled leading to it simulating a lacerated wound. Such wounds are called lacerated-looking incised wounds. These are commonly seen in Scrotum and Axilla.
questions.learning: Incised looking laceration — The image depicts a wound with linear splitting of the tissue, sharp margins, and crushed hair follicles, which is suggestive of an incised-looking lacerated wound.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You have gone from your clinic to a village for screening where people have diabetes and hypertension. What type of screening is done for family members of these patients who show up in large numbers at your clinic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High-risk screening

The given scenario of screening the family members of diabetic and hypertensive patients is an example of high-risk screening.

High-risk or selective screening is done on high-risk groups like in this case. Another example: MRI screening of the breast is done annually in 25-year-old women with BRCA 1, and BRCA 2 mutations in the first-degree relative.

Other options

Option A: Multiphasic screening is the application of two or more screening tests in combination at one time to a large number of people instead of screening separately for individual diseases. This procedure includes a health questionnaire, clinical examination, and investigations that can be performed rapidly with the appropriate staffing organization and equipment.

Option B: Mass screening is a screening of a whole or large population like using chest X-rays for TB screening in large populations. It is done for diseases with high prevalence.

Option D: Anonymous screening is a screening that allows people to take tests without using their name, commonly used for HIV testing. They will receive a number to access the test results instead of providing their name.
questions.learning: High-risk screening — The given scenario of screening the family members of diabetic and hypertensive patients is an example of high-risk screening. High-risk or selective screening is done on high-risk groups like in this case.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a case of a firearm entry wound with an abrasion collar and tattooing, but no singeing or blackening, what is the likely distance between the victim and the firearm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intermediate range

Rrange of fire can be estimated from the characteristic features of a firearm entry wound. An abrasion collar with tattooing (powder stippling) but without singeing or blackening indicates an intermediate-range shot, where unburnt powder particles reach and embed in the skin, while flame and soot do not.

Why not the other options?

• A. Tight contact: The muzzle is pressed against the skin, producing a muzzle imprint, burning, and soot/gases entering the wound; tattooing is usually absent.
• C. Distant range: Only an abrasion collar is seen; tattooing, blackening, and singeing are absent because powder and soot do not reach the target.
• D. Close range: Characterized by blackening (soot deposition) and often singeing of hair/clothes due to flame, in addition to tattooing.

| Range of Fire | Characteristic Findings

| ------------- | -----------------------

| Tight contact | Muzzle imprint, burning, soot and gases in wound

| Close range | Blackening + Singeing ± Tattooing

| Intermediate range | Tattooing present, no blackening or singeing

| Distant range | Abrasion collar only

Exam Tip:

• Tattooing (stippling) is caused by unburnt powder particles, is not washable, and is a reliable indicator of intermediate-range firing.
• Blackening is due to soot deposition and can be wiped off, indicating close-range firing.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a recent history of throat infection presents with a characteristic water hammer pulse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A "water hammer" (collapsing) pulse, also known as Corrigan's pulse, is pathognomonic for aortic regurgitation. The history of a throat infection points to a prior streptococcal infection triggering rheumatic fever, which is a major cause of valvular damage, particularly affecting the aortic valve. Infective endocarditis (Option B) can cause aortic regurgitation but usually presents with acute fever and embolic signs like splinter hemorrhages. Mitral stenosis (Option C) classically presents with a small, low-volume pulse rather than a collapsing one. Aortic stenosis (Option D) features a "pulsus parvus et tardus," which is slow-rising and low-amplitude. The water hammer pulse results from the rapid ejection of a large stroke volume into the aorta followed by immediate backflow into the left ventricle during diastole

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive patient presents with a history of pneumonia. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral interstitial infiltrates. A bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) sample is obtained for diagnostic evaluation. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumocystis carinii

Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly P. carinii) is an opportunistic fungal pathogen causing Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) in HIV patients, especially with CD4 < 200 cells/µL.

• Clinical setting: HIV + pneumonia + bilateral interstitial (ground-glass) infiltrates
• Diagnosis:

o    Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is the most sensitive test

o    Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain shows cup-shaped cysts (“crushed ping-pong ball” appearance)

Why not others:

• Mucor: broad, aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching
• Aspergillus: septate hyphae with acute-angle branching
• Candida: budding yeast with pseudohyphae (not typical lung pathogen)
