questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 46-year-old man is diagnosed with a tumor involving the left lobe of the liver, and a left- sided hemihepatectomy is planned. Which lobes of the liver are removed during this surgical procedure?
questions.explanation: Functional liver anatomy is based on Couinaud’s segments, which are determined by vascular supply and biliary drainage. A left hemihepatectomy involves the surgical resection of the entire functional left lobe, which consists of segments II, III, and IV. Segment I (the caudate lobe) is functionally distinct and is typically not resected in a standard hemihepatectomy unless specifically indicated (Option B). Segments V, VI, VII, and VIII (Option C) comprise the functional right lobe of the liver. Option D is incorrect because Segment V is part of the right lobe. Therefore, segments 2, 3, and 4 are the correct anatomical targets for a left hemihepatectomy
questions.learning: Functional liver anatomy is based on Couinaud’s segments, which are determined by vascular supply and biliary drainage. A left hemihepatectomy involves the surgical resection of the entire functional left lobe, which consists of segments II, III, and IV.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What does the Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) mainly indicate in the context of water quality management?
questions.explanation: The Langelier Saturation Index (LSI) is used in water quality management to predict whether water will be scale-forming or corrosive. It does this by comparing the actual pH of the water with the pH at which the water is saturated with calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). Positive LSI (> 0): Water is supersaturated with CaCO₃ → scale formation likely Negative LSI (< 0): Water is undersaturated → corrosive, tends to dissolve metals and pipe material LSI = 0: Water is in equilibrium (neither scaling nor corrosive) LSI incorporates several chemical parameters, including pH, calcium hardness, alkalinity, temperature, and indirectly total dissolved solids. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Option B: Total dissolved solids are measured separately, not by LSI alone 2. Option C: Water hardness alone does not determine scaling or corrosion 3. Option D: Biological contamination is unrelated to LSI and assessed microbiologically Thus, LSI primarily indicates the balance between scaling and corrosion in water systems

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with throat pain, fever, and ear pain. He is diagnosed with recurrent tonsillitis. Which nerve is responsible for the ear pain in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tympanic branch of glossopharyngeal nerve

The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia from tonsillitis.

The tonsils and tonsillar fossa are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The glossopharyngeal nerve and the styloid process lie in relation to the lower part of the tonsillar fossa. Therefore, any irritation or pain can be referred to the ear along the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal (Jacobson's) nerve.

The image below shows the anatomic relations of the tonsil and tonsillar bed.

The ear receives extensive sensory innervation via four cranial nerves (V, VII, IX, and X) and two spinal segments (C2 and C3).

Referred otalgia transmitted by the glossopharyngeal nerve may be secondary to lesions and/or inflammatory processes of the nasopharynx, palatine tonsil, soft palate, or posterior one-third of the tongue.

Causes of referred otalgia via glossopharyngeal nerve:

• Acute pharyngitis
• Tonsillitis
• Peritonsillitis
• Peritonsillar abscess
• Post-tonsillectomy
• Foreign bodies embedded in the base of the tongue or tonsillar area
• Elongated styloid process

Other options:

Option B: The great auricular nerve provides sensory sensation for the lower two-thirds of the pinna.

Option C: Causes of referred pain via the auriculotemporal nerve which is the branch of the trigeminal nerve include caries tooth, ulcerative lesions of the oral cavity, temporomandibular joint disorders, and sphenopalatine neuralgia.

Option D: Causes of referred pain via the auricular branch of the vagus nerve include malignancy or ulcerative lesion of the vallecula, epiglottis, larynx, and esophagus.
questions.learning: Tympanic branch of glossopharyngeal nerve — The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia from tonsillitis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which treatment kit would you recommend for a 20‑year‑old woman presenting with vaginal discharge and lower abdominal pain after recent sexual intercourse, following the syndromic management approach for sexually transmitted infections at a Suraksha clinic in the local primary health center?
questions.explanation: The syndromic management of Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) uses color-coded kits to simplify treatment based on clinical presentations. For a woman presenting with the syndrome of lower abdominal pain accompanied by vaginal discharge, Kit 6 (the Yellow kit) is the correct recommendation. This kit is specifically designed to treat Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), which is the likely diagnosis in this scenario. It typically contains Cefixime, Doxycycline, and Metronidazole to cover common pathogens like Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and anaerobes. The Blue kit (Option A) is for vaginal discharge alone (Bacterial Vaginosis or Trichomoniasis). The Red kit (Option B) is for vaginal discharge specifically suspected as Candidiasis. The Black kit (Option C) is for inguinal buboes. Because the patient has symptoms suggesting an ascending infection (abdominal pain), the broader coverage provided by the Yellow kit is necessary. This standardized approach ensures that patients receive effective, immediate treatment at the primary care level, even without complex diagnostic laboratory testing

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which of the following TCA cycle intermediate is a part of heme metabolism?

(TCA - tricarboxylic acid)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Succinyl CoA

Succinyl Co-A, an essential part for heme biosynthesis, is an intermediate of the TCA cycle.

The synthesis of heme begins by condensation of succinyl Co-A and glycine to form α-amino-β-ketoadipate, which is then converted to δ-aminolevulinate. These steps are mediated by the enzyme ALA synthase in the mitochrondria.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Galactokinesis is governed by:
questions.explanation: Galactokinesis, which refers to the ejection of milk from the mammary glands, is primarily governed by the hormone oxytocin. This occurs through the "milk-ejection reflex" or "let-down reflex." When an infant suckles, sensory signals are sent to the hypothalamus, triggering the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin into the bloodstream. Oxytocin then causes the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli, forcing milk into the ducts. Prolactin (Option A) is responsible for lactogenesis (milk production) and galactopoiesis (maintenance of secretion) but not the actual ejection. Estrogen (Option B) and Progesterone (Option D) are involved in mamogenesis (development of the breast tissue) during pregnancy but actually inhibit the stimulatory effects of prolactin until their levels drop after delivery. Understanding these specific roles is critical for managing lactation issues; oxytocin's role in ejection means that emotional stress or pain can inhibit the let-down reflex by interfering with oxytocin release

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What physiological response is most likely to occur in a person exercising vigorously in high temperatures to help maintain internal body temperature within a narrow range?
options: Sweating and vasodilation in the skin
Shivering and vasoconstriction in the skin
Increased production of heat by the liver
Decreased heart rate (HR) and respiratory rate (RR)
questions.explanation: To maintain thermoregulation during vigorous exercise in high temperatures, the body must maximize heat loss. The two primary mechanisms are sweating, which facilitates cooling through evaporation, and vasodilation of the skin blood vessels, which brings warm blood to the surface to radiate heat away. Shivering and vasoconstriction (Option B) are responses to cold exposure designed to generate and conserve heat. Increased heat production by the liver (Option C) would be counterproductive in a hot environment. Heart rate (HR) and respiratory rate (RR) actually increase (Option D) during exercise and heat stress to support increased cardiac output and facilitate some heat loss through the lungs. Failure of these thermoregulatory mechanisms can lead to heat exhaustion or heat stroke, a medical emergency characterized by an internal body temperature exceeding 104°F and central nervous system dysfunction

questions.text: What is the diagnosis of this patient from the ECG shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ventricular tachycardia

The rate of the given ECG is around 188 BPM ( >100 BPM) and it shows wide QRS complexes ( ≥ 0.12 s) with abnormal morphology (red arrows) and absence of P waves which suggests a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with type 1 DM presents with acidosis, and blood sugar 400 mg/dl. What is the further management?
options: Normal saline with SC insulin stat
Normal saline followed by insulin infusion after 1 hour
Normal saline and insulin infusion immediately
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Normal saline followed by insulin infusion after 1 hour

A given clinical scenario of a child with type 1 diabetes mellitus (DM) presenting with acidosis and a high blood sugar level (hyperglycemia) describes a scenario suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a serious complication of uncontrolled diabetes. the further management would be Normal saline followed by insulin infusion after 1 hour.

The International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for the management of DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis) in children and adolescents.

Diabetic ketoacidosis is the most serious complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus. Clinical manifestations of diabetic ketoacidosis include:

• Dehydration, tachypnea with deep, sighing respiration (Kussmaul breathing)
• Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain that may mimic an acute abdominal condition
• Confusion, drowsiness, and coma in severe cases.

The diagnosis of DKA is based on the triad of hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. All three biochemical criteria are required to diagnose DKA

• Hyperglycemia (blood glucose >200 mg/dl)
• Venous pH < 7.3 or serum bicarbonate <18 mmol/L
• Ketonemia or ketonuria

Initial management includes management of the airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC) according to Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) guidelines. Following that emergency assessment is done, which includes:

• Immediate measurement of blood glucose, blood or urine ketones, serum electrolytes and blood gases
• Assessment of level of consciousness.
• Two peripheral intravenous (IV) lines should be inserted.

The goal of therapy is to correct dehydration, correct acidosis, reverse ketosis, and gradually blood glucose concentration to near normal. Monitor for acute complications, and identify and treat any precipitating event.

Fluid replacement should always begin before starting insulin therapy. One or more boluses of 0.9% saline at 10-20 mL/kg are given to restore peripheral circulation. Insulin therapy with 0.05–0.1 U/kg/hr must begin at least 1 hour after starting fluid replacement therapy. Insulin of 0.05 U/kg/hr can be considered if pH is > 7.15.

Potassium replacement is given only when potassium is <5.5 mmol/L. In rare cases of hypokalemia with potassium <3.0 mmol/L, defer insulin treatment.

Bicarbonate administration is not recommended except for treatment of severe acidosis (pH < 6.9) or in cases of life-threatening hyperkalemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which among the following is not a growth-promoting oncogene?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. TGF beta

TGF beta is not a growth-promoting oncogene among the listed options.

TGF beta (Transforming Growth Factor beta) primarily acts as a regulatory molecule In normal cells, TGF beta functions mainly as a tumor suppressor by inhibiting cell proliferation, inducing apoptosis (programmed cell death), and promoting differentiation. It helps maintain tissue homeostasis and prevents the uncontrolled cell growth that can lead to cancer. In the early stages of tumorigenesis, TGF beta exerts anti-proliferative effects.

FGF (Fibroblast Growth Factor) is a family of growth factors involved in various processes, including angiogenesis, wound healing, and embryonic development. Some members of the FGF family can act as oncogenes, meaning they promote cell proliferation and survival, which can contribute to the development and progression of cancers. (Option A)

PDGF (Platelet-Derived Growth Factor) is another crucial growth factor that regulates cell growth and division. In the context of cancer, PDGF is often implicated due to its role in promoting cellular proliferation and survival. Dysregulation of PDGF signaling pathways is commonly observed in various tumors, making it a significant contributor to oncogenesis. (Option B)

TGF alpha (Transforming Growth Factor alpha) is a growth factor that binds to the EGF (Epidermal Growth Factor) receptor, promoting cell proliferation and survival. TGF alpha is frequently overexpressed in various types of cancers, where it stimulates the growth of tumor cells. Its ability to drive cellular proliferation through the activation of EGF receptors classifies it as a growth-promoting oncogene, contributing to the malignancy of cancers where it is overexpressed.(Option D)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the amount of milk given to a term baby in the first 24 hours after delivery?
questions.explanation: According to standard pediatric guidelines, the fluid and nutritional requirements for a healthy term baby in the first 24 hours of life are approximately of body weight. This volume accounts for the infant's limited stomach capacity and the physiological weight loss (primarily water) that occurs immediately after birth. This requirement is gradually increased each day, typically reaching by the end of the first week. Option A (40 ml/kg) and Option B (50 ml/kg) are below the standard initial target. Option D (80 ml/kg) is the requirement for Day 2. While early and frequent exclusive breastfeeding is the gold standard, this value serves as the clinical guide for calculating intake if supplementation or IV fluids are medically necessary. Monitoring the baby’s hydration status through urine output and weight tracking is critical during this transitional period

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Given that the stone shown in the image measures approximately 2 mm in size, what would be the most appropriate and recommended management strategy?
questions.explanation: The management of urinary stones is heavily dependent on the size and location of the stone, as well as the presence of complications. For a very small stone measuring only 2 mm, as depicted in the image, the spontaneous passage rate is exceptionally high, often exceeding 80–90%. Therefore, the most appropriate and conservative initial management strategy is a "wait and watch" approach combined with adequate hydration and analgesia. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (Option A) is an invasive surgical procedure reserved for large renal stones, typically those greater than 2 cm. Ureteroscopy (Option B) is an endoscopic procedure used for ureteral stones that fail to pass or are larger in size. Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL, Option C) is a non-invasive treatment for medium-sized stones but is unnecessary for a 2 mm stone likely to pass naturally. Thus, observation remains the definitive primary management for asymptomatic tiny stones

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 15-year-old boy presents with tremors, difficulty in speech, and behavioral changes. On examination, he has hepatomegaly and a golden-brown ring at the limbus of the cornea (Kayser–Fleischer ring). Wilson’s disease is suspected. Which of the following is the best investigation to support the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liver biopsy for copper estimation

Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by defective copper transport and impaired biliary excretion. This results in excess copper accumulation in the liver, brain (basal ganglia), and cornea, producing features such as hepatomegaly, neurological symptoms, behavioral changes, and Kayser–Fleischer rings.

The most definitive investigation to support the diagnosis is liver biopsy for quantitative copper estimation, which directly measures hepatic copper concentration. Markedly increased hepatic copper confirms abnormal copper accumulation.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Serum ceruloplasmin: Often decreased in Wilson disease but can be normal in some cases, so it is not definitive.
• Serum copper: Usually low due to reduced ceruloplasmin-bound copper and is not reliable for diagnosis.
• Urinary copper excretion: Increased in Wilson disease and useful for screening/monitoring but less definitive than hepatic copper estimation.
questions.learning: Liver biopsy for copper estimation Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by defective copper transport and impaired biliary excretion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents with abdominal pain, fever, and vomiting for five days. Examination reveals a mass in the right iliac fossa, and total leukocyte count is decreased. The clinical findings suggest an acute appendicular mass. What is the most appropriate management approach in this case?
questions.explanation: When a patient presents with an appendicular mass (formed by the omentum and bowel loops walling off an inflamed appendix), the standard-of-care management approach is conservative treatment, classically known as the Ochsner-Sherren regimen. This involves making the patient NPO (nil per oral), administering intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and maintaining a careful vital sign and mass-size chart. Attempting an immediate appendectomy (Option D, either open or laparoscopic) in the presence of an inflammatory mass is technically difficult and carries a high risk of bowel injury or fistula formation. Cholecystectomy (Option C) is for gallbladder disease. The Alvarado score (Option A) is a tool for diagnosing acute appendicitis, not managing a mass. Approximately 90% of masses resolve with conservative management. Following resolution, an "interval appendectomy" is traditionally performed 6-8 weeks later to prevent recurrence, although some modern guidelines suggest this may be optional in asymptomatic patients. Any sign of clinical deterioration during conservative therapy warrants emergency surgical exploration
questions.learning: When a patient presents with an appendicular mass (formed by the omentum and bowel loops walling off an inflamed appendix), the standard-of-care management approach is conservative treatment, classically known as the Ochsner-Sherren regimen.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The first line of treatment for glaucoma in adults is?
questions.explanation: In modern ophthalmology, Prostaglandin (PG) analogues (such as latanoprost, bimatoprost, or travoprost) are considered the first-line medical treatment for primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension in adults. They are highly effective at lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) by increasing the uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor. Their advantages include once-daily dosing and a relatively mild systemic side-effect profile compared to other agents. Atropine (Option B) is a cycloplegic that can actually worsen angle-closure glaucoma. Acetazolamide (Option C) is a potent carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used for acute pressure spikes but is not preferred for long-term first-line therapy due to systemic side effects. Pilocarpine (Option D) is a miotic drug that was once first-line but is now rarely used due to frequent side effects like brow ache and blurred vision. Beta-blockers (like timolol) are often the second-line or alternative first-line choice. Consistently maintaining low IOP is critical to prevent progressive optic nerve damage and permanent vision loss
questions.learning: In modern ophthalmology, Prostaglandin (PG) analogues (such as latanoprost, bimatoprost, or travoprost) are considered the first-line medical treatment for primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension in adults.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is caused by exposure to cotton dust?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Byssinosis

Byssinosis is caused by exposure to cotton dust.

Byssinosis is an occupational disease due to chronic exposure to cotton dust as in textile and rope-making industries. Chest X-ray shows hyperlucency, diaphragmatic flattening, and emphysema. A chest CT demonstrates ground glass opacities largely distributed in the basal regions with centrilobular nodules.

Other options :

Option A: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, which accumulate in the connective tissue. Initially, it causes simple coal workers pneumoconiosis with little or no pulmonary dysfunction. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis which is called complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes of the lungs are commonly involved.

Option B: Silicosis is a form of pneumoconiosis which is a cause of permanent disability and mortality. It occurs in people working in sandblasting, pottery, and ceramics industry, mining, and construction work. It occurs due to the inhalation of silica dust. The patient presents with a cough, exertional dyspnea, and chest pain.

Option D: Bagassosis is an occupational lung disease caused by the inhalation of bagasse or sugarcane dust. A thermophilic actinomycete, Thermoactinomyces sacchari is the causative organism. The symptoms are breathlessness, cough, hemoptysis, and fever. Initially, it can result in acute diffuse bronchiolitis, If left untreated it can progress to diffuse fibrosis, emphysema, and bronchiectasis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child is brought to the emergency department with vomiting and loose stools, along with a history of laxative use. On examination, the child is found to have an arrhythmia. What underlying abnormality is most likely present?
questions.explanation: The combination of vomiting, loose stools, chronic laxative use, and cardiac arrhythmia in a child strongly suggests hypokalemia. Hypokalemia is defined as a serum potassium level below 3.5 mEq/L and is a very common result of significant gastrointestinal fluid losses. Low potassium levels disrupt the resting membrane potential of cardiac myocytes, leading to delayed repolarization and life-threatening arrhythmias in severe cases. Hyponatremia (Option A) can occur with GI losses but is not characteristically associated with direct cardiac arrhythmias. Hypocalcemia (Option B) classically presents with neuromuscular irritability (tetany) and a prolonged QT interval but is not the primary driver of arrhythmias in this context. Hyperkalemia (Option D) also causes arrhythmias, but it results from renal failure or acidosis rather than the potassium depletion seen with vomiting and laxatives. Severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mEq/L) requires urgent intravenous potassium chloride replacement with careful monitoring

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most appropriate next step in the management of a 40-year-old man who presents with generalized abdominal pain, has a known history of peptic ulcer disease, and exhibits abdominal rigidity on examination, in light of the findings shown on the abdominal X-ray?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the "classic triad" of hollow viscus perforation: history of peptic ulcer disease, sudden widespread abdominal pain with rigidity (peritonitis), and radiographic evidence of pneumoperitoneum (air under the diaphragm). This represents a surgical emergency. The appropriate next step is urgent surgical exploration (laparotomy or laparoscopy) to identify and repair the perforation. Antibiotics and NPO (Option A) are part of the initial resuscitation but are not definitive treatment. Upper GI endoscopy (Option B) is strictly contraindicated in suspected perforation because the air used to distend the bowel would worsen the pneumoperitoneum and spill more contents into the cavity. A CT abdomen (Option D) is highly sensitive for air but is unnecessary if the plain X-ray already confirms the diagnosis. Delay in surgical intervention significantly increases mortality from septic shock. Therefore, immediate surgical repair is the life-saving priority
questions.learning: The patient presents with the "classic triad" of hollow viscus perforation: history of peptic ulcer disease, sudden widespread abdominal pain with rigidity (peritonitis), and radiographic evidence of pneumoperitoneum (air under the diaphragm).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In judicial hanging, what is the primary cause of death?
questions.explanation: In the context of forensic medicine, "judicial hanging" is distinct from suicidal hanging because it involves a long drop calculated to break the neck. The primary cause of death is the fracture and dislocation of the upper cervical vertebrae (most classically a C2 fracture, known as the "Hangman’s fracture"), which results in the crushing or complete transection of the spinal cord and lower brainstem. This leads to immediate cessation of respiratory and cardiac functions. Vagal inhibition (Option A), cerebral hypoxia (Option C), and asphyxia (Option D) are common causes of death in cases of "typical" or suicidal hanging where there is no significant drop. In those instances, the pressure of the ligature constricts the carotid arteries or the airway. Judicial hanging is designed to ensure a rapid, certain death through mechanical disruption of the central nervous system rather than slow strangulation
questions.learning: In the context of forensic medicine, "judicial hanging" is distinct from suicidal hanging because it involves a long drop calculated to break the neck.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A woman with a history of infertility is currently receiving HMG treatment. Based on the ultrasound findings provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided ultrasound image shows ovaries that are massively enlarged with multiple large, thin-walled cystic follicles bilaterally. In the clinical context of a woman undergoing infertility treatment with HMG (Human Menopausal Gonadotropins), this appearance is pathognomonic for Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) . OHSS is a potentially life-threatening iatrogenic complication of ovulation induction, characterized by increased capillary permeability leading to fluid shifts into the third space (ascites, pleural effusion). Theca lutein cysts (Option B) present similarly but are usually associated with molar pregnancies rather than infertility drugs. PCOD (Option C) would show much smaller, peripheral "string of pearls" follicles rather than these massive cysts. Therefore, the combination of recent HMG use and the characteristic "multicystic" ovarian enlargement confirms OHSS. Management involves intensive fluid and electrolyte monitoring and prevention of further gonadotropin exposure

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A previously healthy child presented with acute-onset dyspnea. A chest X-ray shows unilateral hyperinflation of the lungs. What is true for this patient?
options: Focal area of decreased air entry will be suggestive of foreign body
In complete obstruction, ball and valve mechanism causes hyperinflation
The child has developed acute laryngotracheobronchitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Focal area of decreased air entry will be suggestive of foreign body

The above scenario is suggestive of a foreign body in the airway, most likely in the bronchi. In this condition, auscultation is likely to reveal a focal area of decreased air entry due to incomplete airway obstruction

It is more commonly seen in children below 4 years. The most foreign bodies in the airway are food items. The foreign bodies can be non-irritating types (plastic, glass, or metallic foreign bodies) and irritating types (vegetables, peanuts, beans, and seeds).

The clinical presentation depends upon the site of the obstruction.

Site of foreign bodies
Signs and symptoms

Larynx

• Complete obstruction causes asphyxia
• Incomplete obstruction causes croup, hoarseness, cough, stridor, and dyspnea.

Trachea
Dysphonia, dysphagia, dry cough, and biphasic stridor.

Bronchi

• May be asymptomatic.
• Asymmetric breath sound/air entry, coughing, and breathing.

Foreign bodies in bronchi are more likely to enter the right bronchus because it is wider and more in line with the tracheal lumen.

The initial evaluation is done with a plain X-ray chest in posteroanterior and lateral views (expiratory films are useful). It may reveal:

• The radio-opaque foreign body- size, shape, and location
• In complete airway obstruction- lobar or segmental atelectasis
• In incomplete airway obstruction- the ball valve mechanism is produced when a foreign body incompletely obstructs a bronchus allowing air to enter inside but not leave. This leads to the appearance of hyperinflation or obstructive emphysema of the affected area when an expiratory X-ray film is taken as the air is not allowed to escape.

Management of foreign body airway is as follows:

• Laryngeal foreign body- Heimlich maneuver should be attempted. If it fails, cricothyrotomy or emergency tracheostomy should be done
• Foreign bodies in the trachea and bronchi are removed through a rigid bronchoscope after adequate hydration and emptying of the stomach.
• Appropriate antibiotics are given to prevent secondary infection.

Option D: Laryngotracheobronchitis or croup is caused by the parainfluenza virus. It commonly affects children of age 6 months-3 years. The clinical features include barking cough, biphasic stridor, and low-grade fever. The chest X-ray shows a narrowing of the subglottic region known as the steeple sign.

The image given below shows the steeple sign seen in croup.
questions.learning: Focal area of decreased air entry will be suggestive of foreign body The above scenario is suggestive of a foreign body in the airway, most likely in the bronchi.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 42-year-old obese female presented to the clinic with Schizophrenia. Which of the following anti-psychotic drugs causes the least weight gain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ziprasidone

Out of the following antipsychotics, Ziprasidone causes the least weight gain.

Ziprasidone is an atypical antipsychotic used primarily in the treatment of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. It works by blocking the activity of dopamine and serotonin receptors in the brain. Specifically, it acts as an antagonist at dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors.

The side effects of ziprasidone include orthostatic hypotension, QT prolongation, and minimal weight gain.

Ziprasidone causes prolongation of QT interval and hence should be avoided in patients with a history of cardiac arrhythmias and should not be given in combination with other drugs known to prolong the QT interval.

Atypical agents classified according to their metabolic risk potential:

* Highest: clozapine, olanzapine

* Intermediate: quetiapine, risperidone, paliperidone

* Least: Aripiprazole, ziprasidone, iloperidone, asenapine

Clozapine causes the highest weight gain among all antipsychotics.
questions.learning: Ziprasidone Out of the following antipsychotics, Ziprasidone causes the least weight gain. Ziprasidone is an atypical antipsychotic used primarily in the treatment of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Failure of which mechanism is central to TTN?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ENaC-mediated alveolar sodium absorption

• Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN) occurs due to delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid after birth. Normally, during labor and shortly after delivery, epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the alveolar epithelium actively reabsorb sodium and water from the alveoli into the pulmonary circulation and lymphatics.
• Failure of ENaC-mediated sodium absorption leads to retained lung fluid, causing tachypnea and mild respiratory distress shortly after birth.

Why not the other options?

A. Surfactant production: Deficiency causes Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) in premature infants, not TTN.

C. Type II pneumocyte proliferation: Related to surfactant production; not the mechanism of TTN.

D. Pulmonary vasodilation: Failure causes Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a population with a mean blood glucose level of 105 mg/dL and a standard deviation of 10 mg/dL, assuming a normal distribution, what range of blood glucose values would be expected to include approximately 95% of individuals?
questions.explanation: In a normal distribution (Gaussian distribution), approximately 95% of all data points fall within ±2 standard deviations (SD) from the mean (more precisely ±1.96 SD). Given a mean of 105 mg/dL and an SD of 10 mg/dL, the calculation for the 95% range is: Mean ± (2 × SD) = 105 ± (2 × 10) = 105 ± 20. This results in a range of 85 to 125 mg/dL. Option B (101–110) covers a much narrower range of only ±0.5 SD. Option C (90–125) is an asymmetric range and does not follow the empirical rule. Option D (95–115) represents only ±1 SD from the mean, which accounts for approximately 68% of the population rather than 95%. Therefore, 85–125 mg/dL is the statistically correct range for a 95% confidence interval
questions.learning: In a normal distribution (Gaussian distribution), approximately 95% of all data points fall within ±2 standard deviations (SD) from the mean (more precisely ±1.96 SD).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with unexplained weight loss, fatigue, and hypercalcemia, without any detectable primary tumor or palpable mass. Laboratory investigations show elevated hormone levels that are not normally associated with any identified malignancy. What term best describes this condition, in which systemic symptoms arise due to hormone secretion from an occult tumor?
questions.explanation: A paraneoplastic syndrome describes a group of systemic symptoms and signs that develop in a patient with cancer but are not directly caused by the local presence of the tumor or its metastases. Instead, these syndromes are mediated by hormones, cytokines, or an immune response triggered by the malignancy. The patient’s "hypercalcemia" in the absence of a visible mass is a classic paraneoplastic finding, often due to the secretion of Parathyroid Hormone-related Protein (PTHrP) by an occult squamous cell carcinoma. Pretumor (Option A) and Paratumor (Option C) syndromes are not standard medical terms for this phenomenon. Autocrine phenomenon (Option D) refers to a cell secreting hormones that act on itself, rather than causing systemic syndrome. Therefore, paraneoplastic syndrome is the correct clinical term for these systemic, hormone-mediated manifestations of an underlying, unidentified malignancy
questions.learning: A paraneoplastic syndrome describes a group of systemic symptoms and signs that develop in a patient with cancer but are not directly caused by the local presence of the tumor or its metastases.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: One of the effector mechanisms in cell-mediated immunity involves identifying and lysing target cells whose membrane surface antigens are bound by specific antibodies.NK cells are one of the effector cells capable of this process. What other cells are capable of this process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neutrophils and eosinophils

Neutrophils and Eosinophils are capable of the effector mechanism described along with NK cells.

The effector mechanism being described refers to Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). Antibody dependent cellular cytotoxicity is seen with NK cells. However, it is also seen in macrophages,neutrophils and eosinophil killing certain parasitic worms like helminths via IgE antibodies.
questions.learning: Neutrophils and eosinophils Neutrophils and Eosinophils are capable of the effector mechanism described along with NK cells. The effector mechanism being described refers to Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 66-year-old man presents with urinary symptoms, back pain, elevated PSA, radiolucent pelvic bone lesions on X-ray, and enlarged lower abdominal lymph nodes on MRI, suggestive of advanced prostate cancer with bone metastases and nodal involvement. Which medication is indicated for treatment in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, characterized by elevated PSA and osteoblastic bone lesions. The mainstay of management for advanced disease is Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT) to lower testosterone levels. Goserelin (Option C) is a Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) agonist used for this purpose. It initially causes a surge in LH and FSH, followed by downregulation of the pituitary receptors, which effectively leads to chemical castration. Anastrozole (Option A) is an aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer. Desogestrel (Option B) is a progestogen used for female contraception. Oxandrolone (Option D) is an anabolic steroid which would be contraindicated in prostate cancer as it could stimulate tumor growth. Therefore, Goserelin is the correct pharmacological choice for suppressing the hormonal drive of the malignancy. ADT often provides significant symptomatic relief and can stabilize metastatic bone disease in elderly patients with prostate adenocarcinoma. Consequently, Goserelin is a standard component of systemic treatment protocols for these patients
questions.learning: The patient presents with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, characterized by elevated PSA and osteoblastic bone lesions. The mainstay of management for advanced disease is Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT) to lower testosterone levels.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the type of anemia. • Hb = 8 g/dL • MCV = 68 fL • Ferritin = Low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Iron deficiency anemia (IDA)

Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is the most common cause of microcytic hypochromic anemia and is characterized by depleted iron stores, reflected by low serum ferritin. A low hemoglobin, low MCV (<80 fL), and low ferritin are highly suggestive of IDA.

• Hb = 8 g/dL → Anemia
• MCV = 68 fL → Microcytic anemia
• Low ferritin → Depleted iron stores, the most specific laboratory marker of iron deficiency

Why not the other options?

• A. Aplastic anemia: Typically presents with normocytic anemia and pancytopenia, with normal or increased ferritin.
• B. Hemolytic anemia: Usually normocytic with reticulocytosis, elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin, and low haptoglobin.
• C. Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia: Causes macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia with an elevated MCV.
questions.learning: Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is the most common cause of microcytic hypochromic anemia and is characterized by depleted iron stores, reflected by low serum ferritin.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with renal colic and recurrent urinary tract infections. A CT scan reveals no significant findings. The patient undergoes a percutaneous nephrolithotomy and his urine analysis is as shown. Based on the clinical presentation and the urine analysis findings, what are these crystals made up of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cystine

The image shows a hexagonal crystal, suggesting cystine stones. These stones are a recurrent feature in patients with cystinuria.

Cystinuria is the most common inborn error of amino acid transport. It occurs due to defective basic amino acid transporter in the proximal tubules of the kidney. This leads to the excretion of cystine(dimer of cysteine), ornithine, lysine and arginine, abbreviated as COLA.

The disease manifests as precipitation of cystine stones in the urine leading to renal colic. Oral hydration is the mainstay of treatment.

Crystals in urine are usually associated with kidney stones. Crystals form in the urine depending upon a variety of factors including:

• The degree of concentration of constituent molecules
• The urine pH
• The presence of inhibitors of crystallisation

Calcium oxalate and uric acid crystals can sometimes be found in normal urine that has been left to stand, due to crystal formation ex vivo.
questions.learning: Cystine — The image shows a hexagonal crystal, suggesting cystine stones. These stones are a recurrent feature in patients with cystinuria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-month-old boy who is a known case of cerebral palsy, was brought to the OPD for a routine check-up. The child had a past history of weakness in both upper and lower limbs which improved with time. On examination, residual weakness is present more in the lower limbs and trunk as compared to the upper limbs. What is this condition called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spastic diplegia

The given clinical scenario of a child with cerebral palsy, who has residual weakness in his lower limbs as compared to his upper limbs is highly suggestive of spastic diplegia.

Spastic diplegia is more commonly seen in premature infants with a history of birth asphyxia due to damage to immature white matter. It is 2nd most common type of cerebral palsy in India after spastic quadriplegia. Both the lower limbs are involved. During development, characteristic commando crawling is seen. Brain MRI shows scarring and shrinkage in the periventricular white matter with compensatory enlargement of the cerebral ventricles. IQ of these children is usually normal and has a good prognosis.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a diagnostic term used to describe a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture causing activity limitation that is attributed to nonprogressive disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain. It is the most common cause of motor disability in childhood.

The subtypes of cerebral palsy and the pathology involved are given below:

Cerebral palsy subtype
Pathology

Spastic diplegia
Periventricular leukomalacia

Spastic quadriplegia
Multi-cystic encephalomalacia

Spastic hemiplegia
Middle cerebral artery territory infarction

Dyskinetic cerebral palsy
Basal ganglia

In older children, a scissoring gait is characterized by the knees and thighs pressed together or crossing each other while walking, caused by high muscle tone (spasticity) in the hip adductors.

Option B: Spastic hemiplegia affects one-half of the body (upper and lower limbs on the same side). It is seen due to vascular insult leading to perinatal stroke event. Early hand preference is seen (before 1 year), where one side of the body is always preferred as the other side is weak. MRI shows focal changes and porencephalic cysts due to infarcts.

Option C: Spastic quadriplegia is associated with ischemia of the brain and infections. MRI would reveal severe periventricular leukomalacia and multicystic cortical encephalomalacia.

Option D: Dyskinetic/ Extrapyramidal CP is more commonly seen in term infants. It is likely to be associated with birth asphyxia and kernicterus in the early neonatal period. The upper limb is affected more than the lower limb. Brain MRI reveals lesions in the basal ganglia and thalamus.
questions.learning: Spastic diplegia — The given clinical scenario of a child with cerebral palsy, who has residual weakness in his lower limbs as compared to his upper limbs is highly suggestive of spastic diplegia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): 1. Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor. 2. Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes. 3. Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg body weight) has significantly lower mortality compared to high tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg body weight). 4. PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤100 mm Hg is classified as severe ARDS. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

• Statement 1. Exudative phase lasts from day 7 to day 21 after exposure to a precipitating risk factor: Incorrect. The exudative phase actually lasts from day 1 to day 7 after the precipitating insult (characterized by diffuse alveolar damage, hyaline membrane formation, and neutrophil-rich edema). The timeframe of day 7–21 actually corresponds to the proliferative phase, not the exudative phase.
• Statement 2. Proliferative phase is characterised by proliferation of type II pneumocytes: Correct. The proliferative phase (roughly days 7–21) is marked by proliferation of type II pneumocytes (which attempt to repair the damaged alveolar epithelium), fibroblast proliferation, and organization of the exudate.
• Statement 3. Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg body weight) has significantly lower mortality compared to high tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg body weight): Correct. This is based on the landmark ARDSNet (ARMA) trial, which showed that a lung-protective ventilation strategy using low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) significantly reduced mortality compared to traditional higher tidal volumes (12 mL/kg), along with plateau pressure limitation (<30 cm H₂O).
• Statement 4. PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤100 mm Hg is classified as severe ARDS: Correct. As per the Berlin Definition of ARDS (2012), severity is graded by the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio (with PEEP ≥5 cm H₂O):

• Mild: 200–300 mm Hg
• Moderate: 100–200 mm Hg
• Severe: ≤100 mm Hg

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with a 3 cm soft, non-tender, and fluctuant swelling on the upper back. The lesion has been present for several months and occasionally drains a foul-smelling, cheesy material. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
options: Complete surgical excision including the capsule
Surgical excision of the cyst content leaving behind a portion of the wall
Incision and drainage of the cyst
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Complete surgical excision including the capsule

The clinical vignette is suggestive of a sebaceous cyst and the best management is complete surgical excision including the capsule.

A sebaceous cyst is derived from hair follicle infundibulum or traumatic inclusion. The most common site of a sebaceous cyst is the postauricular sulcus or below and behind the ear lobule. Malignancy is rare.

Clinical features of a sebaceous cyst include:

* Benign swelling that is mobile, fluctuant, and fixed to the skin. It presents with a central punctum in about 70% of cases.

* It is generally an asymptomatic, non-tender swelling. It can be painful and red if inflamed.

* It may ooze out a foul-smelling, cheese-like discharge.

Treatment depends on the clinical state of the cyst. When inflamed or infected, they should be incised and drained initially. After the inflammation subsides, a total surgical excision of the cyst is performed. If the cyst wall is not removed, there is a risk of recurrence. Perilesional triamcinolone injection helps with inflammation resolution but not cyst eradication.

The complications include sebaceous horn, cock’s peculiar tumor, and abscess formation. The treatment involves the excision of the cyst along with normal skin using an elliptical incision.

Below is an image showing an inflamed sebaceous cyst with a central punctum:

Other Options:

Option A: Topical application of antibiotics wont be correct choice for the given case scenario beacuse Antibiotics alone are not indicated for management of sebaceous cyst.

Option C: Surgical excision of the cyst content leaving behind a portion of the wall is also not indicated as it may lead to high rate of recurrence.

Option D: Only Incision and drainage is also not enough .When cyst is inflamed or infected, they should be incised and drained initially. After the inflammation subsides, total surgical excision of the cyst is performed.
questions.learning: Complete surgical excision including the capsule — The clinical vignette is suggestive of a sebaceous cyst and the best management is complete surgical excision including the capsule.
