Absence of neck webbing is associated with higher risk of co-arctation of aorta
Webbing of neck is associated with higher risk of cardiac anomalies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Webbing of neck is associated with higher risk of cardiac anomalies

In Turner's syndrome, webbing of the neck is associated with a higher risk of cardiac anomalies.

The image below summarises the clinical features of Turner's syndrome.

The image given below shows the webbing of neck.

Noonan syndrome is characterised by mutations in the RAS-MAPK pathway. The most common of these is the PTPN11 which encodes a protein tyrosine phosphatase on chromosome 12.

Clinical features include:

• Short stature
• Short webbed neck
• Cystic hygroma
• Tall forehead
• Low posterior hairline
• Dental malocclusion

Although it shares many clinical features with Turner’s syndrome, Noonan syndrome affects both sexes. It follows an autosomal dominant pattern and it also has a different pattern of congenital heart disease, typically involving right-sided lesions.
questions.learning: Webbing of neck is associated with higher risk of cardiac anomalies In Turner's syndrome, webbing of the neck is associated with a higher risk of cardiac anomalies.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with a history of smoking and anemia presents for consultation. His family history includes a sister diagnosed with endometrial cancer. What is the most appropriate method to screen for colorectal malignancy in this patient?
options: Check for occult blood in stool
questions.explanation: For an average-risk adult (starting at age 45-50), a Colonoscopy every 10 years is considered the "gold standard" and most appropriate screening method for colorectal cancer. This patient is at high risk due to his age (60) and family history; the combination of a sister with endometrial cancer may suggest Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC), which significantly increases the risk for colorectal and endometrial malignancies. Colonoscopy is preferred because it allows for both direct visualization and the removal of precancerous polyps (polypectomy) during the same procedure. Fecal Occult Blood Testing (Option C) and Flexible Sigmoidoscopy (Option D) are valid alternatives but are less sensitive and do not examine the entire colon. Barium enema (Option A) is no longer a standard primary screening tool. Given his anemia (a potential sign of right-sided occult bleeding), a colonoscopy is both a screening and diagnostic requirement to rule out synchronous lesions. If Lynch syndrome is formally suspected, the screening interval is shortened to every 1-2 years
questions.learning: For an average-risk adult (starting at age 45-50), a Colonoscopy every 10 years is considered the "gold standard" and most appropriate screening method for colorectal cancer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following consumes the highest energy during assimilation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proteins

Proteins consume the highest energy during assimilation.

The energy wasted in the assimilation of food is represented as diet-induced thermogenesis or specific dynamic action(SDA). Diet-induced thermogenesis (DIT) can be defined as the increase in energy expenditure above the basal metabolic rate and is expressed as a percentage.

The values for diet-induced thermogenesis are relatively higher protein and alcohol consumption and lower at a high-fat consumption, the hierarchy for it, being in the sequence of alcohol> protein> fat> carbohydrate. The value of DIT for protein is 30%, the lipid is 15% and carbohydrate is 5%. Hence, taking into account the loss of energy as DIT, additional 10% calories should be provided in a mixed diet.
questions.learning: Proteins Proteins consume the highest energy during assimilation. The energy wasted in the assimilation of food is represented as diet-induced thermogenesis or specific dynamic action(SDA).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old female patient is diagnosed with pure red cell aplasia and a mediastinal mass. Which of the following can be the likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thymoma

The most probable diagnosis for the clinical presentation of mediastinal mass with pure red cell aplasia is thymoma.

Thymoma refers to the tumors of the thymic epithelial cells. Most of the thymic tumors occur in the anterior mediastinum. Clinical features can be chest pain, dyspnea, cough, or superior vena cava syndrome.

It is associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like myasthenia gravis, pure red cell aplasia, or hypogammaglobulinemia. It is rarely associated with limbic encephalitis, hemolytic anemia, aplastic anemia, and other autoimmune conditions like Sjogren's syndrome.

Pure red cell aplasia: It is a marrow disorder where the erythroid progenitors are only suppressed. The complete absence of red cell progenitors is seen in severe cases.

Causes of pure red cell aplasia: It can be hereditary or acquired. Diamond-Blackfan anemia or congenital pure red cell aplasia is the hereditary cause. Causes of acquired pure red cell aplasia are given below:

• Cancer

• Thymoma
• Lymphoid malignancies (eg. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, large granular lymphocytosis)
• Paraneoplastic to solid tumors

• Connective tissue disorders with immunologic abnormalities

• Systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis

• Viruses

• Persistent B19 parvovirus, hepatitis, adult T cell leukemia virus, Epstein-Barr virus

• Drugs

• Phenytoin, azathioprine, chloramphenicol, procainamide, isoniazid

• Multiple endocrine gland insufficiency
• Antibodies to erythropoietin
• Idiopathic

Other options:

Option B: Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma can cause pure red cell aplasia but it commonly presents as peripheral adenopathy rather than mediastinal mass.

Options C and D: Germ cell tumors and bronchogenic carcinoma are not commonly known to be associated with red cell aplasia.
questions.learning: Thymoma — The most probable diagnosis for the clinical presentation of mediastinal mass with pure red cell aplasia is thymoma. Thymoma refers to the tumors of the thymic epithelial cells.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn born to a diabetic mother develops symptoms 24 hours after birth, and blood glucose estimation shows a level below 35 mg/ dL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Administer IV bolus of Hartmann solution
Administer IV glucose and recheck blood glucose after 20 minutes
questions.explanation: In a symptomatic neonate with blood glucose <35 mg/dL, immediate intravenous correction is required to prevent seizures and permanent neurological injury. The standard treatment is an IV bolus of 10% dextrose (2 mL/kg), followed by a continuous glucose infusion. It is essential to recheck the glucose within 20–30 minutes to confirm stabilization. Infants of diabetic mothers are at exceptionally high risk for this condition due to fetal hyperinsulinism. Hartmann solution (Option A) does not contain glucose and is ineffective. Waiting to recheck glucose without intervention (Option B) is dangerous in a symptomatic baby. Starting oral feeds (Option D) is only appropriate for mild, asymptomatic hypoglycemia. Therefore, immediate IV glucose is the mandatory life-saving intervention
questions.learning: In a symptomatic neonate with blood glucose <35 mg/dL, immediate intravenous correction is required to prevent seizures and permanent neurological injury.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which among the following dementia presents with capgras syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lewy body dementia

Capgras syndrome is a rare delusion of misidentification where the patient believes that someone close to him has been replaced by an imposter who looks exactly the same. Capgras syndrome along with other visual hallucinations are seen in Lewy body dementia or DLW ( Dementia with lew body). Other symptoms include depression, sleep disorders and delusions

Pearl PF1258: Types of delusions

THE TYPES OF DELUSIONS

Delusion of control

False belief that a person’s will, thoughts, or feelings are being controlled by external forces.

Delusion of grandeur or Megalomania

Exaggerated conception of one’s importance, power, or identity.

Delusion of infidelity or morbid jealousy or Othello syndrome

False belief that one’s lover is unfaithful. Sometimes called pathological jealousy.

Delusion of love or erotomania

False belief that another person is in love with them. In De Clerambault syndrome, the woman believes that a man, frequently older and of higher status, is in love with her.

Delusion of misidentification

Capgras syndrome: Belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an exact double i.e. an impostor.

Fregoli syndrome: Person holds a delusional belief that different people are in fact a single person who changes his or her appearance or is in disguise.

Nihilistic delusion

False belief that oneself, others or the world, is non-existent or about to end. When nihilistic delusion is accompanied by ideas concerning bodily function failure e.g. putrefaction of intestine etc, it is called Cotard syndrome.

Delusion of infestation

False belief that one is infested with small but visible organisms. As a monosymptomatic delusional disorder, this is called Ekbom syndrome.

Delusion of persecution

The most common delusion. False belief of being harassed or persecuted.

Delusion of poverty

The person strongly believes they are financially incapacitated.

Delusion of reference

False belief that the behavior of others has a particular and unusual significance, usually of a negative nature. The person may falsely feel that others are talking about them (e.g. the people on television are talking to or about the person).

Delusion of self-accusation

False feeling of remorse and guilt. Seen in depression with psychotic features.
questions.learning: Lewy body dementia Capgras syndrome is a rare delusion of misidentification where the patient believes that someone close to him has been replaced by an imposter who looks exactly the same.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What type of cardiac murmur is depicted in the image shown below?
questions.explanation: The phonocardiogram displays a diamond-shaped (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur occurring during systole, specifically between the first heart sound (S1) and the second heart sound (S2). This pattern is the hallmark of an ejection systolic murmur. It typically begins after a short gap following S1, peaks in mid-systole, and fades before S2. This type of murmur is most commonly associated with aortic stenosis or pulmonic stenosis, where blood is forcefully ejected through a narrowed semilunar valve. A pan systolic murmur (Option B) would maintain a constant intensity throughout the entire duration of systole, commonly heard in mitral regurgitation. Diastolic murmurs (Options A and D) occur after S2 and are linked to conditions like mitral stenosis or aortic regurgitation. The visual "diamond" shape on the phonocardiogram is a definitive diagnostic feature for ejection-type pathology in medical board exams
questions.learning: The phonocardiogram displays a diamond-shaped (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur occurring during systole, specifically between the first heart sound (S1) and the second heart sound (S2).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following treatments are recommended for a pregnant woman suffering from sickle cell disease? I. Folic acid 1 mg daily II. Azathioprine III. Penicillin prophylaxis IV. Thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, III and IV

Pregnancy in women with sickle cell disease (SCD) is considered high-risk because of increased maternal and fetal complications, including vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, and venous thromboembolism. Management focuses on preventing complications and optimizing maternal and fetal outcomes. The following treatments are recommended:

• I. Folic acid 1 mg daily: Correct. Folic acid supplementation is recommended because of chronic hemolysis, which increases folate requirements for erythropoiesis. (Many guidelines recommend an even higher dose, e.g., 5 mg/day during pregnancy.)
• III. Penicillin prophylaxis: Correct. Patients with functional asplenia are at increased risk of infections with encapsulated organisms. Penicillin prophylaxis is recommended in selected patients, particularly those already receiving it.
• IV. Thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin (LMWH): Correct. Pregnancy and sickle cell disease are both prothrombotic states. LMWH thromboprophylaxis is recommended during hospitalization and in the postpartum period, and antenatally in women with additional risk factors.

Why is II incorrect?

• II. Azathioprine: Incorrect. Azathioprine is not a routine treatment for sickle cell disease. Disease-modifying therapy for SCD is hydroxyurea, which is generally avoided during pregnancy because of potential teratogenicity.
questions.learning: I, III and IV Pregnancy in women with sickle cell disease (SCD) is considered high-risk because of increased maternal and fetal complications, including vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, and…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young sexually active female patient presented to the outpatient department with complaints of lower abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. On examination, the body temperature is 103 degrees Fahrenheit, pulse rate is 109 per minute and there is abdominal tenderness. Cervical motion tenderness is present on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelvic inflammatory disease

The likely diagnosis in this patient is pelvic inflammatory disease(PID).

Pelvic inflammatory disease is characterized by inflammation of the upper genital tract including the fallopian tubes as well as the ovaries. This disease is commonly seen in sexually active young women and is usually preceded by a sexually transmitted disease. Gonococcal and chlamydial infections are commonly associated with PID.

Patients present with lower abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, dysuria, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and vaginal discharge. The symptoms also vary depending on the causative organism. On examination, there is a fever of around 103- 104°F, abdominal tenderness, tachycardia, and pelvic mass. Chronic PID is associated with sequelae such as chronic pelvic pain, menorrhagia, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility.

Acute PID is diagnosed if uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness, or cervical motion tenderness is present and other etiologies are excluded or unlikely. One or more of the following can be used to diagnose PID on the clinical findings:

* Oral temperature >38.3°C (101.6°F),

* Mucopurulent cervical discharge or cervical friability,

* Abundant WBCs on saline microscopy of cervical secretions,

* Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP), and

* Presence of cervical N gonorrhea or C trachomatis

Depending on the extent of tissue involved, PID can be classified into five stages

Stage I
Acute salpingitis without peritonitis - No adhesions

Stage II
Acute salpingitis with peritonitis - purulent discharge

Stage III
Acute salpingitis with superimposed tubal occlusion or tubo ovarian complex

Stage IV
Ruptured tuba ovarian abscess

Stage V
Tubercular salpingitis

Other complications of chronic pelvic inflammatory disease:

* Hydrosalpinx

* Chronic pyosalpinx

* Chronic interstitial salpingitis

* Tubo ovarian cyst

Other options:

Option B: Endometriosis is a condition characterized by ectopic benign endometrial tissue that occurs outside the uterine cavity. Patients present with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, menorrhagia, and infertility. There is no foul-smelling vaginal discharge or fever hence this option is incorrect.

Option C: Adenomyosis is seen in multiparous women >40 years. The most common symptom involves menorrhagia and dysmenorrhea. Per-Vaginal examination reveals symmetrical enlargement of the uterus corresponding to <12 weeks of pregnancy.

Option D: Migrating abdominal pain from the periumbilical area to the right iliac fossa is classic for appendicitis. The abdominal pain also causes nausea and vomiting. Other nonspecific signs of appendicitis include low-grade fever, abdominal tenderness, guarding, and rebound tenderness.

Pearl PF1533: Organisms Responsible for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

Sexually transmitted: Gonococcus, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Trichomonas
Aerobes: Staphylococci , Streptococci ,E. coli

Anaerobes: Bacteroides fragilis, Peptococcus, Clostridium, Actinomyces (IUD)

Others: Tubercular salpingitis
questions.learning: Pelvic inflammatory disease — The likely diagnosis in this patient is pelvic inflammatory disease(PID). Pelvic inflammatory disease is characterized by inflammation of the upper genital tract including the fallopian tubes as well as the ovaries.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman with hysteria who was hyperventilating developed carpo-pedal spasm. What could be the likely cause for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Respiratory alkalosis

Respiratory alkalosis, developed secondary to hyperventilation, is the likely cause of the carpopedal spasm.

Hyperventilation leads to the washout of carbon dioxide, resulting in decreased levels of PaCO2 (hypocapnia), which in turn increases the pH (alkalosis). Thus, acute respiratory alkalosis occurs during hyperventilation. An increase in extracellular pH increases the binding of free calcium to albumin, lowering the ionized calcium concentration. This leads to hypocalcemia.

The clinical features of hypocalcemia are:

• Tetany: Increased peripheral neuromuscular irritability. May include perioral paresthesias, muscle spasms, and cramps.
• Trosseau's sign: Induction of carpal spasm when the BP cuff is inflated 20 mm Hg over the systolic BP for three minutes or more.
• Chvostek's sign: Contraction of the ipsilateral circumoral facial muscles when the facial nerve is tapped just anterior to the ear.
• Severe hypocalcemia can cause seizures, carpopedal spasm, bronchospasm, and laryngospasm.

Treatment of the underlying condition is necessary. The patient should be reassured and rebreathing from a paper bag should be done during acute episodes.

The image below shows Trosseau's sign.

The image below shows Chvostek's sign.
questions.learning: Respiratory alkalosis Respiratory alkalosis, developed secondary to hyperventilation, is the likely cause of the carpopedal spasm. Hyperventilation leads to the washout of carbon dioxide, resulting in decreased levels of PaCO2 (hypocapnia), which in turn…

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presented with the following findings on her face. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acne vulgaris

The age of the patient and the presence of papules and pustules with an erythematous base on the face are suggestive of acne vulgaris.

Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit. It is commonly seen in teenagers and young adults.

Comedonal lesions are the earliest lesions of acne. They represent the keratin plugs of the pilosebaceous duct and are non-inflammatory.

When the keratin plug is inside the follicle, it is called a closed comedone/whitehead.
When the keratin plug in the pilosebaceous unit is exposed to the environment, it gets oxidized by the air and turns black, known as open comedones/blackheads.
Inflammatory changes lead to the formation of papules, which may become pustules that rupture superficially or else spread deeper and form cystic lesions.

Management is directed at minimizing inflammation, decreasing keratin production, antibiotics, and antiandrogens to diminish sebum production.

The FDA has recently approved the drug Clascoterone, an androgen receptor inhibitor for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris in patients aged 12 years and older.

Other options:

Option A: Acne rosacea or Rosacea is predominantly a disease with onset in middle‐aged adults (30–50 years old) and involves the convexities of the face.

Option C: Eczema presents more over the flexures and extremities from early adulthood. Features of pruritus and excoriations are predominant.

Option D: Tinea faciei is a fungal infection of the face and presents with a scaly lesion.

Pearl PF1661: Global Alliance Algorithm for Acne Treatment

Global Alliance Algorithm for Acne Treatment

Image: Global Alliance Algorithm for Improving Outcomes in acne

BPO - Benzoyl peroxide
questions.learning: Acne vulgaris — The age of the patient and the presence of papules and pustules with an erythematous base on the face are suggestive of acne vulgaris. Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An African child is found to have a mass in the jaw. A biopsy of the mass was done, and it appears as shown in the image below. The child also had a translocation of t(8;14). What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Burkitt lymphoma

The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the histopathology showing a “starry sky” pattern is Burkitt lymphoma.

Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It is characterized by the translocation of the c-Myc gene on chromosome 8. This leads to increased MYC protein levels. The translocation most commonly seen in Burkitt's lymphoma is t(8;14).

It can occur in 3 forms that have distinct clinical characteristics:

• African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma presents as a mass involving the mandible. It may also involve the abdominal viscera, particularly the kidneys, ovaries, and adrenal glands.
• Sporadic (non-endemic) is often seen as a mass involving the ileocecum and peritoneum.
• Aggressive lymphoma or acute leukemia is seen in immunocompromised individuals

Histopathology shows tumor cells with round or oval nuclei, coarse chromatin, small nucleoli, minimal cytoplasm, and a high mitotic index. The phagocytes have abundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic “starry sky” pattern. Bone marrow aspiration shows tumor cells with royal blue cytoplasm containing clear cytoplasmic vacuoles.

The tumor cells express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6, a phenotype consistent with a germinal center B-cell origin.

Other options:

Option A: Acute myeloid leukemia is most commonly seen in elderly people. Histopathology from bone marrow aspirate reveals Auer rods (needle-like azurophilic granules) in the cytoplasm of the progranulocytes. Myeloblasts have two to four nucleoli and multiple coarse azurophilic granules.

The criterion for making a diagnosis of AML according to WHO requires one of the following:

• Blast cell count of ≥20% either in the peripheral blood or bone marrow
• Blast cell count of <20% in the presence of any one of the following three cytogenetic abnormalities t(15;17), t(8;21), and inversion 16 or t(16;16)

The peripheral blood smear shows numerous Auer rods in the cytoplasm of progranulocytes, characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia.

Option B: Follicular lymphoma presents in middle age with no sex predilection. The most common presenting symptom is painless generalized lymphadenopathy. Most follicular lymphomas have characteristic (14:18) translocation, leading to overexpression of BCL2. Lymph nodes exhibit a nodular or nodular and diffuse growth pattern.

Two cell types are predominantly present in varying proportions:

• Centrocytes - Small cells with a cleaved nucleus and scant cytoplasm
• Centroblasts - Large cells with open nuclear chromatin, several nucleoli, and modest amounts of cytoplasm

The following image shows a lymph node biopsy in follicular lymphoma:

Option C: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm. It is associated with lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, renal failure, and acquired immune abnormalities.

Histopathological findings include

• Flame cells with fiery red cytoplasm
• Mott cells with multiple grapelike cytoplasmic droplets
• Inclusions bodies: Russell bodies (if cytoplasmic) or Dutcher bodies (if nuclear)
questions.learning: Burkitt lymphoma — The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the histopathology showing a “starry sky” pattern is Burkitt lymphoma.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What would be the age of a child who copies crosses, tell stories, and goes to the toilet alone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 4 years

The combination of copying a cross, telling stories, and independent toileting aligns with the developmental milestones of a 4-year-old child.

Developmental milestones
At 1 year

• Motor: Walks with support
• Adaptive: Mature pincer grasp
• Language: Speaks a few words
• Social: Plays simple ball game
• Domestic mimicry at 18 months

At 2 years (Option D)

• Motor: Walks up and downstairs, one step at a time
• Adaptive: Makes a tower of 6 blocks
• Language: Simple sentences, a vocabulary of 50-100 words, uses pronouns at 2.5 yrs
• Social: Asks for food and starts toilet training, listens to stories

At 3 years (Option A)

• Motor: Rides tricycle
• Adaptive: Makes a tower of 9 blocks, handedness is established
• Language: Knows full name, age, gender
• Social: Plays simple games and engages in parallel play with other children

At 4 years

• Motor: Hops
• Adaptive: Draws square and constructs a bridge with blocks
• Language: Tells stories
• Social: Goes to the toilet alone

At 5 years (Option C)

• Motor: Skips
• Adaptive: Draws a triangle
• Language: Asks the meaning of words, names 4 colors
• Social: Dresses and undresses
questions.learning: 4 years The combination of copying a cross, telling stories, and independent toileting aligns with the developmental milestones of a 4-year-old child.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with the lesion shown below in the axillary region. He reports that a similar rash occurs at the same site every time he takes Cotrimoxazole(a sulfa-containing antibiotic). The lesion is mildly itchy and heals with darkening of the skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fixed Drug Eruption

The clinical scenario of a patient having well-defined, dusky lesions that recur at the same spot, with hyperpigmentation after healing, points towards the diagnosis of a fixed drug eruption (FDE). The most likely implicated agent here is Cotrimoxazole.

Fixed drug eruptions/reactions are characterized by sharply demarcated, dull red to brown lesions. But new lesions can occur on different body parts on re-exposure to the offending drug. FDE is a type of delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Cotrimoxazole (sulfa-containing agents) is one of the most common drugs causing FDE.

Drug‐specific clinical patterns have been reported. These include the following:

* NSAID‐induced FDE - lips and genitals

* Tetracycline and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole‐induced FDE - genitals

* Metamizole‐induced FDE - trunk and extremities

* Carbocysteine‐induced FDE - face

Diagnosis is based on history and lesion morphology. Discontinuation of the offending drug is the first step in management.

Other options:

Option A: Drug Allergy usually presents with Drug-induced urticaria, angioedema, and anaphylaxis. There are different clinical features of anaphylaxis identified in different organs. On withdrawal of the offending drug, clinical improvement arises within 24–48h.

Option B: Immunological Drug reaction usually presents with SJS, TEN, DRESS, which are predominantly a T-cell mediated reaction.

Option D: Contact dermatitis is an eczematous reaction with itchy, erythematous papules and papulovesicles that occurs as an immunological response following exposure to a substance to which the immune system has previously sensitized. It is diagnosed using a Patch test. The image below shows Bindi dermatitis.
questions.learning: Fixed Drug Eruption — The clinical scenario of a patient having well-defined, dusky lesions that recur at the same spot, with hyperpigmentation after healing, points towards the diagnosis of a fixed drug eruption (FDE).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which vitamin is given to prevent neural tube defects?
questions.explanation: Folic acid (Vitamin B9) supplementation is the standard of care to significantly reduce the risk of Neural Tube Defects (NTDs), such as spina bifida and anencephaly. NTDs occur during the first few weeks of pregnancy, often before a woman knows she is pregnant. For this reason, women of childbearing age are advised to take of folic acid daily. For those with a prior history of an NTD-affected pregnancy, a higher dose of daily is recommended starting three months before conception. Vitamin B1 (Thiamine, Option A), Vitamin B3 (Niacin, Option B), and Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin, Option D) are essential for general health and fetal development but do not share the specific, evidence-based protective role of folic acid in closing the neural tube. Consequently, ensuring adequate folate levels through diet and supplementation is a critical public health strategy in prenatal care
questions.learning: Folic acid (Vitamin B9) supplementation is the standard of care to significantly reduce the risk of Neural Tube Defects (NTDs), such as spina bifida and anencephaly.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following DMARD use requires regular monitoring of visual acuity and fundus examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine toxicity causes bull’s eye maculopathy. Hence, ophthalmic monitoring every 12 months is necessary.

Hydroxychloroquine is generally used for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and malaria. Chloroquine binds to melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium, causing cytotoxic effects. RPE atrophy occurs in the macula, resulting in dark areas on the autofluorescence image.

Fundus image of bull’s eye maculopathy is shown below
questions.learning: Hydroxychloroquine Hydroxychloroquine toxicity causes bull’s eye maculopathy. Hence, ophthalmic monitoring every 12 months is necessary.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Among the listed laryngeal cartilages, which is least prone to calcification?
questions.explanation: The laryngeal cartilages are composed of either hyaline or elastic cartilage, and this histological difference determines their tendency to calcify with age. The thyroid (Option A), cricoid (Option B), and the majority of the arytenoid (Option C) cartilages consist of hyaline cartilage. Hyaline cartilage characteristically undergoes calcification and even ossification as a normal part of the aging process, which can be visible on radiographic imaging. In contrast, the epiglottis, corniculate, and cuneiform cartilages are composed of elastic cartilage. Elastic cartilage contains a high density of elastic fibers and does not typically undergo calcification regardless of age. This flexibility is essential for the epiglottis to function as a lid during swallowing. Clinically, understanding this pattern is important because a calcified thyroid cartilage on an X-ray can be mistaken for a foreign body by an inexperienced clinician, whereas the epiglottis remains radiolucent throughout life due to its elastic nature
questions.learning: The laryngeal cartilages are composed of either hyaline or elastic cartilage, and this histological difference determines their tendency to calcify with age.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Which of the following instruments are used in the caesarean section?

1. Bard-Parker blade
2. Doyen's retractor
3. Cusco's speculum
4. Allis forceps
5. Shirodkar's uterine clamp
6. Green Armytage forceps
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 4, 6

Of the given list/combination of instruments 1, 2, 4, 6 are commonly used in the cesarean section.

Cesarean section is an operative procedure in which the fetuses are delivered through an incision on the abdominal and uterine walls.

The given image summarizes the various instruments used in the lower segment cesarean section.

Bard-Parker blade (scalpel with blade) has a handle with a notch to fit the blade. It is usually held by pencil grip. Commonly for abdominal incisions, we use blade no: 22. Other uses include incision of skin and sub-cutaneous tissues, cutting the clamped pedicles, and performing sharp dissections.

The given image shows various Bard-Parker blades.

Doyen's retractor is used to retract the abdominal wall as well as the bladder to facilitate better exposure of the lower uterine segment during cesarian operation. It is also used to pull back the soft tissues to widen the surgical field during laparotomy.

The image below shows Doyen's retractor.

Alli's forceps: It is identified by the distal blades and a tip that has teeth that do not oppose each other. There is also a lock in the proximal part.

Uses:

• To catch hold of the margins and angles of the uterine flaps in LSCS after the delivery of the baby in settings where the Green-Armytage hemostatic clamp is not available.
• To catch hold the anterior lip of the cervix
• To hold the apex of the episiotomy wound during the repair.
• To catch hold of the margins of the peritoneum, rectus sheath, vaginal mucosa during the repair.
• To catch hold of the torn ends of the sphincter ani externus prior to suture in the repair of complete perineal tear.

The given image shows Alli's forceps.

Green armytage forceps have a broad tip as shown in the image and hence are used to compress a wide area. It is used as a hemostat in caesarian sections. In LSCS (Lower segment Caesarean section), the cut uterine edges can bleed and Green Armytage forceps are applied to the edge of the incision for hemostasis.

Cusco's speculum is a self-retaining bivalve speculum used for visualization of the cervix, vaginal fornices, and for performing pap smears.

The instrument shown in the image is Cusco’s speculum.

Shirodkar's uterine holding clamp has blades with curved transverse bars with gaps between them when it is locked. This gap makes it atraumatic and is used to lift, hold and steady the uterus during sling surgeries and tubal procedures.

The image below shows Shirodkar's uterine clamp.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 4, 6 Of the given list/combination of instruments 1, 2, 4, 6 are commonly used in the cesarean section. Cesarean section is an operative procedure in which the fetuses are delivered through an incision on the abdominal and uterine walls.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following sites has the least concentration of sodium ions in the fluid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Salivary glands

GI secretions are not static liquids. They get modified along ducts and segments like a river changing chemistry as it flows.

Saliva is the only GI fluid that becomes hypotonic

→ meaning Na⁺ gets reabsorbed more than water

Acinar cells → Secrete isotonic fluid (Na⁺ high)

↓

Ductal cells → Reabsorb Na⁺ & Cl⁻

↓

Final saliva → Hypotonic (Na⁺ ↓↓↓, K⁺ ↑)

Ducts are impermeable to water

→ Na⁺ leaves, water cannot follow → dilution happens

| ---- | ----------------- | -----------

| Saliva | Lowest | Hypotonic

| Stomach | Moderate | HCl secretion dominates

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old male was on maize as a staple diet for a prolonged period. He presented with diarrhoea and lesion over his neck as shown in the image below. The condition occurs due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niacin

The above history and clinical features suggest niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Excessive consumption of maize-based diets can cause pellagra. Corn/Maize has low levels of niacin and tryptophan. Jowar has high leucine content which inhibits QPRTase, an enzyme in the synthesis of Niacin.

Niacin deficiency leads to a disease called pellagra which is characterized by

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia

The lesion in the neck is characteristic Casal’s necklace pattern, seen in pellagra. The Casal collar or Casal necklace is a clinical sign in which there is an erythematous pigmented skin rash in the distribution of a broad collar (dermatomes C3 and C4).
questions.learning: Niacin — The above history and clinical features suggest niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. Excessive consumption of maize-based diets can cause pellagra.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department with diarrhea, profuse sweating, excessive salivation and lacrimation, a garlicky odor, bradycardia (pulse 55/min), and markedly reduced plasma cholinesterase levels (50 U/ mL). Based on these clinical and laboratory findings, what is the most appropriate treatment to administer?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with a classic "cholinergic toxidrome," often summarized by the mnemonic SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, Gastric distress, and Emesis. The bradycardia (HR 55), garlicky odor, and significantly low plasma cholinesterase level (50U/mL) are highly indicative of Organophosphate (OP) poisoning. Atropine is the physiological antidote that works by antagonizing the excess acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, thereby reversing the life-threatening bradycardia and excessive secretions. Neostigmine (Option A) is a cholinesterase inhibitor that would dangerously worsen the condition. Epinephrine (Option C) might raise the heart rate but does not stop the secretions. Benztropine (Option D) is an anticholinergic used for Parkinsonism but is not the drug of choice for acute OP toxicity. Management also involves the use of pralidoxime (oximes) to reactivate the enzyme if administered early. Prompt atropinization (titrated until secretions dry) is the most critical life-saving step in OP poisoning
questions.learning: The patient is presenting with a classic "cholinergic toxidrome," often summarized by the mnemonic SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, Gastric distress, and Emesis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient with longstanding hypertension and diabetes mellitus is evaluated for renal function. In explaining the role of glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which statement correctly describes how GFR is regulated?
options: An increase in sympathetic function increases GFR
An increase in RPF increases GFR
A decrease in RPF increases GFR
questions.explanation: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is heavily dependent on Renal Plasma Flow (RPF). Under physiological conditions, an increase in RPF increases the GFR because it maintains a high hydrostatic pressure across the glomerular capillaries and prevents the rapid rise of oncotic pressure that would otherwise oppose filtration. Afferent arteriolar constriction (Option B) or an increase in sympathetic activity (Option A) both cause a decrease in RPF and a subsequent decrease in GFR by reducing the blood entering the glomerulus. A decrease in RPF (Option D) would lead to a decrease in GFR. GFR is also regulated by autoregulatory mechanisms (tubuloglomerular feedback) and hormones like Angiotensin II. For a patient with diabetes and hypertension, maintaining an optimal GFR is vital to prevent the progression of chronic kidney disease. Understanding that RPF and GFR are generally directly proportional is a core principle of renal physiology, making Option C the only accurate statement

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the name of the pregnancy test kit introduced by the Indian government?
questions.explanation: The Indian government introduced the NISHCHAY kit to provide accessible and reliable pregnancy testing at the community level, primarily through ASHA workers. This initiative aims to ensure early detection of pregnancy, facilitating timely antenatal care and informed reproductive choices. It is a simple urine-based test kit. Understanding the distractors is crucial for public health literacy: NIKSHAY (Option B) is the unified ICT portal for Tuberculosis (TB) patient management and tracking in India. NIKUSTH (Option C) is a similar digital platform specifically designed for the surveillance and management of Leprosy cases. AXSHYA (Option D) refers to a civil society project aimed at improving the reach and quality of TB services. Therefore, while these programs are all vital components of India's health infrastructure, NISHCHAY is the only one dedicated to pregnancy diagnosis. This kit plays a significant role in reducing maternal mortality by bringing diagnostic services directly to the doorsteps of rural and underserved populations
questions.learning: The Indian government introduced the NISHCHAY kit to provide accessible and reliable pregnancy testing at the community level, primarily through ASHA workers.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All the following tests are related to pasteurization of milk except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iodine test

All the above tests are related to the pasteurization of milk except the iodine test. It is done to test if milk is adulterated with starch or cereal flour.

The iodine test is done by adding 2 drops of iodine solution containing potassium iodide and iodine to 1ml of milk. The appearance of a blue color indicates that the milk is adulterated with starch. A control sample of milk that is not adulterated with starch will develop a slightly yellowish color.

Pasteurization can be done by the following methods,

• Holder/Vat method: 63-66 °C for 30 minutes and then quickly cooled to 5°C.
• HTST method (High-temperature short time): 72°C for at least 15 seconds, and then cooled rapidly to 4°C.
• UHT method (Ultra-high temp): Rapidly heated to 125 °C for a few seconds, then cooled and bottled as quickly as possible.

Tests in pasteurization:

• Phosphatase test: It is based on the fact that raw milk contains phosphatase enzyme which gets destroyed at temperatures corresponding to the standard time and temperature required for pasteurization.
• Standard plate count: It is used to determine the bacteriological quality of pasteurized milk.
• Coliform count: The presence of coliform organisms in pasteurized milk indicates either improper pasteurization or post-pasteurization contamination.
• Methylene blue reduction test is an indirect method for the detection of microorganisms in milk. This test is carried out on the milk accepted for pasteurization. Definite quantities of methylene blue are added to 10 ml of milk at a uniform temperature of 37°C. The milk is considered satisfactory if it fails to reduce the methylene blue dye in 30 minutes under standard conditions.
questions.learning: Iodine test All the above tests are related to the pasteurization of milk except the iodine test. It is done to test if milk is adulterated with starch or cereal flour.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
Match the following with the respective ages of fusion:

A. Medial end of clavicle
1. 22-25 years

B. Sacrum as a single bone
2. 50 years

C. Crista scapulae
3. 45 years

D. Lambdoid suture
4. 21-25 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3

The correct match is A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3.

The respective ages of fusion are:

• The medial end of clavicle at 21-25 years
• Sacrum as a single bone at 22-25 years
• Crista scapulae at 50 years
• Lambdoid suture at 45 years

The secondary ossification center at the medial end of the clavicle appears at 18-19 years of age and fuses by 20-22 years of age. This occurs 2 years earlier in females. Thus the complete fusion of the medial end of clavicle can be used for establishment of age of 21 years in medicolegal cases.

The 5 sacral vertebrae are separated by cartilage till puberty. Fusion of epiphysis begins after puberty and ossification start from below upwards. Sacrum becomes a single bone by the age of 25 years.

Ossification of scapulae:

• 30-35 years: lipping starts on ventral margin of glenoid cavity
• 35-40 years: irregular lipping around the clavicular facet and inferior surface of acromion process.
• 45 years: localized bony atrophy
• 50 years: Cristae scapulae

Lambdoid suture starts closing endocranially at 25-35 years and completes fusion by 45-50 years. Endocranial fusion occurs before ectocranial fusion.

The sagittal suture is used for age determination even though age estimation by skull sutures is not considered to be very reliable. The last skull suture to fuse is the squamous temporal suture, which fuses after 80 years of age.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old male patient presented to surgery OPD with a history of intermittent purulent discharge with a slight blood tinge from an external opening located in the perianal region even after multiple drainage attempts.Examination of the perianal region is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fistula-in-ano

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of fistula-in-ano. Laying open fistulotomy is the surest management method to eradicate the disease.

Fistula-in -ano:

A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal hollow tract or cavity that is lined with granulation tissue and that connects a primary opening inside the anal canal to a secondary opening in the perianal skin.

The most common cause is perianal abscess. Other causes include tuberculosis or Crohn's disease.

Symptoms:

* Perianal pain

* Discharge - intermittent purulent discharge (which may be bloody)

Goodsall's rule:

Goodsall’s rule can be used as a guide in determining the location of the internal opening of the fistula.

* Fistulas with an external opening anteriorly connect to the internal opening by a short, radial tract.

* Fistulas with an external opening posteriorly track in a curvilinear fashion to the posterior midline.

Exceptions to Goodsall’s Rule

However, exceptions to this rule often occur: Fistulas with an anterior external opening greater than 3 cm from the anal margin usually track to the posterior midline.

Investigations:

The investigations available for fistula-in-ano are as follows:

* Fistulogram

* Endoanal ultrasound

* MRI

* Computed tomography (CT) scan

* Endocoil MRI

* Hydrogen peroxide–enhanced 3-D endoanal ultrasonography

Fistula-in-ano is surgically managed by fistulotomy, fistulectomy, ligation of the inter-sphincteric fistula tract (LIFT), or setons

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: According to myogenic hypothesis of renal autoregulation the afferent arterioles contract in response to stretch-induced by______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Opening of calcium channels

The afferent arterioles contract in response to stretch induced by the opening of calcium channels. The mechanism is called myogenic autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR.

The stretch of the vascular wall allows increased movement of calcium ions from the extracellular fluid into the cells, causing them to contract. This contraction prevents excessive stretch of the vessel. This prevents excessive increase of renal blood flow and GFR by raising vascular resistance.

This mechanism may be more important in protecting the kidney from hypertension-induced injury.

Autoregulation has two main mechanisms:

• Metabolic mechanism: Tissues produce vasodilatory metabolites that regulate flow e.g. prostaglandins, NO, CO2, H+ and K+
• Myogenic mechanism
questions.learning: Opening of calcium channels — The afferent arterioles contract in response to stretch induced by the opening of calcium channels. The mechanism is called myogenic autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
Which of the following are the objective tests for the hearing?

1. BERA (Brainstem evoked response audiometry)
2. OAE (Otoacoustic emission)
3. PTA (Pure tone audiometry)
4. Tympanometry
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 4

BERA, OAE, and tympanometry are the objective tests for hearing. PTA (pure tone audiometry) is a subjective test for hearing as it relies on patient responses to pure tone stimuli. Other examples of subjective tests include tuning fork tests and speech audiometry.

Tympanometry is an objective test of the middle ear and eustachian tube functions (conductive compartment of hearing). Here, the compliance of the TM, i.e., how much it moves to the pressure differentials applied from the external ear is measured.

The image below shows the types of tympanogram:
questions.learning: 1, 2, and 4 BERA, OAE, and tympanometry are the objective tests for hearing. PTA (pure tone audiometry) is a subjective test for hearing as it relies on patient responses to pure tone stimuli.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: On the same day, a doctor received two summonses: one to appear in court as an expert witness in a rape and murder case, and another for medical negligence after amputating the wrong leg of a patient. What should the physician do in this situation?
options: Attend the summons for the murder case
Attend the summons for the medical negligence case
Attend the court for the summons received first and inform the other court accordingly
Inform both the courts and wait
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Attend the summons for the murder case

If a witness is summoned by both a criminal and a civil court on the same day, priority should be given to attending the summons for the criminal case first, which is the murder and rape case in this scenario. He should also notify the civil court of his inability to attend, providing valid reasons.

A summons is a document compelling the attendance of a witness in a court of law under penalty, on a particular day and time, to give evidence.

In this situation, the physician has a legal and ethical obligation to appear in court as an expert witness for the rape and murder case. This is a criminal case, and a summons to testify in a criminal proceeding is given priority. The medical negligence case is a civil case, and it is of a lower priority. The principle here is that the state's interest in a criminal prosecution, particularly a serious one involving a felony like murder, outweighs the private interests in a civil lawsuit.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Frontline health workers are employed to record the births and deaths in countries which have made slow progress in the development of a comprehensive vital registration system. This approach is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lay reporting

Lay reporting is a method of collecting birth and death data in areas where a complete Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) system is not yet fully developed. In this approach, frontline health workers, teachers, village volunteers, or other community-based workers record vital events and report them to the health system.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Registration of vital events: Refers to the official, continuous, compulsory, and permanent registration of births, deaths, marriages, etc., under the Civil Registration System (CRS).
• C. Sample Registration System (SRS) ✗

• India’s Sample Registration System is a dual-record system involving:

• Continuous enumeration by a resident part-time enumerator.
• Independent six-monthly survey by a supervisor.

• It is not based solely on frontline health workers.

• D. Census: Census is conducted once every 10 years and provides demographic information but does not continuously record births and deaths.
questions.learning: Lay reporting Lay reporting is a method of collecting birth and death data in areas where a complete Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) system is not yet fully developed.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident sustains fractures of both the tibia and fibula. What type of fracture is this classified as?
questions.explanation: A "Bumper Fracture" is a clinical term for a fracture of the proximal tibia and/or fibula, typically caused by a direct blow from a car bumper to a pedestrian's leg. These are often high-energy injuries resulting in comminuted or displaced fractures of both bones at the level of the impact. Patella sleeve fractures (Option B) are specific to the pediatric population and involve an avulsion of the patellar cartilage with a small bone fragment. Depressed skull fractures (Option C) and cervical fractures (Option D) involve the cranium and spine, respectively, and are not descriptive of the leg injuries mentioned. Bumper fractures are significant because they are often associated with soft tissue damage, compartment syndrome, and injuries to the peroneal nerve or popliteal artery. Diagnosis is confirmed with X-rays showing the fracture site. Management depends on the degree of displacement and stability, often requiring surgical fixation
questions.learning: A "Bumper Fracture" is a clinical term for a fracture of the proximal tibia and/or fibula, typically caused by a direct blow from a car bumper to a pedestrian's leg.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The ultrasound of a young woman with infertility is suggestive of a uterine anomaly. Which of the following is used to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hysteroscopy + laparoscopy

Among the given options, hysteroscopy with laparoscopy is used to confirm the diagnosis.

For infertility evaluation, hysteroscopy and laparoscopy can detect müllerian anomalies, screen for co-existent endometriosis, and exclude other tubal or uterine cavity pathology.

This approach can differentiate between a septate and a bicornuate uterus. On laparoscopy, the presence of a uterine fundus indicates that the uterus is septate, while its absence indicates it is bicornuate. The capacity of each horn in a bicornuate uterus and the depth and thickness of the uterine septum prior to surgical resection can also be assessed.

MRI is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of Mullerian anomalies. It clearly delineates both the internal and external uterine anatomy. Complex anomalies and common associations like renal or skeletal anomalies can also be evaluated. It is also less invasive than hysteroscopy and laparoscopy in diagnosing Mullerian anomalies.

Other options:

Option A: Hysterosalpingography (HSG) provides information about the interior contour of the uterine cavity but cannot accurately visualize the external contour of the uterus.

Option C: Laparoscopy alone as a diagnostic procedure cannot visualize the interior contour of a hollow viscus like the uterus. This can be done only with the help of hysteroscopy or imaging such as sonography, HSG, or MRI.

Option D: Transvaginal sonography is used for the initial detection of uterine anomalies causing infertility or spontaneous abortions. Complete evaluation of these anomalies is done by MRI.

Note:

• Hysteroscopy is the gold standard investigation to visualize the uterine cavity and tubal ostia. It also has therapeutic benefits in cases of endometrial polyps, submucous resection of myoma, hysteroscopic adhesiolysis, and resection of uterine septum.
• Laparoscopy is the gold standard investigation to evaluate tubal factors of infertility.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Patient presents to the neurology clinic with complaints of difficulty switching from one movement to another. He also reports having uncontrolled hand movements when trying to perform rapid alternating movements, particularly when asked to tap his fingers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dysdiadochokinesis

The patient has difficulty switching from one movement to another which is suggestive of Dysdiadochokinesia. It is the inability to perform rapid alternate movements.

It is a clinical manifestation of cerebellar dysfunction and is most evident when strength and sensation are intact. Focal lesions in the nervous system may produce highly asymmetric dysdiadochokinesia.

The following movement is the method to check for dysdiadochokinesis. The patient is showing normal movement, with no dysdiadochokinesis.

Other Options:

Option A: Resting tremor is an involuntary, rhythmic muscle movement that occurs when the affected body part is at rest and diminishes with voluntary movement. It is commonly associated with Parkinson's disease and basal ganglia dysfunction.

Option B: Intentional tremor is a slow, rhythmic tremor that occurs during purposeful movement and worsens as the target approaches. It is commonly seen in cerebellar disorders, such as multiple sclerosis or stroke.

Option D: Bradykinesia is the slowness of voluntary movements, often accompanied by reduced amplitude and difficulty initiating actions. It is a hallmark symptom of Parkinson’s disease and other basal ganglia disorders.

Pearl PF1419: Functions of cerebellum

Vestibulo cerebellum

• It is concerned with maintainence of balance and equilibirium.
• It is responsible for regulating the stability of head and body in space.
• It adjusts the tone of the trunk muscle.
• Controls the oculur movements and other postural reflexes.

Spino cerebellum

• Maintains the posture and helps in execution of gross movements.
• It controls the interplay between the agonist and antagonist group of muscles.
• It is essential for the control of rapid muscular activities like running and talking.

Cerebro cerebellum (Neocerebellum)

• Controls fine, highly precise and coordinated movements.
• It is involved in programming of voluntary and skilled movements
• It plays a major role in the timing of the motor activities and rapid progression from one movement to the next.
questions.learning: Dysdiadochokinesis — The patient has difficulty switching from one movement to another which is suggestive of Dysdiadochokinesia. It is the inability to perform rapid alternate movements.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: ‘Masson Bodies’ formed due to proliferation of immature collagen are a characteristic histopathological finding seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia

Masson bodies are the histopathological hallmark of Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP) (formerly called Bronchiolitis Obliterans Organizing Pneumonia [BOOP]). They consist of plugs of loose fibroblastic tissue composed of immature collagen and fibroblasts filling the alveolar ducts, alveoli, and bronchioles, while the underlying lung architecture is preserved.

COP represents an organizing response to lung injury rather than irreversible fibrosis and usually responds dramatically to corticosteroid therapy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Lymphocytic Interstitial Pneumonia (LIP): Characterized by diffuse interstitial lymphocytic infiltration, commonly associated with Sjögren syndrome and HIV, not Masson bodies.
• C. Desquamative Interstitial Pneumonia (DIP): Characterized by accumulation of pigmented macrophages in alveoli, strongly associated with smoking.
• D. Respiratory Bronchiolitis: Also a smoking-related disease, characterized by pigmented macrophages in respiratory bronchioles, not fibroblastic plugs.
questions.learning: Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia Masson bodies are the histopathological hallmark of Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP) (formerly called Bronchiolitis Obliterans Organizing Pneumonia [BOOP]).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor used to treat hypertension. This entire class of drugs is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (Category D/X). ACE inhibitors can cause severe fetal and neonatal injury, including renal failure, limb deformities, lung hypoplasia, and fetal skull defects (ACE inhibitor fetopathy). Paracetamol (Option B) is generally considered the safest analgesic and antipyretic throughout pregnancy. Ranitidine (Option C) is an H2-blocker commonly used for acid reflux and is not contraindicated. Cefixime (Option D) is a third-generation cephalosporin and is a safe antibiotic choice for infections during pregnancy. For pregnant women with hypertension, safer alternatives like Labetalol, Methyldopa, or Nifedipine should be used instead of ACE inhibitors or ARBs. This pharmacological knowledge is vital for preventing iatrogenic fetal harm. Any woman of childbearing age prescribed an ACE inhibitor must be counseled about its teratogenic risks and the need for reliable contraception
questions.learning: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor used to treat hypertension. This entire class of drugs is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (Category D/X).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about the following image?
options: Staph. aureus is the causative organism
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Staph. aureus is the causative organism

The image above indicates that the patient has Fournier's gangrene. It is caused due to mixed infection of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.

Concurrent illnesses like diabetes mellitus and alcoholism, predispose patients to Fournier's gangrene.

The sequence of events is as follows: A mixed infection of the aerobic and anaerobic bacteria → fulminating inflammation of subcutaneous tissue → obliterative arteritis of the arterioles that supply the scrotal skin → gangrene

The testes are usually not affected due to their intraabdominal-origin blood supply.

It is a surgical emergency. In Fournier's gangrene, despite the best therapy, mortality rates are high at 50%.
questions.learning: Staph. aureus is the causative organism The image above indicates that the patient has Fournier's gangrene. It is caused due to mixed infection of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old child with Wilson's disease is being considered for liver transplantation. Which of the following is not a parameter in the selection criteria for transplantation?
options: Jaundice less than 7 days before development of encephalopathy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Jaundice less than 7 days before development of encephalopathy

A 5-year-old child with Wilson's disease is a case of non-paracetamol-induced acute liver failure and jaundice for more than 7 days before the development of encephalopathy is one of the parameters in the King's College criteria for liver transplantation.

It includes the following parameters:

Non-paracetamol-induced acute liver failure:

• PT >100 s (INR >6.5)

or/and

• Any three of the following:

• Age <10 years or >40 years
• Etiology non-A, non-B hepatitis, or idiosyncratic drug reaction
• Jaundice more than 7 days before the development of encephalopathy i.e., not hyperacute
• PT >50 s (INR > 3.5)
• Bilirubin > 18 mg/dl (300 μmol/L)

Paracetamol-induced acute liver failure:

• pH <7.30 (irrespective of the grade of encephalopathy)

or/and

• All three of the following:

• Prothrombin time >100 s (INR >6.5)
• Serum creatinine >3.4 mg/dl (300 μmol/L)
• Grade 3 or 4 hepatic encephalopathy

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Blood supply for the red shaded area in the given image is a branch of which artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vertebral artery

The red shaded area represents the lateral medulla, which is supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA).

PICA is a branch of the vertebral artery and its occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.

Superior cerebellar artery arises from basilar artery, posterior cerebral artery supplies midbrain and occipital lobe, and basilar artery itself does not directly supply this lateral medullary region.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presented with dry mouth, urinary retention, and constipation after consuming an unknown substance. On examination, his PR - 110bpm, and his pupils were dilated. What did he most likely consume?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Belladona

The given clinical scenario with dilatation of the pupil indicates Atropa belladonna consumption.

Atropa Belladonna acts by inhibiting the muscarinic effects of acetylcholine. All the parts of the plants are toxic. The active principle is 1-hyoscyamine.

Heroin, morphine, and malathion cause constriction of the pupil.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young man came to the medical OPD with complaints of early morning backache and stiffness, which improves on exercise, and persistent red eyes. On examination, lung expansion was less than 3 cm. X-ray is shown in the image given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ankylosing spondylitis

The given clinical vignette points towards the diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis.

Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory disease affecting the spine and sacroiliac joint. It is more common in young males and has a strong association with HLAB27.

Clinically, patients present with recurring backache which worsens in the early morning or with inactivity and improves with exercise. Later, they develop fatigue, pain, joint swellings, and heel pain. Extra-articular manifestations include anterior uveitis, aortic incompetence, carditis, and apical lobe fibrosis. Examination findings include loss of lumbar lordosis, increased thoracic kyphosis, diminished spinal movements, and decreased chest expansion.

X-ray findings:

• Erosion of sacroiliac joints - earliest sign
• Periarticular sclerosis in later stages
• Squaring of vertebrae due to the flattening of normal anterior concavity of the vertebral body is the earliest vertebral change
• Bamboo spine appearance due to bridging of adjacent vertebrae
• Wedging of the vertebra, leading to hyperkyphosis

Complications of ankylosing spondylitis include

• Spinal fractures, the most common site is C5–7
• Hyperkyphosis
• Spinal cord compression
• Lumbosacral nerve root compression

Treatment consists of maintaining posture and preserving mobility. Pain and stiffness can be controlled with anti-inflammatory drugs. In severe cases, TNF inhibitors are used. Surgery can be considered to correct the deformity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following medications can be safely used for a pregnant lady diagnosed with hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alpha methyl dopa

Alpha methyldopa is safe for use for hypertension in pregnancy.

Antihypertensives to be avoided in pregnancy:

* ACE inhibitors, ARBs

* Diuretics

* Nonselective beta-blockers

* Nitroprusside

Antihypertensives found to be safe in pregnancy:

* Hydralazine

* Methyldopa

* Dihydropyridine CCBs: should be stopped before labor as they weaken the uterine contractions

* Cardio-selective beta-blockers and those with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity: may be used as a last choice

L-thyroxine is a Category A drug in pregnancy and thus is safe.

Note:

Alpha methyldopa: Methyldopa is preferred for chronic hypertension in pregnancy based on its safety and efficacy data for both mother and fetus. Alpha-methyldopa is converted to methyl norepinephrine centrally to decrease the adrenergic outflow by alpha-2 agonistic action from the central nervous system, leading to reduced total peripheral resistance and decreased systemic blood pressure.

Labetalol: Labetalol acts by blocking both alpha and beta-adrenergic receptors, resulting in decreased peripheral vascular resistance without significant alteration of heart rate or cardiac output. Labetalol is now commonly used as a first-line treatment choice in pregnancy.

Hydralazine: one of the safer drugs in pregnancy. Hydralazine causes preferential dilatation of arteries over veins. It causes a selective decrease in vascular resistance in coronary, cerebral, and renal circulation, with a smaller effect in skin and muscle. Because of preferential dilatation of arterioles over veins, postural hypotension is not a common problem. Hydralazine-induced vasodilation causes reflex activation of the sympathetic system through baroreceptor-mediated reflexes resulting in increased plasma renin activity.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the rate of increment of head circumference in the first three months of life?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 cm per month

Head circumference is a key indicator of brain growth in early infancy, with the most rapid increase occurring in the first few months of life.

Key growth pattern:

• 0–3 months: increases by about 2 cm per month
• 3–6 months: increases by about 1 cm per month
• 6–12 months: increases by about 0.5 cm per month

Clinical importance:

• Rapid head growth reflects normal brain development
• Deviations may indicate conditions like microcephaly or hydrocephalus

Pearl PF1702: The Family as a Social Organization

* A family is a group of biologically related individuals living together under the same roof and eating from a common kitchen.

* It is the most primary and basic unit of all societies.

* The basic and arbitrary model of a family cycle has six phases:

* Types of families:

* A nuclear family or elementary family consists of only the married couple and their offspring while they are dependants.

* The term new family is applied when nuclear families are younger than 10 years and consist of parents and children.

* A joint family or extended family consists of a number of married couples and their children who live together in the same household with usually the men being related by blood. All property in joint families is held in common with the family income going into a common pocket. A senior male member is usually the head of the family who makes decisions.

* A three generation family is one where there are representatives from three different generations in one house.

* A communal family is one in which all the members play a part in its management.

* Functions of the family:

* Residence (patrilocal and matrilocal)

* Division of labour

* Reproduction and raising children

* Socialization and social care

* Economic functions

* Problems families are those that lag behind the rest of the community in terms of standard and quality of life of its members.

* Broken families are those in which the parental or family system has been disrupted by separation, divorce or death.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All are the symptoms of Gaisböck syndrome except?
questions.explanation: Gaisböck syndrome, also known as stress polycythemia or relative polycythemia, is a condition characterized by a pseudo-elevation in the hematocrit. Unlike Polycythemia Vera, the total red cell mass is actually normal; however, the "plasma volume" is significantly reduced, leading to hemoconcentration and a high hematocrit (erythrocytosis, Option B). This syndrome is typically seen in middle-aged, hard-driving, anxious men who are "obese" (Option D) and have a history of smoking and "hypertension." Therefore, hypotension (low blood pressure) is NOT a feature; in fact, hypertension is a defining characteristic of Gaisböck syndrome. The leukocyte counts (Option C) and platelet counts are typically normal, which helps distinguish it from true myeloproliferative disorders like Polycythemia Vera where these are often elevated. Management primarily involves addressing the underlying lifestyle factors, such as weight loss, smoking cessation, and blood pressure control, rather than phlebotomy. Thus, hypertension, not hypotension, is the hallmark clinical finding

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which two structures are shown as dysplastic on left side as compared to right side?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cochlea and vestibule

This is Mondini dysplasia (Mondini malformation), the most common congenital cochlear malformation.

Characteristic abnormalities include:

• Hypoplastic cochlea with only 1.5 turns (normal = 2.5 turns)
• Enlarged/dysplastic vestibule
• Vestibular aqueduct may also be enlarged, but the classic paired dysplastic structures are the cochlea and vestibule.

High-yield NEET PG points:

• Presents with congenital sensorineural hearing loss.
• Diagnosed on HRCT temporal bone and MRI.
• Predisposes to recurrent meningitis due to perilymphatic/CSF fistula.
• Cochlear implantation may be performed in appropriate candidates.

questions.text: Look at the image below and select the linear regression equation corresponding to the graph.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. y=11+2x

Among the given options, the equation y=11+2x corresponds to the linear regression equation of the form y=α + βx.

When 2 variables are correlated, such that the dependent variable is represented on the y-axis and the independent variable on the x-axis, then the value of y can be obtained by using the linear regression equation y = α + βx, where:

y - dependent variable

α - intercept

β - slope of the line

x - independent variable

In the equation y=11+2x, the intercept(α) = 11, while the  slope of the line (β) = 2.

Option A: y=10-x, represents an intercept of 10, and a slope of -1 indicating a negative correlation. However, the given image shows a positive correlation.

Options B and D: They do not fit the linear regression equation of the form y = α + βx.
