questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for evaluation of multiple episodes of seizures and hypoglycemia. A liver biopsy demonstrates hepatocytes with large glycogen stores. Biochemical analysis reveals glycogen with short outer chains. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cori disease

Cori disease (Glycogen storage disease type III) is caused by deficiency of the debranching enzyme, leading to accumulation of abnormally structured glycogen with short outer chains. Affected infants present with hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, seizures, and excess glycogen in hepatocytes. Unlike Von Gierke disease, gluconeogenesis is intact, so hypoglycemia is less severe.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Anderson disease: Defect in branching enzyme → long, poorly branched glycogen causing liver cirrhosis.

C. Von-Gierke disease: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency; glycogen structure is normal.

D. Pompe disease: Lysosomal acid maltase deficiency with cardiomegaly, not hypoglycemia.
questions.learning: Cori disease Cori disease (Glycogen storage disease type III) is caused by deficiency of the debranching enzyme, leading to accumulation of abnormally structured glycogen with short outer chains.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A young man sustained a scorpion sting 2 hours ago. On examination, his blood pressure is 108/ 60 mm Hg; HR, 72 beats/minute, and respiratory rate, 32 breaths/minute. He also complains of breathlessness. How do you manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prazosin

The drug used to manage this condition is prazosin as it can counteract the effects of breathlessness most probably caused by pulmonary edema.

The venom is a potent autonomic stimulator that causes the release of massive amounts of catecholamines from the adrenals. It also has a direct effect on the myocardium.

It can present as neurotoxicity with restlessness or seizure-like activity, abnormal oculomotor function, and loss of pharyngeal muscle control that leads to respiratory compromise. Tongue fasciculations and hypersalivation are also common. Cardiovascular toxicity from systemic envenomation includes tachycardia, hypertension, pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic shock.

If the scorpion has hemolytic venom, the reaction is mainly local, with edema, pain, and reddening. This usually lasts for one to two hours.

Treatment:

• Pain - Paracetamol, NSAIDs, or opioids
• Sedation for agitation, oculomotor abnormalities, uncoordinated neuromuscular activity, and muscle spasms - Benzodiazepines
• Hypertension and pulmonary edema - Prazosin counteracts the adrenergic surge that can lead to these effects
• Cardiogenic shock - Antivenom, prazosin, nitroglycerin, dobutamine
• Cholinergic effects - Atropine
• Supportive care, wound care
questions.learning: Prazosin — The drug used to manage this condition is prazosin as it can counteract the effects of breathlessness most probably caused by pulmonary edema.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Stage the bedsore in the following image:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 4

The given image shows complete skin loss that involves muscles and shows exposed bone indicating a stage 4 pressure sore.

Pressure sores are skin or soft tissue injuries that occur due to prolonged pressure over specific areas of the body. An external pressure of >30 mmHg leads to the formation of pressure sores. The common sites of pressure sores in decreasing frequency are the ischium, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleolus (lateral followed by medial), and occiput.

Pressure sores can be prevented with good skincare, the use of air-fluidized beds, special pressure-dispersion cushions, or foams. Repositioning the patient every two hours can lessen the pressure on the area.

Ulcers of stages 1 and 2 often do not require operative measures. They are managed with regular wound cleaning and dressing with a good antibiotic cover.

Stage 3 and 4 ulcers are adequately debrided, and vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) is used to promote the growth of granulation tissue required for surgical closure. Large skin flaps that have muscle with sensory innervation are best for reconstruction.
questions.learning: 4 The given image shows complete skin loss that involves muscles and shows exposed bone indicating a stage 4 pressure sore. Pressure sores are skin or soft tissue injuries that occur due to prolonged pressure over specific areas of the body.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A woman presents a few weeks after delivery with complaints of fever and bloody discharge from the nipple. On examination, a diffuse lump is palpated beneath the areola. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation—fever, bloody or purulent nipple discharge, and a diffuse lump occurring a few weeks postpartum—is highly suggestive of lactational mastitis. This condition is usually caused by milk stasis followed by bacterial infection, most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. Regarding the distractors, a galactocele (Option A) is a milk-retention cyst that presents as a painless, non-tender lump without fever or bloody discharge. Mondor disease (Option C) is a superficial thrombophlebitis of the breast veins, which presents as a palpable, cord-like structure rather than a diffuse inflammatory mass. Fibrocystic disease (Option D) causes cyclic pain and nodularity in response to menstruation and is not typically associated with the postpartum period or acute infection. Management of mastitis involves frequent breastfeeding and appropriate antibiotics to prevent the formation of a breast abscess
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation—fever, bloody or purulent nipple discharge, and a diffuse lump occurring a few weeks postpartum—is highly suggestive of lactational mastitis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A diabetic patient walks into your clinic and does "namaste". The image is given below. What could be the probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cheiroarthropathy

The image shows the namaste or prayer sign where the patient is unable to touch the palmer aspects of both hands and fingers together. The given scenario is suggestive of diabetic cheiroarthropathy.

Diabetic cheiroarthropathy/diabetic stiff hand syndrome is due to limited joint mobility as a result of the periarticular fibrosing syndrome. This is due to the non-enzymatic glycosylation of collagen. It is seen in both diabetes type 1 and type 2. Its prevalence increases with age and poor glycemic control.

Other options:

Flexor tenosynovitis or trigger finger occurs due to thickening and fibrosis of the tendon sheath.

Dupuytren's contracture is a result of fibrosis of palmar fascia and flexor tendons.

Note: Diabetes is also a known risk factor for Dupuytren's contracture but this condition leads to palmar nodules and flexion deformity of fingers. The image below shows Dupuytren's contracture:

Ankylosis results in limited joint mobility due to joint fusion as seen in osteoarthritis.
questions.learning: Cheiroarthropathy — The image shows the namaste or prayer sign where the patient is unable to touch the palmer aspects of both hands and fingers together.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The therapeutic index of a drug is a measure of:
questions.explanation: The therapeutic index (TI) is a quantitative measure of the safety of a drug. It expresses the margin between the dose that produces the desired therapeutic effect and the dose that causes toxicity. It is commonly defined as: A high therapeutic index indicates a wide safety margin, meaning the drug can be used relatively safely. In contrast, drugs with a narrow therapeutic index—such as digoxin, lithium, or warfarin—require close monitoring because small dose variations may result in toxicity. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Potency refers to the amount of drug needed to produce a given effect. 2. Efficacy refers to the maximum effect a drug can produce. 3. All of these is incorrect because TI does not measure potency or efficacy. Therefore, the therapeutic index is specifically a measure of drug safety
questions.learning: The therapeutic index (TI) is a quantitative measure of the safety of a drug. It expresses the margin between the dose that produces the desired therapeutic effect and the dose that causes toxicity.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During a preoperative assessment, a 45-year- old patient undergoes evaluation of the airway to predict the likelihood of difficulty during endotracheal intubation. On inspection, the soft palate, uvula, fauces (pillars), and tonsils are all fully visible without any obstruction. Based on these findings, which Mallampatti score does this airway correspond to?
questions.explanation: The Mallampati classification is used by anesthesiologists to predict the ease of endotracheal intubation. A Mallampati Score of 1 is assigned when there is complete visualization of the soft palate, uvula, fauces, and tonsillar pillars. This score indicates that intubation is likely to be straightforward. Score 2 (Option B) involves visualization of the soft palate and the majority of the uvula, but the pillars are obscured. Score 3 (Option C) allows for the visualization of the soft palate and the base of the uvula only. Score 4 (Option D) is assigned when the soft palate is not visible at all, and only the hard palate can be seen; this score predicts a "difficult airway." Accurate assessment requires the patient to sit upright, open their mouth wide, and protrude the tongue without phonating. Identifying a Score 1 allows the surgical team to proceed with standard intubation protocols, while higher scores necessitate preparation for advanced airway management techniques
questions.learning: The Mallampati classification is used by anesthesiologists to predict the ease of endotracheal intubation. A Mallampati Score of 1 is assigned when there is complete visualization of the soft palate, uvula, fauces, and tonsillar pillars.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: True about telomeres is:
options: Gradually decreasing length of telomeres with ageing
Telomerase is found in somatic cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gradually decreasing length of telomeres with ageing

Telomeres are repetitive non-coding DNA sequences (TTAGGG repeats) present at the ends of chromosomes that protect them from degradation and fusion.

With each cell division, due to the end-replication problem, telomeres gradually shorten, leading to:

• Cellular aging (senescence)
• Limited replicative capacity of somatic cells

Telomerase is an enzyme that adds telomeric repeats to chromosome ends, thereby maintaining telomere length. However:

• It is active mainly in germ cells, stem cells, and cancer cells
• It is absent or very low in most somatic cells

Why other options are incorrect:

• Increased telomere length with ageing: Opposite is true.
• Telomeres have coding sequences: They are non-coding repetitive DNA.
• Telomerase is found in somatic cells: Generally absent or minimal in somatic cells.
questions.learning: Gradually decreasing length of telomeres with ageing Telomeres are repetitive non-coding DNA sequences (TTAGGG repeats) present at the ends of chromosomes that protect them from degradation and fusion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: You are suturing a laceration in the ER using the interrupted suturing technique. What is the angle of needle placement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 90 degrees

In the interrupted suture technique, the needle is placed at an angle of 90 degrees (at right angles).

Interrupted sutures:

The needle should be inserted and exit the skin at right angles. It should be rotated through the tissue rather than dragged to prevent unnecessary enlargement of the needle hole. The distance from the suture entry point to the wound edge should be approximately equal to the depth of the sutured tissue. There should be twice this distance between two consecutive sutures.

The image below shows interrupted suture:

Other suturing techniques:

Continuous Suture: The first suture is inserted in a manner identical to that in an interrupted suture. The remaining sutures are inserted in a continuous manner until the far end of the wound is reached. Care should be taken to maintain the tension of the suture to avoid excessive tension or leaving it too slack; hence, the use of an assistant is warranted. An Aberdeen knot is used to secure the end of the suture.

Mattress sutures - They can be vertical or horizontal and are used to create either an eversion or inversion of the wound edges. The initial suture is inserted in the same way as an interrupted suture, but then, the needle either moves horizontally or vertically and traverses both edges of the wound once again, as seen in the image below. The main advantage of the mattress suture is that it produces an accurate approximation of wound edges, especially in settings where the edges are not easily approximated.

Subcuticular sutures: It is used for a better cosmetic appearance. It is also employed in situations where the edges of the wound are easily approximated. In this technique, small bites of the subcuticular tissues are taken on alternate sites of the wound, and then, they are gently pulled together. This causes an approximation of the wound edges without the risk of the cross-hatched markings of interrupted sutures.
questions.learning: 90 degrees In the interrupted suture technique, the needle is placed at an angle of 90 degrees (at right angles). Interrupted sutures: The needle should be inserted and exit the skin at right angles.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a case of shoulder dystocia, if the McRoberts maneuver fails, what is the next appropriate step in management?
questions.explanation: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency where the fetal head is delivered but the anterior shoulder remains stuck behind the maternal symphysis pubis. The first-line management is the McRoberts maneuver (hyperflexing the mother's hips). If this fails, the next immediate step is applying Suprapubic pressure (Rubin I maneuver) to help dislodge the shoulder. Woods maneuver (Option A, internal rotation) and Gaskin maneuver (Option B, all-fours position) are subsequent internal or positional maneuvers performed if suprapubic pressure is unsuccessful. The Zavanelli maneuver (Option D) is an extreme "last resort" involving pushing the head back into the uterus for an emergency C-section. A useful mnemonic for the sequence is ALARMER: Ask for help, Legs (McRoberts), Anterior shoulder pressure (Suprapubic), Rubun/Woods, Manual delivery of posterior arm, Episiotomy, Roll (Gaskin). Rapid and sequential application of these maneuvers is critical to prevent neonatal brachial plexus injury or hypoxic brain damage
questions.learning: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency where the fetal head is delivered but the anterior shoulder remains stuck behind the maternal symphysis pubis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. Although his vital signs are stable, he is unable to speak. He has no other neurological deficits, can write normally, and comprehends spoken instructions, responding appropriately by nodding. Based on these findings, where is the most likely site of the brain lesion?
questions.explanation: The patient demonstrates symptoms of Broca’s aphasia, also known as expressive or non-fluent aphasia. Key features include the inability to produce speech despite knowing what to say and having intact comprehension. The preservation of handwriting abilities and the ability to follow spoken commands rule out more global cognitive deficits or sensory aphasias. Broca's area is located in the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) of the dominant hemisphere. Wernicke's area (Option B) involvement would cause fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension. Lesions in the primary motor cortex (Option C) would typically cause physical paralysis (hemiplegia) rather than an isolated speech deficit. Brainstem lesions (Option D) usually result in multiple cranial nerve palsies or altered consciousness. Therefore, the clinical focus on motor speech production with preserved comprehension identifies Broca's area as the lesion site
questions.learning: The patient demonstrates symptoms of Broca’s aphasia, also known as expressive or non-fluent aphasia. Key features include the inability to produce speech despite knowing what to say and having intact comprehension.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man had an episode of jaundice due to HBV one year back. On follow-up now, he has normal levels of liver enzymes. His current profile is shown. • HBsAg: Positive • HBeAg: Negative • Anti-HBe: Positive • Anti-HBc IgG: Positive • Anti-HBc IgM: Negative • HBV DNA: Low • ALT: Normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic Hepatitis B

Key interpretation of markers:

• HBsAg positive (>1 year) → Chronic infection
• HBeAg negative + Anti-HBe positive → Low replication
• Anti-HBc IgG positive, IgM negative → Chronic (not acute)
• HBV DNA low + ALT normal → Inactive carrier state

Why not others?

• Resolved infection: HBsAg would be negative, Anti-HBs positive
• Acute HBV: Anti-HBc IgM positive
• Chronic Hep B (active): ↑ ALT, high HBV DNA, often HBeAg + (Negative HBeAg in Pre-core mutant)
questions.learning: Chronic Hepatitis B Key interpretation of markers: • HBsAg positive (>1 year) → Chronic infection • HBeAg negative + Anti-HBe positive → Low replication • Anti-HBc IgG positive, IgM negative → Chronic (not acute) • HBV DNA low + ALT normal → Inactive…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the order of insertion of muscles on Annulus of Zinn? 1. Medial rectus 2. Inferior rectus 3. Lateral rectus 4. Superior rectus
questions.explanation: The Annulus of Zinn (or common tendinous ring) is a circular fibrous structure at the apex of the orbit that serves as the origin for the four rectus muscles. In standard anatomical descriptions and medical board questions, the order of insertion around the ring is often listed as: 1. Medial Rectus (A) 2. Inferior Rectus (B) 3. Lateral Rectus (C) 4. Superior Rectus (D) This follows a clockwise or counter-clockwise sequence around the optic foramen. This anatomical landmark is critical because it surrounds the optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery. Additionally, several cranial nerves (III, VI, and the nasociliary branch of V) pass through the ring to enter the orbit. Options B, C, and D provide incorrect sequences of these muscles. Understanding the relationships at the orbital apex is essential for diagnosing orbital apex syndrome and planning complex orbital surgeries. The annulus acts as a structural anchor, ensuring the coordinated movement of the eye by the extraocular muscles
questions.learning: The Annulus of Zinn (or common tendinous ring) is a circular fibrous structure at the apex of the orbit that serves as the origin for the four rectus muscles.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to the Open Vial Policy, which of the following—MR vaccine or Pentavalent vaccine—can be reused after opening, and which one must be discarded once the vial is opened?
questions.explanation: The WHO Open Vial Policy allows certain multi-dose vaccine vials to be reused for up to 28 days after opening, provided they are stored under proper cold chain conditions (2–8°C) and the Vaccine Vial Monitor (VVM) is intact. The Pentavalent vaccine, which is a liquid formulation containing preservatives, falls under this policy and can be reused. Conversely, the MR (Measles-Rubella) vaccine is a lyophilized (freeze-dried) powder that contains no preservatives. Once reconstituted with diluent, it must be discarded within 4 hours or at the end of the immunization session, whichever comes first. Other vaccines that must be discarded and cannot be reused include BCG and JE vaccines. Therefore, Option A correctly identifies that the MR vial must be discarded while the Pentavalent vial can be kept for subsequent sessions
questions.learning: The WHO Open Vial Policy allows certain multi-dose vaccine vials to be reused for up to 28 days after opening, provided they are stored under proper cold chain conditions (2–8°C) and the Vaccine Vial Monitor (VVM) is intact.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An HIV-positive patient presents with the following finding. What is the diagnosis & WHO clinical stage of HIV?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral candidiasis & WHO Stage 3

Oral candidiasis (Thrush) is categorized as WHO clinical stage 3.

Oral Candidiasis (Thrush), and oral hairy leukoplakia, are oral lesions characterized in WHO clinical Stage 3. They generally occur in patients with CD4+ T cell counts of <300/μL.

Differentiating oral candidiasis and oral hairy leukoplakia:

* Oral Candidiasis (Thrush) appears as a white, cheesy exudate, on an erythematous mucosa in the posterior oropharynx. The diagnosis is made by direct examination of pseudohyphal elements.

* Oral hairy leukoplakia presents as white, frondlike lesions, generally along the lateral borders of the tongue and sometimes on the adjacent buccal mucosa(image below). Despite its name, oral hairy leukoplakia is not considered premalignant. Lesions are associated with immunosupression and Ebstein-Barr virus (EBV).

Pearl PF1360: Clinical stages of HIV in children/ infants

Stage 1

* Asymptomatic

* Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy

Stage 2

* Unexplained persistent hepatosplenomegaly

* Papular pruritic eruptions

* Extensive wart virus infection

* Extensive molluscum contagiosum

* Recurrent oral ulcerations

* Unexplained persistent parotid enlargement

* Linear gingival erythema

* Herpes zoster

* Recurrent or chronic upper respiratory infections (otitis media, otorrhoea, sinusitis, tonsilitis)

* Fungal nail infections

Stage 3

* Unexplained moderate malnutrition not adequately responding to standard therapy

* Unexplained persistent diarrhea (14 days or more)

* Unexplained persistent fever (above 37.6 °C intermittent or constant, for longer than one month)

* Persistent oral candidiasis (after first 6-8 weeks of life)

* Oral hairy leukoplakia

* Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis/periodontitis

* Lymph node TB

* Pulmonary TB

* Severe recurrent bacterial pneumonia

* Symptomatic lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis

* Chronic HIV-associated lung disease including bronchiectasis

* Unexplained anemia (<8 g/dL), neutropenia (<0.5 x 109/L) or chronic thrombocytopenia (<50 × 109/L)

Stage 4

* Unexplained severe wasting, stunting or malnutrition not responding to standard therapy

* Pneumocystis pneumonia

* Recurrent severe bacterial infections (e.g., empyema, pyomyositis, bone or joint infection, meningitis, but excluding pneumonia)

* Chronic Herpes Simplex infection; (oro-labial or cutaneous of more than one month's duration or visceral at any site)

* Extrapulmonary TB and disseminated non-tuberculosis mycobacterial infection

* Kaposi Sarcoma

* Oesophageal candidiasis (or candidiasis of trachea, bronchi or lungs)

* Central nervous system toxoplasmosis (after one month of life)

* HIV encephalopathy

* Cytomegalovirus infection; retinitis or CMV infection affecting another organ, with onset at age over 1 month)

* Extrapulmonary cryptococcosis (including meningitis)

* Disseminated endemic mycosis (extrapulmonary histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis)

* Chronic cryptosporidiosis and isosporiasis

* Cerebral or B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma

* Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

* Symptomatic HIV-associated nephropathy or HIV-associated cardiomyopathy
questions.learning: Oral candidiasis & WHO Stage 3 Oral candidiasis (Thrush) is categorized as WHO clinical stage 3. Oral Candidiasis (Thrush), and oral hairy leukoplakia, are oral lesions characterized in WHO clinical Stage 3.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 61-year-old university professor presents with a loss of vision in his left eye. He describes the sensation as a curtain being drawn over his affected eye. The patient had a history of flashing lights and floaters 7 days back. He also gives a history of having cataract surgery in the same eye 3 weeks ago. What is the likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retinal detachment

The patient with sudden painless loss of vision has been complaining of floaters and curtain falling sign with a recent history of cataract surgery suggests the diagnosis of retinal detachment.

Retinal detachment occurs due to the accumulation of fluid between the neurosensory retina(NSR) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) due to a retinal tear.

Types of Retinal detachment:

A. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment- fluid accumulates after a break (tear) occurs in the retina.

Causes include High myopes, Retinoschisis-splitting of neurosensory retina plus vitreous degeneration (typical retinoschisis-split at the level of the outer plexiform layer, atypical retinoschisis-split at the level of the nerve fibre layer), trauma, pseudophakia, and aphakia.

The most dangerous type of retinal break is horseshoe tear and the most dangerous location of the retinal break is the superior-temporal retina.

Clinical features include photopsia, floaters, and visual field defects (a black curtain/veil in front of the eye).

Signs

* Hypotony- as the liquefied vitreous in the subretinal space is absorbed through the RPE.

* Shafer sign-pigments in the anterior vitreous (tobacco dusting) are a feature of fresh retinal detachment.

* The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is corrugated with undulations.

Treatment

* Prophylactic laser barrage

* Scleral buckling

* Pneumatic retinopexy

* Pars plana vitrectomy

B. Tractional retinal detachment: Fibro-vascular membranes in the vitreous due to long-standing retinal neovascularization exert traction on the retina.

Causes include proliferative diabetic retinopathy, central retinal venous occlusion, Eale's disease, retinopathy of Prematurity(ROP)

The detached retina is concave in configuration. No breaks are seen

Treatment

* Pars plana vitrectomy with endo photocoagulation.

C. Exudative retinal detachment: Exudative fluid from the choroid, collects in the subretinal space leading to retinal detachment.

Causes include inflammatory conditions like choroiditis, posterior scleritis choroidal tumours like melanoma, toxaemia of pregnancy, malignant hypertension, Coat's disease

Floaters due to vitreous but no photopsia and visual field defect is seen

The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is smooth. No break is seen. Shifting fluid is seen.

Treatment

* Systemic steroids

* Treatment of the cause

The image below shows a fundus which reveals retinal detachment inferiorly from 3-9 o'clock with a tear at 3:30

Pearl PF1407: Causes of loss of vision

Features
Cause

Sudden painless loss of vision

• Central retinal artery occlusion
• Massive vitreous hemorrhage
• Retinal detachment involving macula
• Ischemic central retinal vein occlusion

Sudden painless onset of diminution of vision

• Central serous retinopathy
• Optic neuritis
• Methyl alcohol amblyopia
• Non-ischemic central retinal vein occlusion

Sudden painful loss of vision

• Acute congestive glaucoma
• Acute iridocyclitis
• Injury to eyeball

Gradual painless diminution of vision

• Corneal dystrophy
• Senile cataract
• Primary open angle glaucoma
• Optic atrophy
• ARMD
• Refractive error
• Diabetic retinopathy

Gradual painful diminution of vision

• Chronic iridocyclitis
• Corneal ulceration
questions.learning: Retinal detachment — The patient with sudden painless loss of vision has been complaining of floaters and curtain falling sign with a recent history of cataract surgery suggests the diagnosis of retinal detachment.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A young child with congenital hydrocephalus was treated with a successful ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt. Four months post surgical repair, the child presented with fever, nuchal rigidity, and irritability. You suspect meningitis. What is the next best step?
options: Check shunt patency by nuclear study
Blood culture and take CSF sample from shunt tap
Blood culture and take CSF sample by lumbar puncture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blood culture and take CSF sample from shunt tap

In a child with suspected shunt-associated meningitis, the next best step useful in confirming the diagnosis is by taking a blood culture and a CSF sample from a shunt tap is preferable to a lumbar puncture (LP) (option D).

Shunt aspiration allows for better detection of microbes and avoids the need for a separate procedure, reducing the risk of contamination. VP shunt fluid is obtained from a subcutaneous reservoir using a 25-gauge needle.

Bacterial meningitis may be caused due to meningococcus, streptococcus pneumoniae, or Haemophilus influenzae type b. The clinical presentation of meningitis in children with VP shunts is similar to acute bacterial meningitis in other children. These include fever, rash, vomiting, and refusal to feed. Clinical signs of meningeal irritation (Kernig and Brudzinski signs) are not usually seen in infants.

Blood cultures should be done in all cases of suspected meningitis. Treatment is aggressive with systemic antibiotics. Third-generation cephalosporins along with vancomycin can be used. Wait and watch policy is not followed (option A).

A ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is used to drain excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) due to an obstruction in the normal outflow or there is a decreased absorption of the fluid. A silicone rubber device with a proximal portion inserted into the ventricle, a unidirectional valve, and a distal segment is commonly used for shunt placement.

Complications of the shunting procedure include infection due to skin flora entering the shunt (Staphylococcus epidermidis), intracerebral or intraventricular hemorrhage, shunt over drainage, shunt nephritis, shunt disconnection, obstruction, inguinal hernia, and seizures.

Shunt patency studies are performed to determine whether shunt revision surgery is needed in the malfunctioned ventriculoperitoneal shunt. This is done using radionucleotides (option B)

Hydrocephalus represents a group of conditions that result from impaired circulation or absorption of CSF.

Causes of communicating hydrocephalus (increased production or reduced absorption) includes choroid plexus papilloma, meningeal malignancy, and meningitis. Causes of noncommunicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus include aqueductal stenosis, infectious (toxoplasmosis, mumps), Chiari malformation, Dandy-Walker malformation, and mass lesions.

In infants, signs include rapid head enlargement, bulging fontanel, and downward eye deviation. Long-tract signs and dilated scalp veins may also be observed. Older children may experience irritability, lethargy, poor appetite, vomiting, and headaches. Diagnosis can be done using MRI, ultrasound, and measurement of ICP.

Medical management with medications like acetazolamide and furosemide can provide temporary relief, but long-term outcomes are often unsatisfactory. Most cases require surgical intervention, such as ventriculoperitoneal shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy.
questions.learning: Blood culture and take CSF sample from shunt tap — In a child with suspected shunt-associated meningitis, the next best step useful in confirming the diagnosis is by taking a blood culture and a CSF sample from a shunt tap is preferable to a lumbar…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is an inhibitor of the intestinal mucosal transporter NPC1L1, responsible for the absorption of dietary and biliary cholesterol?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ezetimibe

Ezetimibe is a cholesterol absorption inhibitor that selectively blocks the Niemann–Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) transporter on the brush border of enterocytes in the small intestine. This reduces the absorption of dietary and biliary cholesterol, leading to decreased hepatic cholesterol stores and increased LDL receptor expression, thereby lowering LDL cholesterol.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Atorvastatin: An HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) that decreases hepatic cholesterol synthesis, not intestinal absorption.
• B. Fenofibrate: A PPAR-α agonist that primarily lowers triglycerides by increasing lipoprotein lipase activity.
• C. Metformin: An oral antidiabetic drug that reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves insulin sensitivity; it has no effect on NPC1L1.
questions.learning: Ezetimibe Ezetimibe is a cholesterol absorption inhibitor that selectively blocks the Niemann–Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) transporter on the brush border of enterocytes in the small intestine.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
A pregnant woman presents with fever, retroorbital pain, headache, pulsatile proptosis of the right eye, and tinnitus. BP and fundus were normal. Which of the following structures are involved?

A. Abducens nerve
B. Oculomotor nerve
C. Internal carotid artery
D. Cavernous sinus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A,B,C,D

The structures affected in this patient are A, B, C and D.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) is a septic thrombus formed in the cavernous sinus. It spreads from infection of the sinuses, teeth, ears, nose, and skin of the face.

It presents as fever, severe headache, supraorbital pain, seizures, and edema in the mastoid region. Eye signs include proptosis, chemosis, and diplopia due to ophthalmoplegia from the involvement of oculomotor (CN-III), trochlear (CN-IV), and abducens nerve (CN-VI). Absence of corneal sensation due to the involvement of the ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve (CN-Va). Ipsilateral ptosis, dilated pupil, and absence of direct and consensual pupillary right reflex due to oculomotor nerve palsy. Pulsatile proptosis occurs with the involvement of the internal carotid artery.

Investigation using brain magnetic resonance imaging or magnetic resonance venography should be done urgently. Following early diagnosis, management of cavernous sinus thrombosis typically includes intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, analgesics, anti-inflammatory drugs, and anticoagulants.
questions.learning: A,B,C,D — The structures affected in this patient are A, B, C and D. Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) is a septic thrombus formed in the cavernous sinus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient presents with difficulty in smoothly transitioning between voluntary movements, along with involuntary, uncontrolled movements of the hands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Difficulty in switching between rapid alternating movements, such as pronation and supination of the hands, is termed dysdiadochokinesis. This clinical sign is a classic manifestation of cerebellar dysfunction or ataxia. Intentional tremor (Option B) also occurs in cerebellar disease but specifically refers to tremors that worsen as the hand approaches a voluntary target. Metamorphosis (Option C) typically refers to visual distortions (metamorphopsia) and is unrelated to motor coordination. Resting tremor (Option D) is characteristic of Parkinson's disease, occurring when the limb is at rest and improving with voluntary movement. Other cerebellar signs include ataxia (drunken gait), dysmetria (overshooting), and dysarthria (jumbled speech). The inability to perform these smooth, rapid alternating movements helps localize the lesion to the cerebellum, which normally coordinates the timing and sequencing of motor activities
questions.learning: Difficulty in switching between rapid alternating movements, such as pronation and supination of the hands, is termed dysdiadochokinesis. This clinical sign is a classic manifestation of cerebellar dysfunction or ataxia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 58-year-old male presents to a PHC for a routine check-up. His blood pressure readings on two separate occasions are 148/90 mmHg and 152/96 mmHg. He is asymptomatic and has no known comorbidities. What is the most appropriate next step in management according to current hypertension guidelines?
options: Initiate treatment only if BP exceeds 160/100 mmHg
Start Amlodipine 5 mg once daily and advise lifestyle modification
Refer to a higher center for further evaluation
Start the patient on IV anti-hypertensive drugs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start Amlodipine 5 mg once daily and advise lifestyle modification

Two readings ≥140/90 mmHg confirm Stage 2 hypertension on office measurements. Current practice recommends initiating pharmacotherapy along with lifestyle modification, even in asymptomatic patients.

A long-acting calcium channel blocker (Amlodipine) is an appropriate first-line agent.

IV drugs and referral are unnecessary in stable, uncomplicated hypertension.

A) Initiate treatment only if BP >160/100

This was older guideline practice.

Current recommendations treat ≥140/90.

C) Refer to higher center

Not needed because:

• Patient is stable
• No complications

Primary care can manage.

D) Start IV antihypertensives

Used only in: Hypertensive emergencies

Examples:

• Stroke
• Aortic dissection
• Pulmonary edema

This patient is asymptomatic.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 33-year-old woman presents with complaints of progressive loss of vision in the right halves of both eyes. Where is the lesion located in the optic pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left optic tract

The patient presenting with progressive visual loss in the right halves of both eyes is suggestive of right homonymous hemianopia. The site of the lesion in this case is the left optic tract.

Here, vision is lost in the right half of both eyes, which means:

• in the left eye, the nasal visual field is lost, and
• in the right eye, the temporal visual field is lost.

It means left temporal and right nasal fibers are destroyed which leads to right homonymous hemianopia. Anatomically, this can be explained by the fact that each optic tract contains fibers from the ipsilateral temporal half of the retina and the contralateral nasal half of the retina.

Optic tract lesions can occur due to pituitary adenomas (most common), craniopharyngioma, tumors of optic thalamus, large aneurysm of superior cerebellar or posterior cerebral arteries, demyelinating diseases, and infarction.

Other options:

Option B - Lesion at right visual cortex causes left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

Option C - Lesion at optic chiasma causes bitemporal hemianopia.

Option D - Lesion at the right optic nerve causes blindness in the right eye.
questions.learning: Left optic tract — The patient presenting with progressive visual loss in the right halves of both eyes is suggestive of right homonymous hemianopia. The site of the lesion in this case is the left optic tract.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: For what population size is an urban Primary Health Centre (PHC) typically intended?
questions.explanation: Under the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) in India, the health infrastructure is tailored to the high density of city populations. An Urban Primary Health Centre (U-PHC) is established to cater to a population of approximately 50,000 people. These centers serve as the first point of contact for the urban poor, particularly those living in slums or unauthorized colonies. This differs from rural norms, where a PHC covers 20,000 in hilly/tribal areas or 30,000 in plain areas. A population of 100,000 (Option B) is typically the benchmark for an Urban Community Health Centre (U-CHC), which provides more specialized services and indoor beds. Options C and D (250,000 and 200,000) do not correspond to the standard planning norms for primary health units in India. The U-PHC focuses on delivering essential services like immunization, maternal care, and screening for non-communicable diseases, ensuring that healthcare is accessible within a manageable distance for urban residents
questions.learning: Under the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) in India, the health infrastructure is tailored to the high density of city populations. An Urban Primary Health Centre (U-PHC) is established to cater to a population of approximately 50,000 people.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All the following are criteria for SIRS, except ______.
options: Temperature >38 degree celsius or <36 degree celsius
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Systolic BP <90 mmHg

Systolic BP <90 mmHg is not a criterion for SIRS (systemic inflammatory response syndrome).

SIRS is diagnosed when two of the following are present:

• Hyperthermia (>38 degrees celsius) or hypothermia (<36 degrees celsius)
• Tachypnoea (>20/min) or arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO2) < 32 mmHg
• Tachycardia (>90/min)
• White cell count >12 x 109/litre or <4 x 109/litre or >10% Band forms

Sepsis is SIRS with a documented infection.
questions.learning: Systolic BP 38 degrees celsius) or hypothermia ( 20/min) or arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO2) 90/min) • White cell count >12 x 109/litre or 10% Band forms Sepsis is SIRS with a documented infection.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common cause of macrocytic anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alcohol

Alcohol is the most common cause of macrocytic anaemia.

Macrocytic anemia can be megaloblastic anemia and non-megaloblastic anemia. Alcohol causes non megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.

Other causes of macrocytic anaemia:

* Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency

* Bone marrow disorders

* Liver disease

* Drug-induced

* HIV

* Multiple myeloma

* Complication of bariatric surgery

Megaloblastic anemia is a type of macrocytic anemia with impaired nucleic acid metabolism. Nuclear maturation lags behind cytoplasmic maturation. The causes include:

* Vitamin B12 deficiency

* Folate deficiency

* Drugs (Methotrexate)

Vitamin B12 or cobalamin is a water-soluble vitamin that is derived from animal products such as red meat, dairy, and eggs. Other causes of B12 deficiency includes

* Malabsorption (Pernicious anemia)

* Total or partial gastrectomy

* Ileal resection

* Tropical sprue

Clinical features of cyanocobalamin and folate deficiency (megaloblastic anemia) include:

* Anorexia, weight loss, diarrhea, or constipation

* Oral manifestations: glossitis, angular cheilosis

* Mild fever in more severely anemic patients

* Jaundice (unconjugated)

* Reversible melanin skin hyperpigmentation

* Bruising (thrombocytopenia) and infections (low leucocyte count)

* Complications in pregnancy: recurrent fetal loss and neural tube defects

* Cardiovascular disease: cerebrovascular, peripheral vascular, and coronary heart disease with deep vein thrombosis

* Neurologic manifestations: Bilateral peripheral neuropathy or degeneration of the posterior and pyramidal tracts of the spinal cord (SACDSC). Seen in only B12 deficiency.

* Psychiatric disturbances
questions.learning: Alcohol Alcohol is the most common cause of macrocytic anaemia. Macrocytic anemia can be megaloblastic anemia and non-megaloblastic anemia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presents with a pterygium that has been steadily progressing towards the pupillary area. What is the best means of management in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Excision with conjunctival autograft

The best mode of management in the given options for progressive pterygium is excision with conjunctival autograft.

A pterygium is a degenerative subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a connective tissue disorder and is never inflammatory. Histologically, it comprises elastotic degenerative changes in vascularised subepithelial stromal collagen. It is most commonly seen on the nasal aspect of the eye. It is made up of three parts:

* cap (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge)

* head

* body

Patients may be asymptomatic or present with irritation, grittiness, or episodes of inflammation. As they enlarge, it may obstruct vision and lead to astigmatism.

Treatment:

* A pterygium is best left alone unless:

* It is progressing towards the pupillary area

* Causes excessive astigmatism

* Restricts ocular motility

* Causes disfigurement.

* Excision: A simple pterygium excision often leads to a high chance of recurrence. Measures to prevent recurrence are:

* Mitomycin C drops- applied pre-operatively/ intra-operatively or post-operatively. However, it may lead to complications like scleral necrosis, cataract, and iritis and should be used judiciously.

* Beta-radiation applied postoperatively to the pterygium base was popular for many years, but is associated with late scleral necrosis.

* Conjunctival autografting- limbal tissue from the same or other eye is grafted and secured with fibrin glue or sutures.

* Amniotic membrane graft

* Peripheral lamellar keratoplasty if the lesion is deep.

Currently, the most widely used techniques are conjunctival autografting, amniotic membrane transplantation, and mitomycin-C application either preoperatively or postoperatively (can be applied intraoperatively also), of which conjunctival autografting has fewer recurrence rates and is a simple and quick procedure that reduces the risk of granuloma formation, scleral thinning, and necrosis.

Note:

A combination of conjunctival autografting with intraoperative mitomycin C is the most preferred as it has the least recurrence rates as per studies.
questions.learning: Excision with conjunctival autograft — The best mode of management in the given options for progressive pterygium is excision with conjunctival autograft.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Focal seizures may be associated with which of the following? 1. Jacksonian march 2. Todd’s paralysis 3. Epilepsia partialis continua Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Focal (partial) seizures originate from a localized region of one cerebral hemisphere and may remain focal or progress to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures. They are associated with several characteristic clinical phenomena.

• 1. Jacksonian march: True.

• Refers to the orderly spread of clonic movements from one body part to adjacent parts (e.g., fingers → hand → arm → face) due to the sequential spread of epileptic activity along the primary motor cortex.

• 2. Todd’s paralysis: True.

• A transient focal neurological deficit (usually weakness) occurring after a focal motor seizure.
• Typically lasts minutes to 48 hours and resolves completely.
• It may mimic an acute stroke but is self-limiting.

• 3. Epilepsia partialis continua: True.

• A rare form of focal motor status epilepticus characterized by continuous or repetitive focal clonic muscle jerks involving one part of the body for hours, days, or even longer, with preserved awareness in many patients.
• Common causes include Rasmussen encephalitis, stroke, cortical dysplasia, tumors, and metabolic disorders.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Focal (partial) seizures originate from a localized region of one cerebral hemisphere and may remain focal or progress to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following healthcare personnel does not function at the village level?
questions.explanation: The Indian public health system utilizes various workers to deliver services at the grassroots level. The Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) is a key provider who primarily operates at the Sub-centre level, serving as a link between the village and the Primary Health Center. While she makes village visits, her official headquarters and primary work location are the Sub-centre, not the village itself. In contrast, the Anganwadi Worker (AWW) (Option B) is a village-level worker under the ICDS program focusing on nutrition. The Trained Birth Attendant (TBA) (Option C) and Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) (Option D) are strictly village-based workers who live and work within the community they serve. ASHAs, in particular, are the face of the National Health Mission at the doorstep of the rural population. Therefore, because the ANM represents the first formal link in the facility-based hierarchy rather than community-based living, she is not classified as village-level

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A soldier posted in Siachen is brought to you in the ER. In order to rule out hypothermia, how do you best measure his temperature?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rectal

In the given clinical scenario rectal temperature would be the preferred site to measure the core body temperature.

During low or high temperatures like in Siachen, the axillary and the oral temperatures are highly misleading and should not be used to measure the core body temperatures

Infrared tympanic thermometer measures the temperature of the eardrum which is representative of core body temperature. However, more often the thermometer is not inserted adequately or for safety reasons, they are manufactured in such a way that they do not reach deep into the ear canal, or the ear canal contains cerumen which can disturb the measurement. Hence the infrared thermometer more commonly delivers the temperature of ear canal cerumen and hence not a reliable method of measuring the core body temperature.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman undergoes screening mammography. The figure suggests a likely diagnosis of: (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Involuting Fibroadenoma

The mammogram shows coarse, popcorn-like calcifications within a well-circumscribed mass. This characteristic "popcorn" pattern of calcification is the classic radiographic appearance of an involuting fibroadenoma. These benign breast tumors typically develop in younger women and often undergo calcification during the involution process as women age, particularly after menopause.

Visual Support: The image demonstrates the typical popcorn calcification pattern within a well-defined mass - the hallmark radiographic appearance of an involuting fibroadenoma.

Other Options:

Option A. Intraductal Carcinoma Breast - Incorrect because DCIS typically presents with fine\, linear\, branching or pleomorphic microcalcifications in a segmental or ductal distribution\, not the coarse popcorn-like calcifications seen here.

Option C. Fibroadenosis - Incorrect as fibroadenosis (fibrocystic changes) typically shows multiple small cysts and areas of increased density without the characteristic popcorn calcifications visible in this image.

Option D. Fat Necrosis - Incorrect because fat necrosis typically appears as an oil cyst with a thin calcified rim\, or as spiculated masses with architectural distortion. It lacks the typical popcorn calcification pattern seen in this mammogram.

Educational Objective:

Coarse "popcorn" calcifications within a well-circumscribed mass on mammography are pathognomonic for an involuting fibroadenoma, representing the degenerative calcification of a previously non-calcified fibroadenoma.
questions.learning: Involuting Fibroadenoma — The mammogram shows coarse, popcorn-like calcifications within a well-circumscribed mass. This characteristic "popcorn" pattern of calcification is the classic radiographic appearance of an involuting fibroadenoma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In which of the following diseases is collagen cross linking treatment used for ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratoconus

Collagen cross-linking therapy is used for keratoconus.

Riboflavin eye drops are used in collagen cross-linking therapy for keratoconus. The corneal epithelium is removed and riboflavin eye drops are instilled until the cornea is saturated with riboflavin. The cornea is then exposed to UVA and covered using a soft bandage lens. Riboflavin acts as a photo sensitizing agent and promotes cross-linking of collagen fibers. This stabilizes the corneal stroma and delays the progression of the disease.

Keratoconus:

Clinical Presentation:

* Young male with constantly changing power of glasses with myopia & high cylinder due to myopic astigmatism.

* Corneal topography shows an asymmetric bow tie pattern with the skewed radial axis.

Morphological pattern (3 types):

* Nipple cone (<5mm)

* Oval cone (5-6mm)

* Globus cone (>6mm)

Signs:

* Munson sign

* Enlarged corneal nerves

* Oil droplet reflex

* Rizutti sign (conical reflection on nasal cornea when a penlight is shone from the temporal side)

* Acute Hydrops (percolation of aqueous into stroma through breaks in DM)

* Fleischer ring (at keratoconus base, a brownish ring, probably due to haemosiderin, may form in the epithelium encircling the cone)

* Scissor reflex on retinoscopy

* Vogt striae in slit lamp

Important associations:

* Marfans, Down’s, EDS syndrome

* Osteogenesis imperfecta, MVP

* RP, Leber congenital amurosis

* VKC, aniridia, ectopia lentis

Investigations:

* Corneal topography

* Pachymetry

* Keratometry:

* Steep cornea

* Bow tie pattern

* Paracentral thinning of the cornea (thinnest point)

KISA index is used to classify Keratoconus.

Treatment:

* Spectacle correction

* Contact lens can be used include:

* Rigid Gas Permeable

* Rose K lenses

* Soper lenses

* Corneal collagen cross-linking with Riboflavin

* Intacs

* Surgery
questions.learning: Keratoconus Collagen cross-linking therapy is used for keratoconus. Riboflavin eye drops are used in collagen cross-linking therapy for keratoconus.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Resistance to the airflow through the tube shown below is primarily because of :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diameter

The airway device shown in the image is an endotracheal tube and the resistance to the airflow through it primarily depends on diameter(Internal diameter).

* The size of an endotracheal tube usually refers to the internal diameter in mm. Rarely the French scale is used where the size corresponds to the external diameter multiplied by 3.

* For adults, usually, a 7-mm is used for women and a 7.5 or 8-mm ETT is used for men.

* Generally, high-volume, low-pressure cuffed tubes are used in adults, and cuffless tubes are used in neonates and infants.

* Besides age, the choice of an endotracheal tube also depends on the presence of airway pathologies and the reason behind the placement of the tube.

* Smaller-sized tubes lead to increase airway resistance and increased work breathing.

* Larger tubes have a higher risk of laryngeal and tracheal trauma and sore throat.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The functioning of the thyroid involves the transport of iodine from the blood to the thyroid follicle. Iodine is transported from the follicle to the colloid. Which pump or channel is for transport of iodine from the follicle to the colloid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pendrin

The channel needed for the transport of iodine from the follicle to the colloid is Pendrin.

Steps in synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormone:

• Iodide uptake: The basolateral sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) actively takes up I-(iodide) from the circulation into the follicular cells. It is then transported into the colloid through a pendrin (chloride-iodide) transporter
• Thyroglobulin synthesis: Thyroglobulin (Tg), is a large glycoprotein rich in tyrosine residues. It is synthesized by follicular cells.
• Iodination of Tg: This is regulated by the thyroid peroxidase (TPO) enzyme. TPO has three functions:
• Oxidation: TPO oxidizes I- to I2 (iodine)  in the presence of H2O2
• Organification: TPO links tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin with iodine (I2) to form monoiodotyrosine (MIT), diiodotyrosine (DIT)
• Coupling reactions: TPO combines iodinated tyrosine residues to make MIT + DIT = T3 (triiodothyronine), DIT + DIT = T4 (tetraiodothyronine)
• Storage: Thyroid hormones are bound to thyroglobulin and stored in the follicular lumen as colloids. The colloid has hormone reserves for 2-3 months
• Release: Iodinated thyroglobulin is taken up by the thyroid follicles via endocytosis and fuses with lysosomes. It is cleaved by lysosomal proteolytic enzymes into MIT, DIT, T3, and T4. T4 (80%) and T3 (20%) are released into the blood
• Peripheral T3 conversion: T4 undergoes deiodination in extrathyroidal tissue to form T3, which is the active form of the hormone.

Pendred syndrome: Pendrin is present in the thyroid gland and inner ear. The mutation causes goiter and sensorineural hearing loss.

Other options

Option A: Sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is responsible for transporting iodine from the bloodstream into the thyroid follicular cell, not into the colloid. It works by bringing in iodine along with sodium from the bloodstream into the follicle.

Option B: Calmodulin is structurally and functionally related to troponin. In place of troponin, smooth muscle cells contain a large amount of the regulatory protein calmodulin; it is different in the manner in which it initiates contraction. Calmodulin initiates contraction by activating the myosin light chain kinase.

Option C: Claudin is a transmembrane protein involved in the formation of tight junctions.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: DNA is present in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mitochondria

Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles found in eukaryotic cells. They have their own small circular DNA, known as mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which encodes a limited number of genes.

mtDNA is inherited maternally and is essential for the synthesis of certain proteins involved in energy production through oxidative phosphorylation.

The presence of DNA in mitochondria is a key characteristic that distinguishes them from other cellular structures.

Other Options:

*

Lysosome: Cellular organelles containing enzymes that degrade cellular waste and foreign substances.

*

Cytoplasm: Region within a cell that surrounds the nucleus and organelles. While some cellular activities occur in the cytoplasm, DNA is primarily housed in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells.

* Endoplasmic reticulum: Complex network of membranes involved in protein synthesis, lipid metabolism, and calcium storage. It does not typically contain DNA.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought to the outpatient department by his mother with irritability, poor school performance, and a history of recurrent ear infections. Otoscopic examination shows a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid behind it. There is no blood clot present in the ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Otitis media with effusion

In the given clinical scenario, the patient's history of recurrent ear infections and dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid and absent blood clots points to the diagnosis of otitis media with effusion (OME).

Serous otitis media, also known as secretory otitis media, otitis media with effusion (OME), mucoid otitis media, or glue ear, is characterised by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis, tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, tumors of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, or viral infections).

Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild ear aches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.

* Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Hearing tests suggestive of conductive hearing loss as seen in serous otitis media:

* Rinne negative (BC>AC).

* Weber—lateralized towards the worse ear

* Audiogram—AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present

* Impedance audiometry—flat curve (reduced compliance, shift to the negative side)

A B-type tympanogram is expected in a case of serous otitis media. Here, compliance decreases. The fluid accumulation causes decreased mobility of the tympanic membrane, leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve. This results in a B-type tympanogram, as shown below:

Note: The tympanograph is Flat when there is Fluid in the middle ear.

Other options:

Option B: Cartwheel appearance is seen in acute otitis media. It is an acute infection of the middle ear by pyogenic organisms. It presents with marked earache, and hearing loss is seen in later stages.

Option C: Cholesteatoma is an abnormal collection of keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid that leads to bone destruction. It can be congenital or acquired, with acquired cases arising from tympanic membrane retraction or epithelial migration through a perforation. The expanding mass erodes nearby structures, potentially causing serious complications.

Option D: Tympanosclerosis involves calcification and fibrosis of the tympanic membrane, usually following chronic otitis media. It does not cause bone erosion or a retraction pocket.
questions.learning: Otitis media with effusion — In the given clinical scenario, the patient's history of recurrent ear infections and dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid and absent blood clots points to the diagnosis of otitis media with effusion (OME).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: To establish the cause of death, a post-mortem examination was performed on an 82-year-old man. Histopathological evaluation of a cardiac tissue section revealed the presence of pigment deposition. What is the pigment shown in the image provided?
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin is a yellowish-brown, granular, autofluorescent pigment that accumulates in cells as a result of "wear and tear" or aging. It is composed of polymers of lipids and phospholipids complexed with protein, derived from the peroxidized lipids of subcellular membranes. In an 82-year-old man, its presence in cardiac myocytes is a normal finding of aging, often called "brown atrophy" of the heart. Melanin (Option A) is a black-brown pigment found in the skin or brain (substantia nigra) and is not typical for aging cardiac tissue. Hemosiderin (Option C) and Iron (Option D) would appear as golden-yellow but would stain bright blue with a Perl’s Prussian blue stain; they indicate iron overload (hemosiderosis), not simple aging. Lipofuscin is typically located in a perinuclear distribution, as seen in the slide. Therefore, given the patient's advanced age and the classic appearance of the pigment in the heart, Lipofuscin is the correct identification

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A non-smoker patient with a history of cardiac disease suddenly develops chest pain and breathlessness. An X-ray is performed and given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema

The given chest X-ray shows increased interstitial markings, vascular redistribution, and alveolar oedema in a butterfly pattern points to a diagnosis of pulmonary oedema.

Acute severe hypertension, acute myocardial infarction, or exacerbation of chronic heart failure are some of the common causes of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. It can be precipitated by the discontinuation of medications (non-compliant patient), excessive salt intake, or tachyarrhythmias.

It presents with severe dyspnea, pink frothy sputum production, diaphoresis, and cyanosis. Auscultation reveals rales and rhonchi in all lung fields. Cardiomegaly might be seen in cases of chronic heart failure.

Management of pulmonary oedema includes the use of diuretics, nitrates, and morphine to decrease the preload. Nitroglycerin and isosorbide dinitrate have a rapid onset of action and can be given sublingually. If there is a persistence of pulmonary oedema and no hypotension, it can be administered intravenously.

Oxygen therapy to maintain a saturation of >92% is recommended. If saturation is not maintained even with supplemental oxygen, positive-pressure ventilation through a face mask or endotracheal intubation is required. A sitting position with legs hanging by the side of the bed can be used to reduce venous return in patients without hypotension.

Non-cardiac causes of pulmonary oedema are high altitude, sepsis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Heart failure is a manifestation of most chronic cardiac conditions such as hypertension, valvular heart disease, and coronary artery disease. Symptoms such as shortness of breath, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea point to left heart failure due to pulmonary congestion. In contrast, symptoms such as pedal oedema, weight gain, early satiety, and hepatic congestion are characteristic of right heart failure.

Summary of Pathogenesis of Major Findings in Congestive Heart Failure

Abnormality

Cause

Weakness, exercise intolerance, fatigue

Left ventricle output inadequate to perfuse muscles; especially, failure of output to rise with exercise

Ankle, sacral edema

Increased peripheral venous pressure →increased fluid transudation.

Hepatomegaly

Increased peripheral venous pressure →increased resistance to portal flow.

Pulmonary congestion

Increased pulmonary venous pressure →pulmonary venous distention and transudation of fluid into air spaces

Dyspnea on exertion

Failure of left ventricular output to rise during exercise → increased pulmonary venous pressure

Paroxysmal dyspnea, pulmonary edema

Probably a sudden failure of left heart output to keep up with the right heart output →acute rise in pulmonary venous and capillary pressure →transudation of fluid into air spaces.

Orthopnea

Normal pooling of blood in lungs in supine position added to the already congested pulmonary vascular system; increased venous return not put out by the left ventricle. (Relieved by sitting up, raising the head of the bed, lying on extra pillows.)

Cardiac dilation

Greater ventricular end-diastolic volume.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When assessing Polycystic Ovary Disease/ Syndrome (PCOD/PCOS), which is associated with multiple clinical features and hormonal abnormalities, which of the following parameters or findings is typically evaluated in this condition?
questions.explanation: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS/PCOD) is a complex endocrine disorder defined by the Rotterdam criteria, which include ovulatory dysfunction, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, and clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism. Consequently, measuring serum testosterone levels is a fundamental biochemical study used to document the hyperandrogenism characteristic of the condition. While women with PCOS have a higher incidence of obstructive sleep apnea (making a sleep study, Option B, occasionally relevant) and may have metabolic issues (urine study, Option A, for glucose), these are not the primary diagnostic studies for the syndrome itself. Elevated free or total testosterone supports the diagnosis in patients presenting with hirsutism, acne, and irregular periods. Other relevant studies include the LH:FSH ratio (often increased) and fasting insulin levels to assess insulin resistance. Therefore, among the options provided, serum testosterone is the most direct and standard laboratory investigation used to characterize the hormonal derangement in PCOD, aiding in the differentiation from other causes of virilization
questions.learning: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS/PCOD) is a complex endocrine disorder defined by the Rotterdam criteria, which include ovulatory dysfunction, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, and clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A child is starting to walk and gain upright posture. Which of the following spinal curvatures develops secondarily due to the development of this function?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lumbar

Lumbar curvature develops secondarily when the child starts walking and gaining upright posture.

During embryonic life, the body appears flexed and has 2 primary spinal curvatures.These are the thoracic and the pelvic curves, which are convex dorsally.

After birth, functional muscle development leads to the early appearance of secondary spinal curvatures. These are the cervical and the lumbar curves, both of which are convex forwards (lordosis).

* The secondary cervical curvature occurs with the development of function in the muscles responsible for the head extension.

* The secondary lumbar curvature occurs with the development of function in the muscles responsible for sitting upright and walking.

Normal adult curvatures of the vertebral column are as follows:

* The cervical curve is lordosis (convex forwards)

* The thoracic curve is kyphosis (convex dorsally)

* The lumbar curve is lordosis (convex forwards)

* The pelvic curve is concave anteroinferiorly
questions.learning: Lumbar Lumbar curvature develops secondarily when the child starts walking and gaining upright posture. During embryonic life, the body appears flexed and has 2 primary spinal curvatures.These are the thoracic and the pelvic curves, which are convex dorsally.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During resuscitation, when is the given position indicated?
options: Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing absent
Unconsciousness with pulse present and breathing absent
Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing present
Unconsciousness with pulse absent and breathing present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing present

The position illustrated in the picture is known as the recovery position, and it is used in the management of patients who are unconscious but with pulse present and breathing present.

The recovery position can help prevent complications such as aspiration and airway obstruction in unconscious individuals. Additionally, it is crucial to monitor the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation continuously while they are in the recovery position and seek immediate medical assistance. An unresponsive patient who is breathing spontaneously in the supine position is at risk of airway obstruction from their tongue, mucus, vomit, etc. A modified lateral position is used and the following 6 principles are considered while choosing which variation of recovery position to use,

1.

The victim should be in as near a true lateral position as possible, with the head dependent to allow free drainage of fluid.

2.

The position should be stable.

3.

Avoid any pressure on the chest that impairs breathing.

4.

It should be possible to turn the victim on his or her side and to return to the back easily and safely, with concern for a possible cervical spine injury.

5.

Good observation of and access to the airway should be possible.

6.

The position itself should not cause injury to the victim.

Other options

Option A: Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing absent - In this situation, the patient is in cardiac arrest and requires immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), not the recovery position. CPR involves chest compressions and rescue breaths to support circulation and respiration.

Option B: Unconsciousness with pulse present and breathing absent - In this case, the patient is experiencing respiratory arrest. Rescue breathing or bag-valve-mask ventilation should be initiated to support the patient's breathing. The recovery position is not indicated in this scenario.

Option D: Unconsciousness with pulse absent and breathing present - This option is not physiologically plausible, as the absence of a pulse implies a lack of circulation, and breathing cannot be present without circulation.
questions.learning: Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing present — The position illustrated in the picture is known as the recovery position, and it is used in the management of patients who are unconscious but with pulse present and breathing present.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 70 yr old female presents with extracapsular neck of femur fracture. What is the best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dynamic hip screw

Intertrochanteric fractures are the most common type of extracapsular fracture. Dynamic hip screw is the managament for undisplaced intertrochanteric fractures.

In elderly patients, internal fixation is preferred because inthem prolonged bed rest in traction may cause complications related to recumbency i.e., bed sores, pneumonia etc.

Intertrochanteric fractures of the femur can be treated by:

• Extramedullary implants - dynamic hip screw
• Intramedullary implants - proximal femoral nail and gamma nail.

Dynamic hip screws are used in undisplaced intertrochanteric fractures, whereas proximal femoral nails are used in displaced intertrochanteric fractures.

Conservative methods like Russels traction or skeleton traction in Thomas Splint are nowadays not preferred due to the success rate of operative methods.
questions.learning: Dynamic hip screw Intertrochanteric fractures are the most common type of extracapsular fracture. Dynamic hip screw is the managament for undisplaced intertrochanteric fractures.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Notochord

The correct answer is Notochord.

The marked midline structure is the notochord, a rod-like axial mesodermal structure extending cranio-caudally beneath the neural tube.

It plays a key role in neural induction and later contributes to the nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs.

Primitive streak is caudal and transient, neural groove is dorsal ectodermal, and neural crest cells migrate laterally rather than forming a midline rod.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the most common complication of this condition, if left untreated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cubitus valgus

Cubitus valgus is the most common complication, as the given condition is untreated lateral condyle of humerus fracture.

5–15 degrees of valgus is the normal carrying angle of the elbow. An angle more than this or an asymmetry between the two sides is called a valgus deformity. Long-standing non-union of a fractured lateral condyle is considered the most common cause.

Features of ulnar nerve palsy, such as the weakness of the hand, numbness or tingling of the ulnar fingers are also seen with cubitus valgus

Lateral condyle of humerus fracture is seen mostly in children up to 16 years of age. Falling on the hand with an extended elbow is the mechanism of injury. It is classified into types 1 and 2: the fracture is lateral to the trochlea in type 1 and through the middle, in type 2.

A back slab with the elbow flexed 90 degrees is used if there is no displacement. Reduction and internal fixation are needed for a displaced fracture.

Recurrent dislocations and malunion are the other complications. Since it is a Salter-Harris type IV injury, an imperfect reduction can result in growth arrest.

The image below shows cubitus valgus deformity:

Other options:

Option B: Cubitus varus deformity is also called gunstock deformity. It happens due to the malunion of supracondylar fracture in childhood. Injury to the brachial artery is an important complication.

Option D: Myositis ossificans is a tender swelling seen in the area of injury. It is often confused as a malignant tumor. Calcified lesions are seen in radiological studies. However, the swelling soon becomes less painful.

The X-ray image below shows myositis ossificans:
