questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During the clinical examination of the nervous system, which of the following nerves can be tested by touching the highlighted structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IX

The structure marked in the given sagittal section of the head and neck is the uvula. The sensory supply to the uvula is by the glossopharyngeal nerve and it is tested in this case.

Nerve supply by glossopharyngeal nerve:

• Sensory fibers to the uvula, tympanic cavity, pharyngotympanic tube, tonsils, fauces, nasopharynx, and posterior third of the tongue.
• Motor fibers to the stylopharyngeus muscle
• Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland
• Gustatory fibers for the postsulcal part of the tongue.

Pharyngeal plexus:

The nerve supply of the pharynx is mainly from the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. It is formed by the pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion. The vagus nerve provides the motor supply and the glossopharyngeal nerve provides the sensory supply.

Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve:

• All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve)
• All the muscles of the pharynx(except stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve)

Note:

Previously cranial root of the spinal accessory nerve was thought to contribute to the motor functions of the pharyngeal plexus, but recent evidence suggests that it is not a major part of the motor drive to the pharyngeal plexus.

Innervation of the soft palate:

General sensation - It is mostly carried by the lesser palatine nerve which is a branch of maxillary nerve. The sensation from posterior part is carried by the pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and from the plexus around the tonsil which is formed by the tonsillar branches of the glossopharyngeal and lesser palatine nerves.

Taste sensation - There are taste buds in the oral surface of soft palate and sensation from them is carried by the lesser palatine nerve.

Secretomotor supply - It is by the lesser palatine nerve via postganglionic fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion.

Motor supply - It is by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve except for tensor veli palatini which is supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.learning: IX The structure marked in the given sagittal section of the head and neck is the uvula. The sensory supply to the uvula is by the glossopharyngeal nerve and it is tested in this case.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Artery supplying near marked structure is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior interventricular artery

The correct answer is Anterior interventricular artery (LAD).

The LAD, a branch of the left coronary artery, runs in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior wall of left ventricle and anterior 2/3 of interventricular septum.

The left circumflex artery supplies the lateral/posterior left ventricle, the left marginal artery supplies the obtuse margin, and the posterior interventricular artery supplies the posterior septum and inferior wall.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 68-year-old man with chronic heart failure presents to the emergency department in shock, with hypotension and reduced urine output. The physician starts low-dose dopamine therapy. Based on the pharmacological effects of dopamine at low doses, which beneficial effect is most likely to be achieved in this patient?
questions.explanation: Dopamine has dose-dependent effects on various receptors. At "low doses" (typically <5 mcg/kg/min), it primarily stimulates dopaminergic ( and ) receptors, which causes vasodilation in the renal, mesenteric, and coronary vascular beds. This leads to an "increase in renal blood flow" and improved urine output, which is the intended benefit in a patient with heart failure and low perfusion. "Intermediate doses" (5–10 mcg/kg/min) stimulate receptors to increase cardiac contractility (Option A). "High doses" (>10 mcg/kg/min) stimulate receptors, leading to significant vasoconstriction (Option B) and potential tachycardia (Option C). While the concept of a specific "renal-dose" dopamine is debated in modern critical care, physiologically, the low-dose stimulation of dopaminergic receptors is responsible for the selective vasodilation of the renal arteries
questions.learning: Dopamine has dose-dependent effects on various receptors. At "low doses" (typically 10 mcg/kg/min) stimulate receptors, leading to significant vasoconstriction (Option B) and potential tachycardia (Option C).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 20-year-old man is brought for psychiatric evaluation due to intellectual disability, with an IQ of 45. He has a long face, large ears, and macroorchidism, along with a cardiac murmur on examination and a paternal family history of intellectual impairment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of intellectual disability, a long face with large ears, and macro-orchidism (large testes) is pathognomonic for Fragile X syndrome (Option C) . This is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and is caused by a CGG triplet repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene. The "cardiac murmur" mentioned likely represents mitral valve prolapse, which is common in these patients. William syndrome (Option D) features a "pixie-like" face, hypercalcemia, and great social skills ("cocktail party personality"). Rett syndrome (Option B) is an X-linked disorder seen almost exclusively in females, characterized by loss of hand skills and purposeful movements. Cushing's syndrome (Option A) involves cortisol excess with different physical findings like a buffalo hump and striae. Because the classic triad of facial features, macro-orchidism, and moderate intellectual disability is present, Fragile X is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical combination of intellectual disability, a long face with large ears, and macro-orchidism (large testes) is pathognomonic for Fragile X syndrome (Option C) .

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which type of programmed cell death primarily involves the action of caspase-1?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyroptosis

Pyroptosis is a form of programmed inflammatory cell death mediated by activation of caspase-1. Occurs in:

• Macrophages
• Infected cells

Caspase-1 is activated via inflammasomes and leads to cleavage of IL-1β and IL-18. This causes pore formation in the cell membrane, cell swelling, and membrane rupture.

Pathogen / Danger signal

↓

Inflammasome activation

↓

Caspase-1 activation

↓

Gasdermin pore formation

↓

Cell swelling + membrane rupture

↓

Release of IL-1β, IL-18 → Inflammation

Apoptosis involves caspase-3, 6, 9. Necroptosis is caspase-independent, and necrosis is unregulated cell death.

| Feature | Apoptosis | Pyroptosis | Necroptosis | Necrosis

| ------- | --------- | ---------- | ----------- | --------

| Type | Programmed | Programmed | Programmed | Uncontrolled

| Inflammation |  No | Yes | Yes | Yes

| Key enzyme | Caspase 3,9 | Caspase-1 | RIPK3 | None

| Cell size | Shrinks | Swells | Swells | Swells

| Membrane | Intact | Ruptures | Ruptures | Ruptures

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the gold standard method for intraocular pressure measurement?
questions.explanation: The Goldmann applanation tonometer (GAT) is universally recognized as the gold standard method for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP). It works on the Imbert-Fick principle, measuring the force required to flatten a constant area (3.06 mm) of the cornea. It is highly accurate and is the standard against which all other tonometers are compared. Hertel's exophthalmometer (Option A) measures the degree of eyeball protrusion (proptosis) from the orbit, not pressure. A Gonioscope (Option B) is used to visualize the drainage angle of the eye. The Tonopen (Option D) is a portable handheld device that is useful for patients who cannot sit at a slit lamp, but it is less accurate than GAT. Accurate IOP measurement is fundamental for the diagnosis and management of glaucoma. GAT readings can be influenced by central corneal thickness, which must be accounted for using pachymetry. Regular GAT assessment is the cornerstone of monitoring glaucoma patients to ensure they remain at their target pressure to prevent optic nerve damage
questions.learning: The Goldmann applanation tonometer (GAT) is universally recognized as the gold standard method for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP). It works on the Imbert-Fick principle, measuring the force required to flatten a constant area (3.06 mm) of the cornea.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which opening is present posterior to the marked structure in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Eustachian tube

The Eustachian tube (pharyngotympanic tube) opens into the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, posterior to the nasal cavity structures.

• The opening lies behind the inferior turbinate and choana
• It is surrounded by a prominence called the torus tubarius
• Connects nasopharynx → middle ear cavity

Functions:

• Equalizes middle ear pressure
• Drains middle ear secretions
• Maintains ventilation of middle ear

Clinical relevance:

• Dysfunction → otitis media with effusion
• Enlarged adenoids can obstruct this opening
• Landmark during endoscopic nasal surgery

Why other options are incorrect:

• Onodi cell: Posterior ethmoid air cell near optic nerve
• Sphenopalatine foramen: Opens into lateral nasal wall (posterior nasal cavity)
• Sphenoid sinus: Located posterior-superior in skull base, not directly behind this structure

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is indicative of severe pre-eclampsia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)

Severe preeclampsia is diagnosed when preeclampsia is associated with severe hypertension or evidence of end-organ dysfunction. Features suggesting severe disease include:

• BP ≥160/110 mm Hg
• Thrombocytopenia
• Elevated liver enzymes
• Pulmonary edema
• Renal insufficiency
• Neurologic symptoms
• Fetal growth restriction (IUGR)

Intrauterine growth restriction occurs due to uteroplacental insufficiency caused by abnormal placental vascular remodeling and is considered a marker of severe placental disease.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Diastolic BP 90 mm Hg → mild hypertension
• Systolic BP 145 mm Hg → not severe range
• Proteinuria 2 g/24 h alone does not define severe preeclampsia
questions.learning: Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) Severe preeclampsia is diagnosed when preeclampsia is associated with severe hypertension or evidence of end-organ dysfunction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: An elderly patient with overactive bladder develops confusion and memory issues after starting therapy. Which alternative drug would be least likely to worsen cognition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trospium

Trospium is a quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic that poorly crosses the blood–brain barrier, making it least likely to cause central anticholinergic effects such as confusion and memory impairment in elderly patients. Hence, it is preferred in overactive bladder when cognitive safety is a concern.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Oxybutynin: Tertiary amine with high CNS penetration; commonly causes confusion.

B. Tolterodine: Tertiary amine; can cross the BBB and impair cognition.

D. Solifenacin: M3-selective but still a tertiary amine with potential CNS effects.
questions.learning: Trospium Trospium is a quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic that poorly crosses the blood–brain barrier, making it least likely to cause central anticholinergic effects such as confusion and memory impairment in elderly patients.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An AIDS-positive patient presents with fever, vomiting, and signs of meningitis. Which investigation is most useful for the rapid diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis?
options: Urine lateral flow assay for cryptococcal antigen
questions.explanation: The urine lateral flow assay (LFA) for cryptococcal antigen is the preferred test for rapid bedside diagnosis, especially in resource-limited settings. It is highly sensitive and specific, often detecting the antigen even before clinical symptoms of meningitis develop in AIDS patients. While India ink preparation (Option A) can detect the capsulated yeast Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF, it has relatively low sensitivity compared to antigen tests. Blood culture (Option B) can identify disseminated infection but takes several days to yield results. CSF culture (Option C) remains the gold standard for definitive diagnosis but is time-consuming, typically requiring three to seven days for fungal growth. Therefore, for immediate clinical decision-making in an acute presentation of meningismus, the urine LFA provides the fastest reliable results
questions.learning: The urine lateral flow assay (LFA) for cryptococcal antigen is the preferred test for rapid bedside diagnosis, especially in resource-limited settings.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A middle-aged male patient presents with protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet. Which of the following is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pegvisomant

The clinical features of protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet are suggestive of acromegaly. Pegvisomant is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used to treat this condition.

Acromegaly is commonly caused due to growth hormone-secreting somatotroph adenoma. It occurs secondary to mutations of the pituitary-specific gene PIT-1.

Patients present with frontal bossing, increased hand and foot size, mandibular enlargement with prognathism, widened space between the lower incisor teeth, soft tissue swelling resulting in increased heel pad thickness, coarse facial features, and large fleshy nose.

Serum IGF-1 levels (elevated) and GH suppression test with oral glucose are useful in the diagnosis. The levels of GH do not reduce in response to the oral glucose load.

Transsphenoidal surgical resection of the tumor, octreotide, and pegvisomant will be helpful in the management of this condition.

Other options:

Option A: Octreotide is a synthetic analog of somatostatin. It is used for the treatment of acromegaly and secretory diarrhea.

Option C: Cabergoline is a dopamine D2 receptor agonist. It is used as a first-line drug for the treatment of hyperprolactinemia.

Option D: Oglcegepant is a calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) antagonist. It is used for the treatment of migraine.
questions.learning: Pegvisomant — The clinical features of protrusion of the chin, excessive sweating, impaired glucose tolerance, and enlargement of hands and feet are suggestive of acromegaly.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman presents to a psychiatrist with a two-month history of persistent low mood, loss of interest in routine activities, reduced appetite, and sleep disturbances. Following detailed assessment, she is diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD). In view of this diagnosis and the requirement for appropriate pharmacological management, which medication would be most suitable to initiate treatment?
questions.explanation: For the initial treatment of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) like Fluoxetine are the first-line pharmacological agents of choice. They are preferred due to their superior safety profile, lower side-effect burden compared to older antidepressants, and high patient acceptability. Divalproex (Option A) and Lithium (Option C) are mood stabilizers primarily used for Bipolar Disorder and are not first-line for unipolar depression. Buspirone (Option B) is an anxiolytic used for Generalised Anxiety Disorder but is not effective as a primary treatment for MDD. Fluoxetine works by increasing the synaptic concentration of serotonin, which helps alleviate the core symptoms of low mood and anhedonia over a period of several weeks. Clinicians must counsel patients that the full therapeutic effect typically takes 2 to 4 weeks to manifest. Monitoring for early side effects like nausea or increased anxiety is essential during the initiation phase of therapy to ensure long-term medication adherence. **************
questions.learning: For the initial treatment of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) like Fluoxetine are the first-line pharmacological agents of choice.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What can be said about this graph?
options: The baseline shows that the fetus has tachycardia.
The beat to beat variability is less/inadequate.
This is a uterine contraction graph.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. This is a non-stress test.

The given graph showing only the tracing for the fetal heart rate (FHR) is a non-stress test (NST).

The NST is a screening test for fetal wellness. It describes fetal heart rate acceleration (measured by a doppler) in response to fetal movements (perceived by the mother).

• Reactive (reassuring) NST - Two or more accelerations of 15 seconds duration and amplitude of 15 beats/min, in a 20-minute testing time
• Non-reactive (non-reassuring) NST - Absence of any fetal reactivity.

Other options:

Option B: Fetal tachycardia is defined as a baseline FHR above 160 beats/min, whereas this tracing shows FHR below 160 beats/min.

Option C: Beat-to-beat variability is the change in baseline fetal heart rate (excluding the accelerations and decelerations) in response to sympathetic and parasympathetic stimulation. A beat-to-beat variability of 6-25 beats/min is considered normal. This tracing shows normal beat-to-beat variability.

Option D: Cardiotocography (CTG) includes tracings for fetal heart rate and uterine contractions.
questions.learning: The given graph showing only the tracing for the fetal heart rate (FHR) is a non-stress test (NST). The NST is a screening test for fetal wellness.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which ion is most responsible for the resting membrane potential (RMP):
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. K+

Resting membrane potential is primarily determined by potassium permeability across the cell membrane. High resting K⁺ conductance through leak channels allows outward diffusion, making the inside negative. The membrane potential closely approximates the K⁺ equilibrium potential. Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ have minimal resting permeability compared to K⁺.

High intracellular K⁺

↓

K⁺ diffuses out via leak channels

↓

Loss of positive charge from inside

↓

Cell interior becomes negative

↓

Electrical gradient opposes further K⁺ loss

↓

Equilibrium reached → Resting membrane potential
questions.learning: K+ Resting membrane potential is primarily determined by potassium permeability across the cell membrane. High resting K⁺ conductance through leak channels allows outward diffusion, making the inside negative.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Lipotrophic factors are all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arginine

Arginine is not a lipotropic factor.

Lipotropic factors are those factors that mobilize triacylglycerol from the hepatocytes. Following are the example :

* Choline

* Folic acid

* Betaine

* Vitamin B12

* Methionine

* Glycine

* Inositol

* Serine

Lecithin (option b) is a phospholipid (phosphatidylcholine) that is important for VLDL formation and its secretion from the liver. So the best answer is arginine

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The years of potential life lost could be attributed to______.
options: Years lost due to premature death
Years lost to poor quality of life
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Years lost due to premature death

The years of potential life lost could be attributed to the years lost due to premature death.

It is a mortality indicator that shows the number of years that a dying person could have expected to survive (usually taken as 75 years). Mortality indicators are used as the starting point in the evaluation of health status. They are used as indirect indicators of health.

The concept of years of potential life lost (YPLL) is used to estimate the societal impact of premature death. It helps prioritize public health interventions and allocate resources to address significant health problems. YPLL, along with other metrics like DALYs and QALYs, aids in assessing the burden of disease and the effectiveness of healthcare interventions. These measurements can help inform policymakers and healthcare providers in making informed decisions about healthcare delivery and resource allocation.

Strategies to reduce YPLL include prevention and early intervention, improving access to healthcare, and addressing social determinants of health that contribute to health disparities and premature death.

Other options:

Option A: Years lost to morbidity refers to the time spent living with a disease or disability, which is not directly related to the concept of years of potential life lost.

Option C: Years lost to disability is a component of disability-adjusted life years (DALY). DALY indicates the number of years lost due to ill health, disability, or early death.

DALY = YLL +YLD

• Years lost to disability (YLD): Here, the number of cases due to injury and illness is multiplied by the average duration of the disease and a weighting factor. (Severity of the disease on a scale of 0 (perfect health) to 1 (dead))
• Years of lost life (YLL) - Here, the number of deaths at each age is multiplied by the expected remaining years of life. (according to a global standard of life expectancy)

Option D: Quality-adjusted life year (QALY) indicates how the health status of an individual impacts his quality and quantity of life. It shows the years of life lost due to injury or illness. It is commonly used in evaluating the outcomes of medical interventions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The spinal sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve has 2nd order neurons to carry which sensation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pain

The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensory input from the face, as well as motor functions such as chewing. Its sensory pathway involves three branches: the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions. The first-order neurons for each division originate from different sensory ganglia:

1.Ophthalmic Division (V1):
First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion (also called the semilunar or Gasserian ganglion).

2. Maxillary Division (V2):
First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

3. Mandibular Division (V3):
First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

These first-order neurons carry sensory information from the face to the brainstem. Upon entering the brainstem, the fibers synapse with second-order neurons in specific nuclei:

1. Principal Sensory Nucleus (Main Sensory Nucleus):
a.Receives input from all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve.
b.Located in the pons.
c.Second-order neurons here carry discriminative touch and proprioceptive information.

2. Spinal Trigeminal Nucleus (Spinal Nucleus of Trigeminal):
a.Receives input mainly from the maxillary and mandibular divisions.
b.Located in the medulla.
c.Second-order neurons here carry pain and temperature sensations.

After synapsing in these nuclei, the sensory information is further relayed to higher brain centers for processing and perception.
questions.learning: Pain — The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensory input from the face, as well as motor functions such as chewing. Its sensory pathway involves three branches: the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
A 6-year old boy complains of cough and throat pain. On examination of the oral cavity, a white pseudomembrane was visualized. A swab was taken from it and stained as given in the image below. What is the procedure for the following staining?

1. Albert's stain- I
2. Acid alcohol
3. Gram's iodine
4. Safranin
5. Methylene blue
6. Crystal violet
7. Carbol fuschin
8. Acetone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6, 3, 8, 4

The image shows Gram's stain of Corynebacterium diphtheria and the staining procedure is crystal violet, Gram's iodine, acetone, and safranin.

Corynebacterium diphtheria (also called Klebs-Loeffler bacillus) is a gram-positive bacillus with clubbing at both ends. They possess characteristic polymetaphosphate granules also called metachromatic granules.

Gram's stain procedure:

• Fix the smear using heat or methanol.
• Cover with crystal violet stain for 10–30 seconds.
• Gram’s iodine stain used as mordant for 10–30 seconds.
• Decolorize with 30% acetone–alcohol for 10–30 seconds, until the stain cannot flow off the slide.
• Cover with safranin stain for 10–30 seconds.

Image shows gram staining of Corynebacterium diphtheria

Other stains used for corynebacterium diphtheria:

• Albert's stain shows green bacilli with purple-blue metachromatic granules arranged in typical Chinese letter or cuneiform arrangement. The stain requires two reagents:

• Albert’s I solution contains toluidine blue, malachite green.
• Albert's II contains iodine and potassium iodide.

• Loeffler's methylene blue: The granules take up the bluish-purple color.
• Immunofluorescence: This is more specific as the smear is stained with a specific antibody.

Image shows Albert's stain of C. diphtheria

The incubation period of diphtheria is usually 2–5 days (range: 1–10 days).

Respiratory diphtheria is characterized by mild fever, sore throat, difficulty swallowing, malaise, loss of appetite, hoarseness (if the larynx is involved). The hallmark is a gray-white pseudomembrane over the mucous lining of the tonsils (most commonly), pharynx, larynx, or nares. It is tightly adherent to the underlying tissue, and any attempt to dislodge the membrane may cause bleeding.

A few patients develop massive swelling of the tonsils and present with bull-neck diphtheria, due to edema of the submandibular and paratracheal region. Cutaneous diphtheria may present as a scaling rash or as ulcers with clearly demarcated edges and membrane.

The images below shows pseudomembrane, bull-neck, and cutaneous diphtheria respectively.

Treatment of diphtheria includes administration of diphtheria anti-toxin. Recommended antibiotics include penicillin G and erythromycin. Prevention is with the diphtheria toxoid vaccine. It is coadministered with tetanus and acellular pertussis (DPT) and should be given according to the National Immunization Schedule.
questions.learning: 6, 3, 8, 4 The image shows Gram's stain of Corynebacterium diphtheria and the staining procedure is crystal violet, Gram's iodine, acetone, and safranin.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the defect shown in the image:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herbert pits

The image shows tiny lesions at the limbus, indicating Herbert's pits. This finding is seen in trachoma, which is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, more specifically the trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis (TRIC) serovars A, B, Ba, and C.

Trachoma is a form of chronic infective conjunctivitis and is one of the leading causes of blindness. It has an ‘active’ inflammatory stage and a ‘cicatricial’ chronic stage.

The active inflammatory stage is more prevalent in children and presents with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (often mild symptoms). Examination findings at this stage show:

* Conjunctival follicles contain Leber cells (multinucleated lymphocytes)

* Limbal Herbert's follicles (similar to conjunctival follicles)

Cicatricial chronic stage is seen in middle age. And when the chronic infection with sequelae sets in, the patient complains of pain, lacrimation, photophobia, and later blurring, and finally loss of vision. The conjunctiva shows concretions (whitish deposits of inspissated mucus in depressions called glands of Henle). Corneal signs include:

* Herbert pits (pitted scars in the limbal, which are remnants of healed Herbert follicles)

* Corneal opacity is seen in later stages.

There can be associated trichiasis (when at least one eyelash rubs the eyeball) and entropion.

At present, WHO grading with 'FISTO' is in use.

Trachoma is treated according to the WHO classification using the SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial hygiene, and Environmental improvement). Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice, and surgery involves the correction of trichiasis and entropion. In case of significant corneal scarring, penetrating keratoplasty is done.

Other options:

Option B: Horner–Trantas dots (image below) are distinct white, chalky, gelatinous nodules made up of eosinophils and epithelial debris that appear at the limbus, and they are characteristic of limbal vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

Option C: In giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC), gelatinous papillae initially appear as small, elevated nodules on the conjunctiva. These papillae eventually grow larger, forming macropapillae and giant papillae, and may be accompanied by Trantas dots at the limbus.

The image below shows giant papillae in the conjunctiva:

Option D: Progressive pannus in trachoma involves the infiltration of the cornea with new blood vessels developing in the upper part, lying between the epithelium and Bowman's membrane. As the condition advances, these superficial vessels contribute to the destruction of Bowman's membrane, with corneal infiltration occurring before significant vascularization.
questions.learning: Herbert pits — The image shows tiny lesions at the limbus, indicating Herbert's pits. This finding is seen in trachoma, which is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, more specifically the trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis (TRIC) serovars A, B, Ba, and C.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with developmental delay has absence of the developmental milestone of social smile by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 months

The social smile normally appears at 6–8 weeks (around 2 months). Failure to develop a social smile by 3 months is considered abnormal and is an early marker of developmental delay, warranting further evaluation for visual impairment, hearing impairment, autism spectrum disorder, or global developmental delay.

Why not the other options?

• A. 6 weeks ❌: Social smile is just beginning to appear; absence is still within normal limits.
• B. 10 weeks ❌: Many infants develop it by this age, but the upper limit of normal is 3 months.
• C. 3 months ✔️: Correct. Absence beyond this age is abnormal.
• D. 4 months ❌: Delay should be recognized earlier, by 3 months.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016, human anatomical waste is to be carried in which colour plastic bags?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Yellow

Under the Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016, human anatomical waste (human tissues, organs, body parts, fetus, and placenta) is segregated into yellow non-chlorinated plastic bags and disposed of by incineration, plasma pyrolysis, or deep burial (where permitted).

High-Yield Pearls

• Yellow Bag: Human/animal anatomical waste, placenta, fetus, soiled waste, microbiology waste, expired medicines.
• Red Bag: Contaminated recyclable plastics (IV sets, tubing, catheters, gloves).
• White Container: Sharps (needles, scalpels, blades).
• Blue Container: Glassware, vials, ampoules.

questions.text: How much per cent of GNP does WHO recommend being spent on the healthcare sector?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 5%

The WHO has set the target of at least 5% expenditure of each country's GNP on healthcare

India spends about 1% of its GNP on health and family welfare. The National Health Policy, 2017 aims to increase public health expenditure from 1.15% of GDP to around 2.5% by 2025.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a newborn presenting with features of intestinal obstruction, where X-ray and CT abdomen findings suggest the presence of an annular pancreas?
questions.explanation: A annular pancreas is a congenital anomaly where a ring of pancreatic tissue encircles the second part of the duodenum. This ring can cause extrinsic compression and narrowing of the duodenal lumen, leading to duodenal atresia or stenosis (Option C). Clinically, this presents shortly after birth with signs of high intestinal obstruction, such as bilious vomiting and upper abdominal distension. The pathognomonic radiological sign on an abdominal X-ray is the "double bubble" appearance (air in the stomach and the dilated proximal duodenum). Esophageal atresia (Option B) presents with excessive salivation and inability to swallow feeds. Jejunoileal atresia (Option A) and Colonic atresia (Option D) would show multiple dilated loops of bowel and different radiological signs. Surgical treatment for an annular pancreas involves bypassing the obstruction via a duodenoduodenostomy rather than dividing the pancreatic ring itself. Thus, duodenal atresia is the definitive clinical result of this anatomical malformation
questions.learning: A annular pancreas is a congenital anomaly where a ring of pancreatic tissue encircles the second part of the duodenum. This ring can cause extrinsic compression and narrowing of the duodenal lumen, leading to duodenal atresia or stenosis (Option C).
